10765-thrilling-adventures-by-land-and-s:
James O. Brayman edited Thrilling Adventures by Land and Sea as a book of remarkable historical facts gathered from authentic sources. Its preface defends true adventure against cheap, harmful fiction, arguing that readers who seek amusement deserve stories that also inform. Flood and field supply its motto, borrowed from Othello's tale of moving accidents.

The volume collects escapes, wrecks, battles, and survivals, chosen for excitement and truth together. Brayman's aim is wholesome thrill, not sensation for its own sake. Readers get a sturdy anthology of real-life adventure, in the taste of an earlier age of popular history.
10849-saved-at-sea:
Mrs. O. F. Walton wrote Saved at Sea as a lighthouse story for young readers. Its hero is born on a stormy day when waves beat the lighthouse rock and wind rages against all within. His grandfather, keeper of the light, had never known such a storm since coming to live on the rock. Chapters follow a flare at sea, a bundle saved, and little Timpey.

The tale moves through fog, waiting boats, a change of light, and a new neighbor, toward the claiming of the Sunbeam. Walton writes with Christian warmth and seaside detail. Children get adventure and faith together, in a story that made Walton a favorite of Victorian nurseries.
11058-jack-archer-a-tale-of-the-crimea:
G. A. Henty wrote this boys' adventure about Jack Archer, a midshipman in the Crimean War. Jack begins at the King's School, Canterbury, where term starts dull after holidays, then sails to Gibraltar, Gallipoli, and the Crimea. Battles at the Alma, Balaklava, and Inkerman, a great storm, and the siege of Sebastopol follow, with chapters on prisoners, escapes in disguise, and Polish insurgents.

Jack is taken prisoner, held on parole, and escapes, while a Russian count's daughter, Katinka, and court intrigues add romance to the war story. Henty writes with his usual energy for schoolboys, mixing history with heroics. The novel gives young readers a vivid, if dated, view of the Crimean War through one boy's service.
12150-north-south-and-over-the-sea:
M. E. Francis, Mrs. Francis Blundell, gathered these stories in 1902 for the Country Life Library of Fiction, with illustrations by H. M. Brock. Several had appeared before in the Cornhill Magazine, Longman Magazine, and Country Life.

The book divides into three parts. North holds Lancashire and Yorkshire tales like Golden Sally and The Conquest of Radical Ted. South holds village romances, and Over the Sea holds Irish and emigrant stories. Francis writes in dialect and local color, favoring plain folk, stubborn lovers, and small moral turns. The stories suit readers who like regional England and Ireland rendered with affection and a light comic touch.
12173-the-two-lovers-of-heaven-chrysanth:
Denis Florence Mac-Carthy translated Calderon drama The Two Lovers of Heaven from Spanish in 1870, with dedicatory sonnets to Longfellow and others. Calderon, the great dramatist of Counter-Reformation Spain, set the play in early Christian Rome.

Chrysanthus, a young Roman noble, converts to Christianity and falls in love with Daria, a vestal virgin who shares his faith. Pagan priests, family pressure, and imperial law drive the lovers toward martyrdom, and the motto Por la fe morire, for the faith welcome death, frames their choice. Mac-Carthy verse keeps Calderon baroque imagery and theological argument. The play offers English readers a rare taste of Spanish Golden Age drama in full.
12483-reminiscences-of-scottish-life-cha:
This 1874 volume, twenty-second edition enlarged, gathers reminiscences of Scottish life and character by Dean E. B. Ramsay of Edinburgh, with a memoir by Cosmo Innes. Friends, publishers and relatives asked Innes to write the memoir, giving him authentic facts, dates and the dean's own views.

Chapters cover Scottish religious feeling, old conviviality, domestic servants, judges, humour from Scottish expressions and proverbs, and stories of wit. Ramsay's anecdotes preserve a Scotland of kirk, court and household talk, fondly recalled. The book is a classic of Scottish social memory, humorous, affectionate and rich in dialect colour.
13367-hills-and-the-sea:
Hilaire Belloc writes of walking, sailing, and looking at old places in a work of travel and reflection. He dedicates it to Philip Kershaw, the other man of a pair who loved each other like brothers yet quarrelled on nearly all things. One of the Faith and the other certainly not.

Belloc reads walls built in a fashion forgotten since the Antonines, watches Rome fall asleep as sculpture loses power. He finds a Pyrenean valley fit for camping, fishing, and walking up all the way. Hills and sea become a way to think about history, faith, and friendship. The prose moves between guidebook detail and a walker's sudden, personal judgment.
13518-the-journey-to-the-polar-sea:
Sir John Franklin's Journey to the Polar Sea tells of an overland Arctic expedition in simple, faithful prose, praised in its introduction for revealing the character of its writer. Mr. Beck misses his ship at Yarmouth and rejoins her at Stromness after nine successive days of travel, a small sign of the hardships and changes that fill the narrative.

Guides sketch the Copper-Mine River on the floor and name the Copper Indians who know its lower course to the sea. Hunters follow animal tracks north to a strait, keep deer skulls from dogs and wolves by hanging them in trees, and live by rules learned from the land. Franklin's account remains a classic of Arctic travel, plain in style and rich in northern detail.
1354-chronicles-of-avonlea:
L. M. Montgomery returns to Avonlea, the Prince Edward Island village of Anne of Green Gables, for short stories of its people. Her subjects are lovers, gossips, old maids, and children, each with a small drama of pride, love, or forgiveness. Anne herself appears at the edges, now grown.

Montgomery writes the island with warmth and humor, and her tales are gentle, romantic, and full of local color. The book suits readers who loved Anne and want more of her village, in stories that stand on their own. Montgomery's Avonlea tales still welcome readers back to the island.
1407-a-message-from-the-sea:
Set in a steep Cornish fishing village, this Christmas story opens with the arrival of Captain Jorgan, a bluff American sailor. He brings talk of the sea and a message that stirs an old local sorrow. A young villager long thought lost may still be alive, and a family must face hope it had buried.

Told in short chapters, the tale moves between the cliff village, the shore, and the ships that link it to the wider world. It mixes humour, sea lore, and feeling, and ends with a homecoming of sorts. It is a gentle seasonal story about news long delayed and ties renewed.
14352-patty-and-azalea:
Carolyn Wells wrote this 1919 Patty book, a light novel of family life and house parties. Patty, now a mother, keeps house with her husband Bill and their small daughter Fleurette. Guests stream in from New York for weekends of talk, meals, and fun. Into this cheerful house comes Azalea, a new relative whose odd manners upset the household. The tale is told with warmth, jokes, and a keen eye for social gaffes.

Patty frets that Azalea cannot be made to blend, like a figure against its background. At dinner Azalea yawns openly across the flowers, and the family calls her queer. Yet Azalea gets her chance, and a sampler, a picture play, and a house party all shape her story. Philip Van Reypen and other friends drift through the weekend fun. The novel charms as a sunny tale of manners, kin, and second chances.
14432-a-dream-of-the-north-sea:
James Runciman's 1889 book describes the lives of North Sea fishermen and the mission work that reached them aboard smacks and in port towns. Runciman knew the fleet from earlier reporting, and he writes with sympathy for men at sea.

Chapters follow storms, long voyages, drink, gambling, and the preaching and confession meetings that offered an alternative fellowship. The title points to a vision of a kinder, more hopeful life for sailors. The book blends reportage, sermon, and sea story, and it helped raise support for missions to deep-sea fishermen. Its portraits of hardship aboard the smacks remain vivid.
14832-a-maid-of-the-silver-sea:
John Oxenham's romance, partly written on a verandah at Sark looking toward France, follows Nance, a maid of the silver sea. Two lie in a cleft, Nance comes to be herself, and a new mine captain arrives, while Gard makes new acquaintances and shines through modest veiling.

Grannie schemes schemes, Gard fights gales and Tom, Tom wants to but does not dare, and old Tom finds a silver heart. Oxenham writes island life with warmth: sea, mines, families and courtship in a Channel Island world. Dedicated to Edward Baker of La Chaumiere, Sark, the novel is a gentle love story set where land, sea and silver meet.
15411-a-voyage-to-the-south-sea:
William Bligh published this account in London in 1792, by permission of the Admiralty, with charts. The voyage had a royal order behind it: carry the breadfruit tree to the West Indies in His Majesty's ship Bounty, under Bligh's command. The title page promises the full story, including the mutiny and the open-boat voyage that followed.

Chapters trace the plan, the outfit, and the sailing from England, with stops at Tenerife, the Cape of Good Hope, Van Diemen's Land, and the Pacific islands. After the mutiny, part of the crew sailed in the ship's boat from Tofoa to Timor, a Dutch settlement in the East Indies. Bligh's narrative, written to correct a hasty first account, remains the classic firsthand record of the Bounty affair.
15420-broken-homes-a-study-of-family-des:
Joanna C. Colcord, superintendent of New York's Charity Organization Society, published this social work study in 1919 for the Russell Sage Foundation. It asks why men desert their families, and how charities should answer. A district secretary's line opens the argument: before the deserter, there was a broken man, bankrupt for the time in health, hopes, or prospects.

Chapters move from causes to treatment: finding the missing husband, gathering facts, and shaping help case by case. Colcord also treats the home-staying non-supporter, and closes with next steps in corrective and preventive work. The book is practical, not sentimental, drawing on case records to show what aid could and could not do. It remains a clear record of early social work facing family breakdown.
16142-the-communist-threat-in-the-taiwan:
Released by the State Department in September 1958, this pamphlet gathers official American papers on the Taiwan Straits crisis. It prints Secretary Dulles's statement of September 4, a White House statement, President Eisenhower's report to the American people, and Eisenhower's letter to Premier Khrushchev. The series number is Far Eastern Series 76.

Dulles states that Taiwan, Quemoy, and Matsu had never been under Communist authority, remaining under Free China since the Second World War, and that the United States stood bound by treaty. The pamphlet lets readers follow Washington's public case during artillery attacks on the offshore islands. It remains a compact primary source on Cold War Asia.
16243-journal-of-landsborough-s-expediti:
William Landsborough's journal, published in Melbourne in 1862 by F. F. Bailliere, records his expedition from Carpentaria in search of Burke and Wills. Anxiety for the lost explorers raised four parties within a short time: Howitt from Melbourne, McKinlay from Adelaide, Walker from Rockhampton, and Landsborough from Brisbane. The steamer Victoria, under Commander Norman, sailed to the Gulf of Carpentaria to support them.

Landsborough's route, shown on a map, crosses the Gulf country toward the interior, through heat, flood, and rough ground. His daily entries give the search its human scale, with horses, stores, and native guides. Readers of Australian exploration will find a plain, gripping record of a famous rescue quest.
16347-miscellanea:
Juliana Horatia Ewing's Miscellanea, published by the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge, gathers papers republished to complete her collected works. The preface admits the pieces were not republished in her lifetime, a sign she did not rate them highly, yet each holds a special interest that justifies bringing them forward. Ewing's gift for mimicry shapes the book, since she acted above the average of amateurs and could imitate any style she wished.

The first four stories show that mimic power at work, copying other voices with wit and accuracy. Later pieces add sketches, verses, and odds and ends from a busy writing life. Readers who know Ewing's children's classics will enjoy these slighter, revealing extras.
16936-parker-s-second-reader-national-se:
Richard G. Parker, principal of the North Johnson School in Boston, wrote this second reader in the National Series of selections for reading, adapted to the standing of the pupil, issued by A. S. Barnes and Burr in New York in 1851. Part second is designed for younger classes in schools and academies. A motto from Acts asks, understandest thou what thou readest.

Parker gathers short prose and verse for young readers, graded to their level, with lessons in reading, morals, and knowledge. The book served thousands of American schoolrooms. Modern readers get a clear window on 1851 schooling, and teachers of reading history will find a useful, plain sample of how children once learned to read aloud.
17480-the-digger-movement-in-the-days-of:
Lewis H. Berens, author of Towards the Light, published this study of the Digger movement in London in 1906 with Simpkin, Marshall, Hamilton, Kent and Company. He dedicates it to the Society of Friends, whose doctrines he learned to love while writing. The subtitle calls Gerrard Winstanley, the Digger, a mystic and rationalist, a communist, and a social reformer.

Chapters run from the Reformation in Germany and England, through the great civil war, to the Diggers themselves. Winstanley, his exposition of Quaker doctrines, the new law of righteousness, and the Diggers' manifestoes follow. Readers get a careful history of England's first communist movement, drawn from Winstanley's own writings.
17694-adventures-in-new-guinea:
James Chalmers of Port Moresby wrote this account of adventures in New Guinea, published in London in 1886 by the Religious Tract Society, with six pictures. Chalmers notes that public attention had lately turned to New Guinea, whose name often appeared in newspapers and missionary reports. His introduction sets the scene for a missionary's travels among coastal peoples.

Readers get a Victorian missionary adventure, mixing exploration, encounter, and evangelism in the Pacific. The book suits readers of mission history and of New Guinea's colonial past. Its Tract Society origin marks its earnest, improving tone.
17910-the-mafulu-mountain-people-of-brit:
Robert W. Williamson wrote The Mafulu Mountain People of British New Guinea in 1912, printed in London by Macmillan, with a preface by A. C. Haddon. Williamson studied a mountain folk of Papua, then little known to outsiders, and he gives their life in full, careful detail.

The book covers homes, dress, food, rites, law, and trade, with pictures and a map to aid the reader. Haddon, a famed anthropologist, lends his name to the work. It is a classic early ethnography, written with the era's colonial gaze, and it stays a key source for the Mafulu, best read with modern Papuan studies at hand.
18062-stories-of-ships-and-the-sea:
Jack London wrote these Stories of Ships and the Sea, printed as Little Blue Book number 1169 in Girard, Kansas, by Haldeman-Julius. The copyright stands in the name of Charmian London, his widow, and the set was reprinted by arrangement for cheap, wide sale.

Five tales fill the book: Chris Farrington, able seaman, a typhoon off Japan, a lost poacher, the banks of the Sacramento, and a stay in Yeddo Bay. Chris, a lad of seventeen, spars with a Swedish sailor over rank and manners. The stories are brisk, salty, and full of sea life, a fine pocket sample of London at his best.
18268-ballads-of-lost-haven-a-book-of-th:
Bliss Carman, author of Low Tide on Grand Pre and Songs from Vagabondia, published this book of sea ballads at Boston in 1897. Lamson, Wolffe and Company issued the volume, printed at the Norwood Press. Carman writes of sailors, ships, and shore towns, with the sea as both workplace and fate.

Contents open with A Son of the Sea, whose speaker was born for deep-sea faring and bred to put to sea on stories of his father's daring. Later ballads give The Gravedigger, The Yule Guest, The Marring of Malyn, The Nancy's Pride, Arnold master of the Scud, and The Ships of St. John. Legends of Lost Haven, The Shadow Boatswain, and The Last Watch close the set. Readers get sea poetry in ballad form: storms, legends, and the pull of the tide.
1861-an-old-town-by-the-sea:
Thomas Bailey Aldrich's Old Town by the Sea is a portrait of Portsmouth, New Hampshire, sung first through the Piscataqua River, which sings by gleaming isles, woods, and fields of corn. Aldrich, writing from a city and full of vague unrest, looks back to the town of his boyhood with affection.

The sketches walk the reader past great houses with oaks and elms, tessellated marble walks, and small square buildings abutting the street. They dwell on the town's sea captains and old families. The book is a gentle work of local memory, and it remains a charming introduction to a New England port before it changed.
1880-the-pathfinder-or-the-inland-sea:
Natty Bumppo, older now, works as a guide on Lake Ontario — the inland sea of the title — where forest war meets naval war. Cooper's preface explains the plan: to join seamen and savages in incidents that might be supposed to happen on the great lakes, where forest war meets naval war.

The tale follows Pathfinder's love for Mabel Dunham, a young woman who has come to the frontier, and his rivalry with officers and Indians alike. Cooper writes the lake country with the care of a man who knew it. The novel's set pieces — canoes, storms, and night attacks — give it the shape of the Leatherstocking Tales at their most adventurous.
19005-the-rose-of-dawn-a-tale-of-the-sou:
Helen Hay wrote this short verse tale of the South Sea in 1901, with a drawing by John La Farge. It opens before dawn on a still island shore, where palms, stars, and sea wait for first light. The poem's music carries the story more than plain plot does.

A youth named Malua meets Taka on the beach and follows her to the hut of old Akau, who gives him a carved kava bowl of great worth. Love, honour, and the gifts of age shape the brief action. Readers get a lyrical island romance, rich in colour and gentle in tone.
19119-cerberus-the-dog-of-hades-the-hist:
This short study traces the idea of Cerberus, the hound of Hades, through Greek and Indian myth. Its front piece shows Herakles dragging two-headed Cerberus from the underworld past Persephone, Hermes, and Athene. The author follows the hound's image across vases, poems, and rites.

A key section reads the two dogs of Yama in the Rig-Veda as kin to Cerberus, guarding the road to bliss and barring unfit souls. Hymns, funeral lore, and sky lore are weighed together. Readers get a learned myth study on how one fearsome dog grew from old beliefs about death and the heavens.
19220-irish-wit-and-humor-anecdote-biogr:
This 1872 volume gathers Irish wit and humour in anecdote biographies of Swift, Curran, O'Leary, and O'Connell. Dean Swift fronts the book, with tales of his birth, marriage certificate, grace after dinner, three crosses, and quarrels with Chief Justice Whitshed. Each anecdote is short and pointed.

Swift's resolutions when old warn against marrying a young woman, keeping young company unasked, peevishness, scorning new ways, and telling the same story over and over. Such rules show his sharp self-knowledge. Readers get a lively store of Irish jokes, sayings, and lives, rich in bite and humour.
1958-hermann-and-dorothea:
Johann Wolfgang von Goethe's Hermann and Dorothea, is a verse epic of German village life. It follows Hermann, a young man who falls in love with Dorothea, a refugee girl fleeing the French Revolution. The poem is set in a small town on the Rhine, where war arrives as a column of wagons on the road.

Goethe writes the story in hexameters, giving a village romance the dignity of epic. The poem's fame rests on its balance: love and war, home and exile, held in a single, calm narrative. It remains one of Goethe's most loved works, and a good entry point to his poetry for readers new to it.
19993-childhood-s-favorites-and-fairy-st:
Childhood's Favorites and Fairy Stories is a young folks' treasury of classic tales. Its contributors' list reads like a hall of fame. Joel Chandler Harris, creator of Uncle Remus, appears there. Franklin K. Lane, the Interior Secretary, lends his name. Ernest Ingersoll the naturalist writes for the young here too. The Hamilton Wright Mabie circle edited the treasury in 1909. Famous pens were gathered to stock one family volume.

Treasuries like this decided which stories counted as childhood's favorites. Fairy tales, animal stories, and poems fill the big book. Editors promised parents the best, pre-selected and safe. The famous-contributor list was the selling point and the standard. Many American childhoods were furnished from such volumes. This one shows the canon being packaged.
20190-the-handy-cyclopedia-of-things-wor:
The Handy Cyclopedia of Things Worth Knowing is a manual of ready reference for daily use. Its pages define hard words and give brief facts in strict order. Copperas is ferrous sulfate, one short entry tells the reader plainly. Diathesis means a bodily bent toward a certain kind of illness.

Other entries cover fines, pay for office, and Greek myth alike. Erebus is the dark region the dead cross toward Hades. Such handbooks put a small library on one shelf for busy homes. Readers get a quaint, handy store of the facts its era prized most.
21087-the-ghost-ship-a-mystery-of-the-se:
John Conroy Hutcheson's mystery of the sea opens at a blazing sunset aboard the ocean steamer Star of the North. The weather has looked threatening all day. Soon the officers face a puzzle that pulls the tale in and out of the supernatural.

Again and again the ship meets the same vessel sailing in a direction that seems impossible. Her officers check their position and grow more baffled each time. Hutcheson grounds the mystery in daily life aboard a late nineteenth-century steamer, with its watches, routines, and weather. Readers get a ghost story tested against charts, compasses, and hard-headed sailors.
21088-the-white-squall-a-story-of-the-sa:
Tom is thirteen, and his father is a naval officer on half pay who has bought property in the West Indies. John Conroy Hutcheson sends the boy home to school in England after an accident delays his start. A ship's captain takes charge of him for the voyage.

That voyage brings nearly every mishap a sailing ship could meet. A white squall, a sudden line squall, strikes and capsizes the vessel in the Sargasso Sea. Tom and the crew must right her and carry on to England. Hutcheson wrote the tale as a lively first guide to ships for young readers.
21104-afloat-at-last-a-sailor-boy-s-log-:
Allan Graham, a country vicar's son, signs on as an apprentice aboard the Silver Queen at Wapping Docks for a voyage to Shanghai. Irish bosun Tim Rooney takes to the lad and teaches him the ropes. John Conroy Hutcheson logs the ship warping out of dock and down the Thames under a steam tug.

Seasickness in the Bay of Biscay, a stowaway in the forepeak, and friendship with the Chinese cook Ching Wang fill the outward run. Past the Cape of Good Hope, Malay pirates trail the ship through typhoon weather. She grounds on the Pratas shoal before the voyage ends.
21301-bunyip-land-a-story-of-adventure-i:
Joe Carstairs works on an Australian farm, poring over maps, in George Manville Fenn's New Guinea adventure. His father, a keen naturalist, set off years before to collect specimens in New Guinea and was never heard of again. Joe plans a search expedition, taking a local doctor and an Aboriginal worker from the farm.

A stowaway, Jimmy, joins them with his dog Gyp. In New Guinea they hire porters and push inland, finding Joe's father held prisoner with another Englishman whose mind has broken under captivity. Fenn supplies the usual close shaves, strange creatures, and jungle dangers before the party brings the lost men home.
21366-sail-ho-a-boy-at-sea:
Alison Dale is seventeen and already a practised yachtsman from his father's boats. He ships out on his first real cruise in George Manville Fenn's later sea tale. His skipper is an unpleasant man, and the crew holds worse: a half-French troublemaker named Jarette leads a mutiny. The ship is taken, and officers and passengers are cut off from her.

Most of the loyal party are cast adrift to die, with two of their number left aboard. Rescuers return for them just as the drunken mutineers set the vessel afire and flee. A fight for the burning ship follows, with Jarette at its centre until the end.
21367-sappers-and-miners-the-flood-benea:
George Manville Fenn sets one of his tensest tales in Cornwall. Its scene is an old tin mine whose workings run far out beneath the sea. Colonel Pendarve's son Gwyn starts the book at breakfast, hungry from dawn work by the boats. The mine may date to Roman or even Phoenician tin traders.

Fifty-two chapters give Fenn room for his chapter-end perils, and the flood beneath the sea of the subtitle hangs over every descent. Boys, miners, and old workings meet in passages where one wrong step brings the Atlantic in. Fenn's transcriber called it among his very best, and the underground setting makes the suspense tighter than his open-sea tales.
21373-syd-belton-the-boy-who-would-not-g:
Sydney Belton dines with his father, a naval captain, and his uncle, an admiral, and disappoints them both: he does not want the navy. Rounds with the local doctor have turned his head toward medicine. George Manville Fenn sets the tale in the mid-eighteenth century, cocked hats and all, with France as the coming enemy.

Syd runs away with the gardener's son, comes home, and finds his mind changed toward the sea after all. His father's old connections reach the First Sea Lord himself, and the outcome gives Captain Belton command of the Sirius. The boy who would not go to sea becomes the title's joke and its lesson.
21392-happy-jack-and-other-tales-of-the-:
Happy Jack, and Other Tales of the Sea gathers sea stories by W. H. G. Kingston. The title tale opens on the Naiad, a small brig working the run between London and Leith. Her young narrator joins her at about fourteen, in far from grand style.

Kingston paints shipboard life in plain detail, from the dark forecastle to the captain's cabin. Leaks, pumps, watches, and rough weather shape each day at sea. The tales that follow share that close feel for work aboard sailing craft. For readers who want the daily grind and risk of the old merchant sea, the set is rich fare.
21403-the-pirate-of-the-mediterranean-a-:
Malta opens the scene of W. H. G. Kingston's long sea novel The Pirate of the Mediterranean. Kingston praises the island's fine climate, bright skies, and deep store of history. From there the tale moves out over the eastern seas.

A Greek pirate preys on Italian, Greek, and Turkish ships in those waters. Kingston builds the chase through tense scenes and narrow escapes at sea. The book runs long, some nineteen hours read aloud, and it earns its length. Readers who want Barbary corsairs should note this pirate is a different foe. The craft, coasts, and crews are drawn with Kingston's usual care.
21450-ben-burton-born-and-bred-at-sea:
Ben Burton is born to a sailor's wife in W. H. G. Kingston's Ben Burton, or Born and Bred at Sea. His father Dick, a quartermaster of the old Boreas, comes home wounded from a cutting-out raid. News of the baby greets him as he climbs the ship's side.

The tale follows Ben from birth to senior naval rank through a string of sea and shore scenes. A drifting dinghy brings an ayah and a small white girl into the tale. She grows up alongside Ben, spared his hardest fights. Years fly fast, as they do in such tales, and incident crowds upon incident.
21717-battles-with-the-sea:
Lifeboat crews are the heroes of this Ballantyne book, which frames their work as a war that never ends. The foe is the sea itself, which strikes without warning and takes hundreds of lives each year. Against it stand the men of the lifeboats and rocket crews, ready day and night to launch into storms.

Ballantyne tells true-style tales of wrecks, rescues, and brave deeds along the British coast. He wrote the book so boys would know this quiet war and honor those who fight it. The chapters mix stirring sea stories with plain facts about how rescues were made and what they cost.
21761-synopsis-of-some-genera-of-the-lar:
Fungi with names few readers will know fill this slim scientific pamphlet by C. G. Lloyd, printed at Cincinnati in January 1917. Lloyd works over three groups of large pyrenomycetes: Camillea, Thamnomyces, and Engleromyces. A fine specimen of Camillea Cyclops, sent by the Reverend Torrend from Brazil, set the study going. Photographs taken in European museums back the text.

Lloyd argues that the known species can be told apart from good figures, even without close study of their structure. He warns that many tropical finds now filed under other names are really Camilleas. The work is dry, exact, and meant for specialists. It shows the careful sorting work behind every tidy shelf of natural history.
22056-the-mountain-that-was-god-being-a-:
John H. Williams called his 1905 volume The Mountain That Was God, a little book about the great peak of the Northwest. The mountain is Rainier, the huge extinct volcano that rules the skyline near Tacoma and Seattle. Native peoples had treated the white summit as a god. Williams set out to show it from every side.

Glaciers, forests, and climbing routes all enter his account. He compares the text to a glacial river, narrow but swift, running through grand scenery. Photographs and sketches support the words. The book helped turn Rainier from a distant landmark into a place Americans wanted to visit and protect.
22275-vc-a-chronicle-of-castle-barfield-:
V.C., published by David Christie Murray in 1904, joins Castle Barfield to the Crimean War. Murray opens on a stormy night above his fictional parish. Darkness brings one sign of cheer: the lights of the grey-stone mansion on Beacon Hill. Window after window glows until the whole house seems charged with warmth, while the tempest pours its strength against the walls.

From that house a hero goes to the Crimea, where the Victoria Cross was born. Murray, who had reported wars himself, writes battle with a correspondent's eye. The home parish and the trenches test the same men. The novel is a late-Victorian tribute to the V.C. and the villages that bred its winners.
23271-sunk-at-sea:
Sunk at Sea follows castaways who build a new life after a wreck. In time they return to a village, where a mission is set up. A small church with a spire goes up, and that spire soon proves its worth in a moment of danger.

Another vessel calls for water. Its crew would have fired on the settlement out of spite. Seeing the spire, the crew restrain themselves. The heroes then persuade the captain to take them aboard, though Will now loves the missionary's daughter. Readers get shipwreck, mission work, and romance, with a sequel promised in a companion tale.
23273-john-deane-of-nottingham-historic-:
John Deane of Nottingham tells the historic adventures, by land and sea, of a real Nottingham man. After service in Russia, Deane became British consul at Ostend. He held that post for many years before returning home to honours in his native town.

Deane was made a burgess of Nottingham and settled in the nearby village of Wilford. There he died in 1760. His tomb stands there beside his beloved wife Elizabeth's, in the quiet churchyard. Readers get a true-life adventure: a sailor and soldier whose travels ended in office, honour, and a marked grave.
23377-the-lively-poll-a-tale-of-the-nort:
R. M. Ballantyne set this tale among the North Sea fishing fleets, where an Admiral of the fleet orders a hundred or more boats so their trawl nets do not tangle. After a night's work, crews gut, fillet, and box the catch, and a steam carrier takes it to Yarmouth, Gorleston, and on to London tables by the next day.

Trade with Dutch copers brings a darker note, as tobacco and schnapps flow aboard in exchange for fish, and drink ruins more than one good man. Ballantyne follows the Lively Poll and her crew through work, temptation, and storms, with plain detail of fleet life. Readers get both a working picture of sea fishing and a temperance tale of the dangers that wait when the fleet is far from home.
23539-where-angels-fear-to-tread-and-oth:
Morgan Robertson gathered these sea tales in eighteen ninety nine, with the title story first printed in the Atlantic Monthly and others in the Century, the Saturday Evening Post, Collier's, and more. Dedicated to its godfather John S. Phillips, the book ranges from salvage and trade winds to the brain of a battleship, wigwag messages, millstones, and battles of monsters.

Robertson, a seaman author, writes ships, crews, and storms with first hand force, mixing adventure with a keen sense of the sea's danger and beauty. The title tale, of a place where angels fear to tread, sets the daring tone. Sea story fans will enjoy the set as a prime sample of Robertson's craft, brisk, salty, and full of the risks men took on late nineteenth century waters.
23853-ran-away-to-sea:
Captain Mayne Reid's Ran Away to Sea tells of a boy, just sixteen, who runs away to sea against his parents' wishes. He leaves a fond and indulgent father, a kind and gentle mother, and sisters and brothers who lament him long after he is gone. No one, he says, had more cause to regret the act than himself.

His trouble deepens when he takes a place aboard a ship whose officers and crew are villains, trading in slaves though the trade was banned half a century before. Reid tells the story with his usual humor, but the treatment of the cargo brings harrowing moments. This edition appeared fifty years after the first, and may be slightly condensed from the longer original.
24384-365-luncheon-dishes-a-luncheon-dis:
This cook book gives a luncheon dish for every day in the year, selected from Marion Harland, Christine Terhune Herrick, the Boston Cooking School Magazine, Table Talk, Good Housekeeping, and others. It was published by George W. Jacobs and Company in Philadelphia in September 1902. Its transcriber notes that spelling inconsistencies were retained, with some words accented in the index but not in the body.

January opens with stewed breast of lamb on the first, cut small, seasoned, and stewed tender in gravy, thickened, flavored with wine, and garnished with green peas. Chicken creams follow on the second, herring's roes on toast on the third, and a French omelet on the fourth. Readers get a year's lunches, day by day, in one plain book.
24502-owen-hartley-or-ups-and-downs-a-ta:
William H. G. Kingston wrote this tale of land and sea for young readers. Owen Hartley, a well-educated teenager lately orphaned, is taken to a shipping firm in Wapping, London, run by a family relation. He proves his kinship, wins a clerk's place, and does his work so well that the firm sends him to sea to learn the business.

At sea, the kind captain falls ill, and a nasty mate takes his place. Owen, meant to travel as an honoured passenger, loses his cabin and faces hardship and danger. Kingston's story follows his ups and downs with energy and good humour, giving young readers a stirring picture of merchant seafaring.
25164-the-flag-of-distress-a-story-of-th:
Captain Mayne Reid's Flag of Distress is a long sea adventure. It opens with a strange sight in mid-Pacific: a barque under full sail, wearing the Chilean flag upside down, the signal of distress. Yet she refuses to heave to for a British naval vessel. Only two figures appear on her deck, dressed in reddish fur.

The mystery takes the whole book to explain. Her captain and his passenger lie bound below, her crew are gone, and the fur-clad figures prove to be orang-outangs. Reid, best known for Wild West tales, sets much of the action on the San Francisco sea-front of 1849, and the story mixes humor, suspense, and sailor talk.
26952-eric-or-under-the-sea:
Mrs. S. B. C. Samuels's 1870 children's novel, second in her Springdale Stories, sends Eric and his friends traveling across Europe. The preface promises incidents drawn from real life, plus one set piece readers would remember: Eric's descent to the sea floor in diving armor.

Chapters take in a Dutch city, Strasbourg, and other stops, with scrapes along the way: Eric in trouble, a real thief unmasked, and a friend proved in need. Written for young readers, it mixes travel sights with moral lessons, and the underwater dive gives the journey its thrill.
27069-sonnets-from-the-crimea:
Adam Mickiewicz's Sonnets from the Crimea, translated by Edna Worthley Underwood and published in San Francisco in 1917, gathers the Polish poet's Crimean sequence with a biographical sketch. Mickiewicz, born in 1798, wrote the sonnets in his youth during the Vilna period.

Exiled to southern Russia for his part in a student society, he began the sonnets on the road toward Odessa, and their success was quick and astonishing. The poems move from the Ackerman steppe and Baktschi Serai to the grave of Countess Potocka and the ruins of Balaclava, in classic sonnet form bent to a new landscape.
27356-chelsea:
G. E. Mitton wrote this short guide to Chelsea, edited by Sir Walter Besant, as part of the Fascination of London series from Adam and Charles Black in 1902. The series set out to survey London district by district, preserving each place's history, its historical and literary associations, and its mighty buildings, past and present.

Chelsea Old Church, pictured from an etching, stands at the front of the book, and companion volumes covered Westminster, the Strand district, and Hampstead. Besant, who had walked about London for thirty years, called the survey the work that fascinated him most. The book still serves walkers who want the stories behind Chelsea's streets.
2765-the-lady-from-the-sea:
Henrik Ibsen wrote this play about Ellida Wangel, a lighthouse keeper's daughter married to Dr. Wangel, a widower in a small Norwegian fjord town. Ellida loves the sea with a longing her husband cannot share, and she waits for a stranger from her past.

The Stranger, a sailor to whom she once bound herself, returns to claim her, and Ellida must choose freely between husband and sea. Ibsen writes with symbolic power about marriage, freedom, and the pull of wild nature. The play endures as a haunting study of a woman choosing her own life.
27982-the-ocean-waifs-a-story-of-adventu:
Captain Mayne Reid wrote The Ocean Waifs, a story of adventure on land and sea, opening with small vessels drifting after a fire and explosion aboard a slave ship. Ben Brace escapes on a raft with a boy seaman of sixteen, while the captain's gig and a barrel carrying Snowball, an African cook, and a little girl drift nearby.

The survivors join together. Reid, a natural historian, fills the tale with fish and creatures of the deep, until a whale-ship rescues the good and the wicked perish. The novel mixes sea adventure with natural history, in Reid's instructive and exciting manner.
27986-judith-lynn-a-story-of-the-sea:
Annie Hamilton Donnell published Judith Lynn, a story of the sea, with David C. Cook Publishing Company in 1906. The novel opens with Judith in tarpaulin and oilskins, mistaken for a boy by a little girl from the hotel, who is surprised to learn her name.

Judith tends lobster traps sunk to the bottom of the sea, marked by little wooden floats, and her rare, salty laugh brightens a rough life. Blossom, a frail child Judith loves, is the one sweet and beautiful thing in her world, and the story follows sea work, friendship, and growing up on the coast.
29051-account-of-a-voyage-of-discovery-t:
Captain Basil Hall of the Royal Navy wrote this 1818 account of a voyage of discovery to the west coast of Corea, now Korea, and the Great Loo-Choo Island, now Okinawa. Published by John Murray in London, the work adds an appendix of charts and hydrographical and scientific notices, and a vocabulary of the Loo-Choo language by Lieutenant H. J. Clifford. Hall dedicates it to Captain Murray Maxwell, whose conduct of the voyage made the book possible.

Hall drew his narrative from journals written at the time, with help from Clifford's notes, since Clifford, on half pay and free of duty, could devote himself to learning. The voyage met Korean and Okinawan people with care for their dispositions and goodwill. Readers get a classic early account of East Asian shores, valuable for navigation, natural history, and first contact alike.
29909-a-singer-from-the-sea:
Amelia E. Barr published A Singer from the Sea in New York in 1893, with Dodd, Mead and Company. The tale runs along the wild Cornish coast from Padstow Point to Lundy Race, where a tossing sea and a stiff breeze never rest. Barr dedicates the book, in the words of Guillaume de la Laudelle, to the sailors themselves, the true authors of its frank simplicity.

Denas Penelles heads the first chapter, and the cottage by the sea, Roland, and Elizabeth follow. A seed of change, a sea of sorrow, and a piece of money and a song mark the middle course. A visit to St. Penfer, a cowardly love, and death as dawn lead to sorrow bringing all home. The Darling Denas of the later chapters gives the book its warm, sea-sung heart.
31497-the-brassbounder-a-tale-of-the-sea:
David W. Bone's The Brassbounder, a tale of the sea, was published in London by Duckworth, first published in 1910 and reprinted in 1911, with a popular edition in 1913. Bone, author of Broken Stowage, dedicates the book to James Hamilton Muir. The brassbounder of the title is a young apprentice at sea, learning his trade before the mast in the last days of sail. Bone writes from knowledge of ships and seamen, and the novel carries the salt air of real experience.

Readers of sea fiction will find a story of a boy's first voyages, with storms, shipmates, and the discipline of a sailing ship. Bone's prose is plain and workmanlike, suited to its subject. The book belongs with the best apprentice tales of its period, where the sea itself is the school and the test.
32024-the-motor-girls-on-the-coast-or-th:
Margaret Penrose's girls' adventure story, copyrighted in 1913, sends the Motor Girls to the coast in a tale also called The Waif from the Sea. Its thirty chapters open with a flash of fire and a strange woman with a strange story. They move on through motoring on the road, a lost boy named Jack, and a girl whose identity is in question. The cove, a lighthouse maid, and the keeper's story follow. The list signals a mix of motoring fun, mystery, and seaside incident.

Later chapters raise the stakes with gathering clouds, a storm, a wreck, and a rescue. Floating spars, a safe landing ashore, and the story of Nancy Ford follow. A bold attempt and a strange message at the Shark's Tooth lead toward happy days. Readers get a fast-moving series adventure, built for young readers who liked cars, coastlines, and mystery.
32223-specimens-of-german-romance-vol-ii:
Specimens of German Romance, volume two, Master Flea, selected and translated from various authors, was printed in London for George B. Whittaker in Ave-Maria-Lane in 1826, and printed by Thomas Davison in Whitefriars. The volume belongs to a three-volume set of German romance in English dress, and its tale is Hoffmann's Master Flea. An illustration shows Master Flea himself.

The First Adventure opens with an introduction, wherein the gentle reader learns enough of Mr. Peregrine Tyss's life to follow the tale. Christmas-boxes are presented at the bookbinder Lemmerhirt's in Kelbecker-street, and the adventure begins, with two Alinas in play. The narrator jokes against beginning once upon a time, which the modern reader calls obsolete and tedious, preferring to plunge in medias res. Readers get an early English Hoffmann, playful, fantastical, and self-aware.
32338-toilers-of-the-sea:
Victor Hugo's novel appears here in Everyman's Library, number 509, newly completed from W. Moy Thomas's translation and first issued in this edition in 1911. The story centres on Gilliatt, an unpopular man linked by rumour to a haunted house and a strange seat on the rocks. It also follows Mess Lethierry, whose steamship Durande gives one part of the book its name.

Déruchette, Lethierry's kin, stands at the heart of its love story. Later parts follow Sieur Clubin, the bagpipe, and the sea itself as a force shaping work, wreck, and rescue. Hugo writes at length about ships, tides, and island life, turning labour at sea into a test of courage and endurance. This edition suits readers who want Hugo's Channel Islands epic in a compact, well-made library volume.
32516-a-marriage-at-sea:
W. Clark Russell's novel A Marriage at Sea, first published in two volumes in February 1891 and issued cheaply in 1919, opens at midnight in Boulogne harbour. The narrator's dandy-rigged yacht Spitfire, twenty-six tons, lies hidden in deep shadow against a harbour wall, while a double-funnelled steamer looms ahead and the Capécure pier runs seaward in gloom. Contents promise an elopement, sweethearts in a dandy, dirty weather, and sweethearts in a storm.

Later chapters bring the Carthusian, outward bound, much observation, a singular proposal, Grace's consent, and the marriage at sea itself, followed by the Mermaid and homeward bound. Russell, a master of sea fiction, mixes romance, seamanship, and adventure on a small yacht. Readers who enjoy Victorian nautical romance will find the book brisk, salty, and romantic.
32598-earth-and-sky-every-child-should-k:
Julia Ellen Rogers's Earth and Sky Every Child Should Know, copyrighted in 1910, teaches earth science and astronomy through short studies for any time and place. Part one moves from fossils, granite, and the crust of the earth to wind, rain, rivers, glaciers, coal, and the ages of fishes, reptiles, mammals, and man.

Part two turns families into star clubs, tracing the dippers and the pole star, winter constellations, Orion, and the twenty brightest stars. With thirty-one pages of photographs and drawings, Rogers invites children to look closely at rocks, skies, and seasons close to home.
32710-doom-of-the-house-of-duryea:
Earl Peirce Jr. tells of Arthur Duryea, a young man who meets a father he has never known, after twenty years apart. Doctor Henry Duryea, fresh from Paris, waits in suite six hundred of a hotel, tall, pale, and trembling with joy at the reunion. Father and son share cigars, tears, and talk.

The pair then travel to a lone house in the Maine woods, where a storm blows a door open and cold air floods the lodge. Arthur takes a room upstairs, beside a spare room full of furniture, and the house itself seems to watch him. Horror gathers slowly, and the doom of the name Duryea closes in.
33649-thoughts-and-counsels-of-the-saint:
The Reverend Bonaventure Hammer, a Franciscan, collected this daily devotional of thoughts and counsels from the saints for every day of the year. Saints and blessed figures quoted include Alphonsus, Anselm, Antoninus, Benedict, Bernard, Catherine of Siena, Gregory the Great, Ignatius, Mechtildis, Teresa, Thomas Aquinas, Vincent de Paul, Vincent Ferrer, and Albert the Great. Saints and blessed figures quoted also include Henry Suso, Jordan of Saxony, and others.

Each day offers a short saying to carry into conduct. Thought before action and self-command afterward, resignation in affliction, perfection in the love of God, and prayer as the field where virtues grow. Arranged month by month from January through December, the book gives readers a brief, steady companion for morning reflection or evening review, rooted in the Catholic spiritual tradition.
33909-the-school-by-the-sea:
Angela Brazil wrote this school story, published in London and Glasgow by Blackie and Son with pictures. The frontispiece shows a girl gasping that somebody or something is inside the barred room. Chapters open with an interloper and a kingdom by the sea, setting a school tale beside the shore.

Brazil, author of many school books, writes for girls in a world of forms, friendships, and small mysteries. The barred room gives the term its thrill, while school life carries the heart of the story. The book remains a lively example of Brazil's seaside school tales.
33945-the-unknown-sea:
Clemence Housman wrote this romance, published in London in 1898 by Duckworth. A solitary fisher ploughs a southern sea, a youth of northern race with fair hair and clear grey eyes, tanned red-brown by southern skies. His boat races forward, bright of paint and ruddy of canvas, against old, blackened tackle.

Nets and weighted cross-beams mark him as a coral fisher, bound toward a coast of gaunt and desolate cliffs. Housman writes the sea with color and music. The book offers a dreamlike tale of a young fisher and an unknown shore.
34949-some-reptiles-and-amphibians-from-:
Robert G Webb, J Knox Jones Jr, and George W Byers reported on reptiles and amphibians from Korea. The University of Kansas issued the study on January 31, 1962, as Volume 15, Number 2. It spans pages 149 to 173 of the museum series. A plate list and fine notes on names open the work.

Jones and Byers gathered 382 specimens in Korea in 1954, during fever field studies. The snakes, frogs, and toads rest at Kansas and at the University of Michigan. Notes treat twenty-two kinds, all known from Korea before this study. Field workers gain fresh facts on range, form, and habits.
35530-fundamental-peace-ideas-including-:
Fundamental Peace Ideas is a pamphlet by Arthur Mac Donald, an anthropologist of Washington. It was reprinted from the Congressional Record of the first of July 1919, for the United States Senate, and printed at Washington that year. The pamphlet links the Westphalian Peace Treaty of 1648 and the League of Nations of 1919 to international psychology and revolutions.

Mac Donald opens with the new League. It may be only a first step toward permanent peace, he writes, and not a few persons doubt its use. But the League may be the lesser evil, set against the old order, which failed after a very long and fair trial. The one encouraging thing, he argues, is that peoples and leaders alike have come to see the need of peace and the senselessness of war. His question is what ordinary people are to do now.
36456-the-autobiography-of-an-electron-w:
The Autobiography of an Electron is a science tale told by a spark mote. Charles Gibson cast new physics in a fresh and gay form in the book. A front photo shows the flash of storm light that such motes make. No year is shown in the front pages of the hosted text.

The mote tells its own life to teach the new lore of the atom. Storm flash is shown as a vast rush of such motes from cloud to cloud. Past books by the hand treat wires, rays, and the spark age at large. Plain talk and bright scenes aim the hard lore at home readers. The book stands as a gay gate to the physics of its day.
36495-astronomical-myths-based-on-flamma:
John F Blake based a book on Camille Flammarion's History of the Heavens, published in London in 1877. Blake's preface says the French work held accounts of ideas, some mythical and some serious, about the heavenly bodies and Earth. It also gave a popular history of astronomy's start among ancient peoples. The French original used conversations at the seaside.

Blake dropped that form, judging English readers would like it less. He added much new matter, including a whole chapter on the Pleiades, drawn from recent research. So the book is founded on Flammarion rather than a strict translation. Blake stresses that early astronomy mixed with all of life, even religion.
38406-in-the-yellow-sea:
Henry Frith wrote In the Yellow Sea, a boy’s tale of war in China seas. Henry Frowde and Hodder and Stoughton issued the book in London. A young teller tells his own tale in the first person. Cast out of a navy path, he ships east for fate.

Doctors claim his sight is weak and bar him from the fleet. His stepfather calls the lad no good for sea work. A storm, the Osprey, and the steamer Feng Shui bear him to China. Hong Kong cash and war talk greet him on shore. A hid task, a kidnapping, and a sea murder crowd the tale. The Kowshing gives up to a Japanese war ship in one scene. Port Arthur’s fall and Wei-hai-wei end the grim cruise.
38587-the-victory-at-sea:
A war memoir by Rear-Admiral William Sowden Sims. Sims commanded the American naval forces in European waters. Burton J Hendrick helped him write the book. John Murray published it at London in 1920. Sims dedicates it to his officers and men. The story opens in March 1917. A secret summons called him from the Naval War College to Washington.

The chapters then survey the whole naval war. The adoption of the convoy comes early. American destroyers, decoy ships, and subchasers follow. One chapter describes the North Sea mine barrage. Another meets German submarines off the American coast. The transport of two million soldiers closes the account. No senior American sailor left a fuller record.
39904-the-life-of-crustacea:
The Life of Crustacea, a natural history by W T Calman, was first published by Methuen and Company of London in 1911. Thirty two plates and eighty five figures go with the text. Calman takes the lobster as the type of the whole class, crabs, shrimps, and their kin. An appendix teaches how to collect and preserve specimens, with notes on books.

Early chapters set out the lobster's build and the classification of the class. The metamorphoses of crustacea follow, stage by stage. Then come the peoples of each realm: the seashore, the deep sea, the open sea, fresh waters, and the land. Crustacea as parasites and messmates get a chapter. Their relation to man, as food and as pest, and their fossil past close the survey.
39924-down-the-river-to-the-sea:
Down the River to the Sea, by Miss Machar, was published in New York in 1894. Chapter one is set at Niagara Falls. May Thorburn sits on the Clifton House veranda in July sun. She gazes at the Horseshoe Fall in silent delight. Days before, her life was home duties, mending, and small snatches of poetry and music. Her cousin Kate Severne has now invited her on a grand trip.

The route runs from Niagara all the way to the Saguenay. Kate's two Scots cousins, Hugh and Flora Macnab, join the party. May came by way of Hamilton, through peach orchard country. The tale promises river scenery, travel talk, and young company. It suits readers who like gentle tour stories with a romantic thread.
40631-in-the-roar-of-the-sea:
S Baring Gould wrote In the Roar of the Sea, issued in New York by the National Book Company with a copyright of eighteen ninety one. Baring Gould had earlier written The Pennycomequicks and Urith. More than fifty chapters fill the long novel. Chapter heads name Captain Cruel, Uncle Zachie, Jessamine, and Una. Caves, shingle, and tamarisks set a Cornish sea coast scene.

Early chapters promise a passage of arms, a patched peace, and a warning of danger. Later chapters bring chains, a fight for life or death, and folk bought and sold. Jamie ride, a night excursion, and an unwilling prisoner add pace. Sea wolves, a diamond butterfly, and a whip that falls close the head list. Gould writes of wreck, smuggling, and love on a wild shore. Readers who love long, stormy tales of Cornwall will find full measure here.
42455-the-mystery-of-the-sea:
The Mystery of the Sea, by Bram Stoker, was published in London in 1902. Heinemann issued the novel. Stoker's name rides on Dracula, named beneath his own. Publisher's adverts for new six-shilling novels lead the front matter. A Gaelic verse and its translation stand as motto. To win the mystery of the sea, three weirds must meet: a golden moon on a flowing tide, Lammas floods, and a golden man with death for his bride. Contents run near forty chapters. Second Sight opens the tale, and Gormala follows.

An ancient rune and the Lammas floods set the mystery working. Crom Castle, the Pope's treasure, and a rising tide drive the close. Voices in the dark and a secret passage promise the thrill of the cavern chapters. Stoker mixes Scots coast lore with treasure romance.
42569-the-radio-detectives-under-the-sea:
A Hyatt Verrill wrote a boys' adventure novel in 1922, one of a series about radio detectives. Tom Pauling and Frank Putney sail from New York and sight the Bahamas after three days. Flying fish, sargassum weed, porpoises, and a sperm whale delight them on the way. The blue water of the Gulf Stream strikes them as a revelation.

Chapters promise a mysterious disappearance, radio magic, and a narrow escape. The boys trail a submarine and fight an octopus. They are lost, taken prisoner, and rescued by radio. A figure named Smernoff pays his debt near the end. Verrill blends new radio craft with sea adventure.
43780-the-lettsomian-lectures-on-disease:
Heart Disease in Middle and Advanced Age is the printed form of the Lettsomian Lectures on diseases and disorders of the heart and arteries. Mitchell Bruce, physician to Charing Cross Hospital, delivered them before the Medical Society of London in the session of 1900 to 1901. Harrison and Sons published the lectures in London in 1902.

The first lecture sets out the natural state of the heart and arteries after forty, then the causes of cardiovascular disorder. Bruce lists physical stress, nervous influences, cardiac poisons, and disturbances of metabolism among them. Gout, syphilis, acute fevers and chronic affections each get their place in the scheme. Bruce opens by thanking the society for the honour of the lectureship. The book preserves specialist teaching of its day on how hearts fail in later life, written for fellow doctors.
45082-the-daisy-or-cautionary-stories-in:
The Daisy is a book of cautionary stories in verse for children from four to eight years old. It was printed in London in 1807 by Harris, successor to Newbery, the great children's publisher. Thirty engravings illustrate the poems. Each short piece teaches a small lesson through a child, an animal, or a toy.

Pretty Puss opens the book. A child calls the cat to be patted, and the dog Tray is scolded for barking her away. The Fairing tells of a sister who bought a doll at the fair because the little girl had been good. The Good Boy shows Philip keeping still while his mother is ill, as the doctor and nurse ordered. The verses are simple, the morals plain, and the pictures do half the teaching. Books like this one formed the nursery shelf of Georgian England.
4544-the-cell-of-self-knowledge-seven-ea:
Edmund G. Gardner edited this collection of seven early English mystical treatises, first printed by Henry Pepwell in 1521 and reissued with an introduction and notes in 1910. The opening work, called Benjamin, comes from Richard of Saint Victor, and it traces how dread, sorrow, hope, love, and other powers of the soul rise toward true contemplation. Other pieces draw on Saint Catherine of Siena and on Margery Kempe.

Further treatises include Walter Hilton on the song of angels, an epistle of prayer, and kindred short works on the inner life. Together they show how medieval English writers pictured self-knowledge as a cell, or quiet room, where a person learns their own nothingness and God's goodness. Readers get a scholarly doorway into medieval devotion, with old texts made readable for modern study.
46392-illustrations-of-the-family-of-psi:
Edward Lear published his Illustrations of the Family of Psittacidae, or Parrots, in London in 1832. Lear issued the work himself from Albany Street, Regent's Park, and dedicated it, by permission, to the Queen. The book holds forty-two lithographic plates. Lear drew the birds from life and drew them again on the stone, a method that kept the prints close to the birds.

Cockatoos come first: salmon-crested, sulphur-crested, and Leadbeater's. Macaws follow, including the hyacinthine macaw and the red and yellow macaw. Parrakeets fill most of the later plates, many of them species never pictured before, as the title promises. Lear was twenty when the work appeared, years before his nonsense verse made him famous. Naturalists prize the plates for their accuracy and life. The book stands at the start of his art, and among the finest parrot books ever made.
46823-ten-years-in-india-in-the-16th-que:
Gould, once a sergeant in the 16th Queen's Lancers, wrote a memoir of army life issued at Toronto in 1880. The long title tells the scope: ten years in India with the Lancers, then three years in South Africa with the Cape Corps Levies. Gould says tales told by his own father, a Tenth Royal Hussars man, first drew him to the ranks.

The book names fights at Ghuznee, Cabul, Maharajpoor, Aliwal, and Sobraon, plus the Kaffir War of 1850 and 1851. Gould adds tales of elephant hunts and notes on the ways of Hindu, Muslim, and Kaffir peoples he met. It reads as a plain old soldier's record of service.
47-anne-of-avonlea:
Anne Shirley becomes Avonlea's schoolteacher in this sequel to Green Gables. Lucy Maud Montgomery's Anne of Avonlea finds Anne at sixteen, teaching, keeping house, and raising twins. Marilla adopts Davy and Dora, a lively pair.

Schoolroom mishaps, an irate neighbor, and Miss Lavendar's romance fill the chapters. Anne's ideals meet the daily work of duty and patience. Gilbert Blythe's friendship deepens through the year. The book keeps Anne's humor while she steps toward adulthood. The Avonlea books together trace Anne from orphan arrival to teacher, friend, and young woman of purpose.
47513-the-flea:
The Flea is a small science book by Harold Russell, issued at Cambridge in 1913. It belongs to the Cambridge Manuals of Science and Literature. Nine illustrations accompany the text. A drawing of the oriental rat flea serves as frontispiece. The contents run to eight chapters. The first sets out what a flea is. Fleas were little studied until lately, Russell notes.

Later chapters treat the flea's outer and inner build. Mouth parts and sense organs follow. The human flea and other species are then described. Chigoes and their allies get a chapter. Fleas and plague fill the most urgent chapter. Rat fleas and bat fleas close the survey. Appendices list British fleas and their hosts. Advice on collecting fleas ends the book. Russell writes as a fellow of the zoological society.
48003-a-road-book-to-old-chelsea:
A Road-Book to Old Chelsea is a walking guide by Stuart, published in London in 1914. Hugh Rees issued it with a sketch map and five illustrations. A letter of Queen Katharine Parr from Chelsea in 1547 supplies the motto. She wondered how time was so well shortened there. Eight chapters lead the walker road by road. The first chapter takes the bus routes as its starting point.

The guide presumes the stranger arrives by motor bus from Kensington or Piccadilly. It sets him down at Chelsea Town Hall and turns down Oakley Street. The old church gets three chapters: north side, south side, and nave. Church Street, Cheyne Walk, and the road to the Royal Hospital follow. Leigh Hunt's home and Carlyle's Cheyne Row appear on the walk. Side streets and back gardens close the tour.
49608-the-collected-works-in-verse-and-p:
Poems Lyrical and Narrative forms the first volume of the Collected Works in Verse and Prose of William Butler Yeats. The Shakespeare Head Press at Stratford on Avon imprinted the set in MCMVIII. A charcoal drawing of Yeats by John S Sargent faces the title page. The Wind among the Reeds stands first in the contents. Short lyrics fill most of the volume.

Poems include The Hosting of the Sidhe, The Everlasting Voices, and The Moods. The Lover Tells of the Rose in His Heart and The Host of the Air follow. The Song of Wandering Aengus, Into the Twilight, and A Cradle Song show Yeats early range. Later poems include The Cap and Bells, The Valley of the Black Pig, and The Secret Rose. Readers get Yeats in his faery, lovelorn youth, before his harder later voice.
49610-the-collected-works-in-verse-and-p:
Volume three of the Collected Works of William Butler Yeats holds three plays. The Shakespeare Head Press at Stratford-on-Avon imprinted the set in 1908. The Countess Cathleen opens the volume, given to Maud Gonne at its head. The Land of Heart's Desire follows, then The Unicorn from the Stars. Lady Gregory shares the credit for that last play with Yeats himself.

Shemus Rua, his son Teig, and the bard Aleel people the first play. Two demons dressed as merchants come to buy souls in famine times. The Countess Cathleen gives her own soul to free her starving folk. Angel beings, spirits, and faeries crowd the stage of the old tale. The scene lies in Ireland in old times, the playbill states plainly. An appendix and notes on the Countess play close the volume out. Strange things walk the land in those hungry days of the tale.
49611-the-collected-works-in-verse-and-p:
Volume four of Yeats collected works holds three plays and an essay. The Shakespeare Head Press printed it at Stratford-on-Avon in 1908. Contents list The Hour-Glass, Cathleen ni Houlihan, and The Golden Helmet. The Irish Dramatic Movement essay fills most of the volume here.

Appendices give notes on each play and first performance dates. The Hour-Glass, a morality, opens with a Wise Man at his desk. He seeks a passage writ by a beggar on Babylon walls. It speaks of two living countries, visible and invisible to men. A Fool with shears and an outheld hat enters to test the Wise Man.
49613-the-collected-works-in-verse-and-p:
Ideas of Good and Evil is a book of essays by William Butler Yeats, printed at the Shakespeare Head Press in 1908. It forms the sixth volume of his Collected Works in Verse and Prose. Yeats writes on poetry, magic, painting, and the theatre from the standpoint of the Irish literary revival.

Essays ask what popular poetry is, discuss speaking to the psaltery, and defend magic as a serious study. Others treat Shelley's philosophy, William Blake and his illustrations to the Divine Comedy, and the symbolism of poetry. The Celtic element in literature and Ireland and the arts stake his national claims. The opening essay recalls Young Ireland Society debates, when young men honoured Irish poets in English while privately judging most of them poor writers.
49614-the-collected-works-in-verse-and-p:
Volume seven of the Collected Works of William Butler Yeats came from the Shakespeare Head Press in nineteen hundred eight. The volume gathers his tales under The Secret Rose and two short prose works. John Sherman and Dhoya close the book as early stories. A portrait of the poet from a drawing by his father opens the volume.

Yeats told a friend the tales share one theme. That theme is the war of the spirit world with the plain order of life. He drew his signs from Irish legend and old belief. Tales name an outcast on a cross and old men of the dusk. Rosa Alchemica and The Tables of the Law add lore of secret orders. Readers meet the young Yeats in full myth making mood.
50078-the-forlorn-hope-a-tale-of-old-che:
Anna Maria Hall wrote The Forlorn Hope, a story of old Chelsea transcribed from the edition of 1844. The tale is set at Chelsea Hospital, the home of the old soldiers called pensioners. Hall opens on a warm morning in April 1838. Sun shines along the colonnade, and the veterans who hid from winter indoors come out to pace beside the pillars, inhaling the breeze from the Thames.

Hall insists on the men's dignity. The college is theirs, she writes, and they walk its courts in full consciousness of the fact. They fear rheumatism more than they ever feared steel or bullet. Onto this stage she brings her story of the forlorn hope, the name soldiers gave to the first storming party in a siege. The book mixes description of old Chelsea with sentiment, in the manner that made Hall a popular writer of her day.
50484-the-first-days-of-man-as-narrated-:
The First Days of Man is a children's book by Frederic Arnold Kummer, the first volume of a series called The Earth's Story. It was published in New York by Doran in 1922. Its full title promises the story of man's first days, narrated quite simply for young readers.

A preface for parents explains the design. Every child between five and fifteen, Kummer writes, asks constant questions to grasp the basic facts of the world. Those facts took the race centuries to gather, yet the child must take them in within ten or twelve years. Parents, he says, usually dismiss the questions or answer them badly. His book answers them straight. The pictures show Mother Nature sending Heat away and calling for his brother Cold, whose white wings glitter with frost: deep time told as a family tale.
52126-a-dream-of-the-north-sea:
A Dream of the North Sea is a tale of the trawling fleets by James Runciman, author of Among the North Sea Trawlers and Skippers and Shellbacks. James Nisbet and Company published it in London in 1889. Runciman dedicated the book to the Queen, patron of the Mission to Deep Sea Fishermen.

His dedication letter praises the despatch of hospital cruisers to the smacksmen as perhaps the most valuable event of her reign. In wild weather, he writes, when the struggle for life never slackens on the trawling grounds, the great work of the Mission shines like a pharos over the troubled darkness. The story itself opens in a hard gale over a torn sea, with the drift sweeping past and the moon slipping in and out of cloud. Runciman knew the smackmen's world minutely, and wrote to win them help.
52143-fairview-boys-at-lighthouse-cove-o:
Fairview Boys at Lighthouse Cove, or Carried Out to Sea, is a boys' adventure by Frederick Gordon, with copyright in 1914. Gordon wrote a line of Fairview Boys books, from Afloat and Ashore to On a Ranch. They sold at seventy-five cents a volume. Fifteen chapters carry this tale from vacation plans to two mysteries cleared up.

The tale opens on the last day of school, with three boys shouting hurray over the coming summer. Bob Bouncer, the jolly one with mischief in his eyes, trips Sammy in the school yard for a joke. Ahead lie the lighthouse, a dark beacon, a boat, and a storm. The boys are carried out to sea and drift until rescue, as the front picture shows them crowding to a rail.
5221-the-satyricon-volume-04-escape-by-s:
This fourth volume of Petronius's Satyricon, in W. C. Firebaugh's translation, follows Encolpius, Giton, and Eumolpus as they escape by sea. From chapter ninety-nine onward, the fugitives board ship, quarrel, scheme, and face shipwreck and new dangers, carrying the picaresque adventures of the Roman novel into its maritime episodes.

The volume contains only this stretch of the story, not the whole Satyricon, and its bracket code marks later additions and forgeries woven into the text. Readers following the novel in order will find here its sea-borne middle passage, told with the same mix of low comedy and literary parody.
52340-the-salving-of-the-fusi-yama-a-pos:
The Salving of the Fusi Yama, by Westerman, is a sea story. Blackie published it in London, Glasgow, and Bombay. Westerman served as a lieutenant in the air force. Hodgson drew the illustrations for the tale. A submarine duel forms the frontispiece plate. Thirty two chapters make the book. Rocks ahead and to the rescue open it. Signing on and the Fusi Yama follow. A yacht, the Titania, enters at chapter six. Sand-bagged and sunk in collision darken the middle. The wrong island and a mutiny raise the stakes. Von Giespert hears news at chapter twenty two. Eureka, a hurricane, and the duel come late. Exit the Zug and settling accounts close the list.

Westerman's earlier sea tales are listed at the front. Zeebrugge, Jutland, and submarine hunters stand among their titles.
52786-the-open-sea:
The Open Sea, by Edgar Lee Masters, was published in New York in November 1921. Masters is named at the front as the author of Spoon River Anthology. Contents split the book into parts and named sets. Part one, called Brutus, opens at a feast in Rome. Lucilius tells how he let himself be taken in Brutus's place at Philippi. Antony forgave him, and he stayed Antony's friend till death. The scene is told in verse.

Later parts treat Lincoln, John Wilkes Booth, and Boston Corbett. A set called The New Apocrypha retells Bible tales in modern dress. Pieces on Ulysses, Celsus, and Nebuchadnezzar widen the range. A monody on a dead editor and a poem on the Indiana dunes close the book. Masters mixes stage speech and lyric in one restless volume.
5340-further-chronicles-of-avonlea:
L. M. Montgomery's Further Chronicles of Avonlea gathers more tales of the village that was home to Anne of Green Gables. Its stories include Aunt Cynthia, The Materializing of Cecil, David Spencer's Daughter, Jane's Baby, The Failure of Robert Monroe, The Return of Hester. The Little Brown Book of Miss Emily appears among them.

Later tales follow Sara's Way, The Son of Thyra Carewe, The Education of Betty, The Selflessness of Eunice Carr, The Dream-Child, and finally Tannis of the Flats. Readers return to Avonlea's personalities and events in a warm companion volume, told with Montgomery's humour and affection for Prince Edward Island life.
53418-a-summer-on-the-borders-of-the-car:
A Summer on the Borders of the Caribbean Sea, by Dennis Harris, was published at New York in 1860. Burdick issued the book from Nassau Street. George William Curtis wrote the introduction. Letters at the front back Harris and his plan. One endorses Blair's scheme of land in Central America. Free Black families who wished could settle there, in a warmer climate. The writer hopes the efforts prosper. A second letter praises the manuscript's account of San Domingo.

Bryant, who wrote that letter, notes how little was known of the Spanish part of the island. Contents run as letters from the Dominican Republic. The voyage from New York opens the set. Customs officers, the standing army, and fine scenery follow. Harris writes travel with a colonizing plan behind it.
53541-the-law-of-the-sea:
The Law of the Sea is a handbook of the rules that govern ships and shipping, written for students, mariners, and ship operators. The authors are Canfield of the Michigan bar and Dalzell of the District of Columbia bar. The Project Gutenberg text follows the Appleton issue of 1921, in a series on training for the steamship business.

The book sets out the main rules of admiralty law in plain form. Court remarks on cases are printed in smaller type. Two long appendices close the work. The first sums up the navigation laws of the United States, and was written by Brinton. The second prints the Merchant Marine Act of 1920 in full, in thirty-nine sections.
53636-the-martyrdom-of-belgium-official-:
The Martyrdom of Belgium is a state report of war wrongs by the German host. A Belgian board of high law men and state men made the probe. Eye proof of calm folk, wives, and babes slain fills its pages. Names of some who spoke are held back to shield kin in foe lines. The front words vow the proof bears court weight in full.

Belgium had done naught to bring the war on, the report states at once. Each shot by a German in that land broke a sworn pact of faith. That pact held the land free of war by the word of all great states. Report eleven of the board stands in the leaves of this print. A German staff book quote on war use heads the grim front leaf.
53751-secrets-of-earth-and-sea:
Secrets of Earth and Sea, by Ray Lankester, was published in New York in 1920. Macmillan issued the book, with many pictures. A restored Dimetrodon, seven feet long, fronts the volume. Gilmore of the national museum made the model from Texas bones. Its high back crest puzzles the experts, the note says. Twenty two chapters make the book. The earliest picture in the world opens the set. Portraits of mammoths by men who saw them follow. Cave art and Vesuvius in eruption come next.

Later chapters ask what a species is, and watch species in the making. Hybrids and cross-breeding take two chapters. Wheel animalcules and suspended animation fill the middle. The swastika gets three chapters on its origin. Coal, oil boring, and the story of lime-juice and scurvy close the book.
53975-annie-laurie-and-azalea:
Annie Laurie and Azalea is a girls tale by Elia Peattie, out in nineteen thirteen. A Reilly and Britton house of Chicago brought it out that year. Nuyttens drew the cuts for this print of the tale in full. Azalea McBirney runs from a hut on a high shelf of Tennyson mount at start. Red clay road winds down from that hut through white frost blooms.

Smoke shafts rise from hid huts round the vale of Lee in that dawn. Her dam calls, has Jim brought the nags round yet, from the hut door. Jim at the barn bids her stay put, her work is done for the day. Part names run through a trial with no jury and a wet night. The Summers, a sign, a dark tale, and the Disbrows fill mid parts.
54092-a-bundle-of-letters-from-over-the-:
Louise Robinson wrote home a set of letters from a trip over the sea. The book came out in Boston in 1890. She gave it to her mother with warm love. A verse on lost days heads the front pages. The letters run in a clear road order for the reader.

Liverpool, Chester, and Stratford-on-Avon start the tour. London and Paris take long letters of their own. Geneva, Chamouni, and the Mer de Glace thrill the mid part. Berne, Lucerne, and the Rigi close the Swiss leg. Each town gets fresh eyes and a glad pen. Armchair tours of that age had few more bright guides.
55608-the-war-in-the-east-japan-china-an:
Trumbull White, lately a correspondent of the North China Daily News and the Kobe Herald, wrote a full history of the war between Japan and China, copyrighted in 1895. An introduction comes from Julius Kumpei Matumoto of Tokyo. Pictures by Teitoku Morimoto, J C Fireman, and others illustrate the campaigns. A front view shows the battlefield of Ping Yang.

White promises the causes and results of the war, its fights on sea and land, and its victories and defeats. A preliminary account treats the customs, habits, and history of the three peoples involved. Their cities, arts, sciences, amusements, and literature are described. The book sold the recent war to American readers while it was fresh.
55780-the-strife-of-the-sea:
The Strife of the Sea is T Jenkins Hains's book of sea stories, published in New York by the Baker and Taylor Company in October 1903. Hains had written The Wind-Jammers. The stories first appeared in magazines between 1901 and 1903, in Harper's, the Independent, and others.

The first tale belongs to a bird: the old man of Sand Key, an aged pelican the lighthouse keepers know by sight. He fishes alone over the coral ledges of the Gulf Stream, and head keeper Sandy Shackford trusts his judgment on where the fish run. The outcast, the sea dog, and the Cape Horners follow.
