The loggerhead, the white follower, and King Albicore fill the middle, with Johnny Shark and a tragedy of the South Atlantic. In the Wake of the Weather-Cloth closes the book. Fish, birds, ships, and weather share the strife of Hains's title.
56623-quaint-korea:
Louise Jordan Miln wrote a book on Korea printed in London in 1895. Miln had written When We Were Strolling Players in the East. She gives the book to her dear chum and son Crichton. Some pages first ran in London papers such as the Times, the Pall Mall Gazette, and the Daily Chronicle.

A few words about Hamel, an early Dutch visitor, open the book. Curious Korean customs, Soul from the city wall, and Korea's king follow. Two long chapters treat Korean women. Architecture, amusements shared with China and Japan, Korean art, irreligion, and history in a nutshell round out the survey. Miln writes as a warm, sharp eyed guest of a land then little known in Britain.
56832-the-london-burial-grounds-notes-on:
The London Burial Grounds, notes on their history from the earliest times to the present day, by Mrs Basil Holmes, was printed in London by T Fisher Unwin in 1896. A George Herbert verse heads the book, bidding church goers take a turn or two in the churchyard first. A plate shows St Peter, Cornhill, in 1817.

Holmes gives the details of the dwellings of the dead to those who love the living. A Wordsworth line stands with the gift, first learn to love one living man, then may you think upon the dead. The text opens by saying every chronicler of London history who can claim the name of antiquarian has tried to gather the fragmentary evidence. City fans get a grave by grave history.
57255-a-history-of-the-trial-of-castner-:
A member of the Philadelphia bar wrote a history of the Christiana treason trials, issued in Philadelphia in 1852. Castner Hanway and others were tried for treason at Philadelphia in November 1851, after a clash over the return of men who had fled slavery. A long front essay traces the slave question up to the case.

The writer built his tale from the shorthand court report, the dockets of Lancaster and Philadelphia officers, prison records, and the Evening Bulletin. A full report by order of the court had been planned but not yet printed, so the daily papers were all the public had. He also picks out wild flaws in a rival pamphlet sent to Governor Lowe of Maryland.
59012-young-jack-harkaway-fighting-the-p:
Young Jack Harkaway Fighting the Pirates of the Red Sea is a dime novel by Bracebridge Hemyng. Frank Tousey published it in New York on the twenty seventh of August 1897, as number 1334 of the Five Cent Wide Awake Library. The library was issued every Friday at five cents a copy.

The cover scene promises the thrills inside. A cavernous pair of jaws opens wide with a hiss like a locomotive blowing off steam. Harry, seeing his chance, throws two dynamite shells, one after the other, into the snake's mouth. An inset shows young Jack a prisoner on the pirate ship. The first chapter heading announces that Jack's friends grow anxious about him, a mysterious message arrives, and Harry Girdwood meets Hunston. Other Harkaway numbers sent the boy hero to Armenia, Cuba, and against the slave traders of the Soudan.
596-rivers-to-the-sea:
Sara Teasdale gathers poems of city, sea, and war in this volume, in five parts. Spring night, Broadway, a Woolworth tower at night, and a subway station open the book; Indian summer, the sea wind, and the carpenter's shop follow. Later parts hold songs overseas and a closing sequence on Sappho.

Teasdale writes in short, musical lines, with images of fog, light, and water. Love, longing, and the sea recur, never dressed in heavy show. The book marks her growth from love songs to a wider world, where a park at night can hold as much feeling as a lover's face.
59741-my-experiences-at-nan-shan-and-por:
My Experiences at Nan Shan and Port Arthur, with the Fifth East Siberian Rifles, is a war memoir by a Russian general who commanded that regiment. A portrait of the author in uniform fronts the volume. The title names the two great fights of his service in the war with Japan. Nan Shan was the narrow hill line that guarded the road to Port Arthur.

Port Arthur itself, the besieged fortress at the tip of the Liaodong shore, was the prize of that war. A regimental commander who held both fields writes here from inside the Russian line. His account stands among the few full Russian tellings of a siege the whole world watched. Maps and illustrations in the full edition support the tale of trenches, guns, and sorties.
6041-stories-by-english-authors-the-sea:
Sea stories fill this volume, headed by W. Clark Russell's extraordinary adventure of a chief mate. Newspapers of 1876 reprinted a merchantman's log. The ship Hercules of Liverpool reported a volcanic island hove up in the North Atlantic, while chief officer Michael Balfour fell overboard and vanished despite a boat lowered within fifteen minutes.

Sir Walter Besant's Quarantine Island, the Rock Scorpions, the master of the Chrystolite, Petrel and the Black Swan, Grant Allen's Melissa's Tour, and Vanderdecken's message home complete the set. The tales mix wreck, quarantine, and ghostly messages, all told in the salt air of the merchant service.
60424-a-treatise-on-the-art-of-making-go:
Fredrick Accum wrote a treatise on the art of making good and wholesome bread. Accum taught chemistry and its use in the arts and trades. His book came out in London in 1821.

Accum sets out the chemical rules behind sound bread making. He treats wheat, oats, rye, barley, rice and potatoes as bread stuffs. He shows why some grains make light, porous loaves and others do not. Yeast bread and its marks get close study. He also weighs the food value of each kind. Bakers and housewives alike could learn from his plain tests. The title page lists bread corn of many lands as his scope.
61803-tales-of-shipwrecks-and-other-disa:
Thomas Bingley gathered true tales of wrecks and sea disasters into a book for young readers, issued in Boston with engraved art. The tales are told by a kind Uncle Thomas to a ring of boys by the fire. He starts with the wild adventures of Captain Richard Falconer, then moves to famed wrecks one by one.

Later tales cover the mutiny of the Bounty, the loss of the Kent and the Winterton, and the wreck of the French frigate Medusa. The steamers Killarney and Forfarshire bring the set near his own day, with Grace Darling shown rowing out to save lives. The Royal George and the Albion packet close a grim but gripping set.
61952-spawn-of-the-venus-sea:
Spawn of the Venus Sea is a science fiction story by Harry Walton. It ran in Planet Stories in the fall of 1941. A steel cable snaps aboard the Mermaid, a floating cannery on Venus. The net has likely bottomed on the floor of the planet's largest ocean. That sea is called the Deadly Sea because it teems with unpleasant life. Second Mate Stanley Kort holds the deck command.

Kort came from passenger service and lacks the cannery men's training. The crew waits for his orders, yet would act faster under another mate. He knows he is not wanted aboard the ship. A grapple at last brings the lost net back to the surface. The teaser asks what ghastly inhabitant the sea holds. A multiple life monstrosity is promised by the blurb. Sea horror in space drives the short tale.
62150-the-danube-from-the-black-forest-t:
The Danube, from the Black Forest to the Black Sea, was written by F D Millet and published by Harper and Brothers in eighteen ninety-two. Millet illustrated the book with Alfred Parsons. His subject is a canoe journey down Europe's great river, from source to mouth.

The first chapter settles the quarrel over the Danube's true source among the Brigach and the Brege. Millet starts at Donaueschingen, outfitting canoes under swans and spectators. Contents promise weirs, monasteries, crags and castles, and the first spoiled breakfast in camp. Ulm, Blenheim, lumber rafts, and Roman remains follow downstream. Millet was a war artist by trade, and his travel book reads like dispatches from a peaceful campaign. The river itself is the hero.
62483-quarterdeck-and-fok-sle-stories-of:
Quarterdeck and Fok'sle joins two sea stories by Molly Elliot Seawell between one set of covers. W A Wilde and Company of Boston and Chicago copyrighted the book in 1895. 

The quarterdeck story follows young Brydell, a midshipman, and his friendship with Grubb the marine. Brydell fails, fails again, strikes out for himself, and rises through a summer cruise and a question of honor to command of the squadron and a safe return. Admiral Beaumont, a tender-hearted bachelor possessed by a demon of neatness, rules the navy yard where it begins, warring with nursemaids over his grass. The fok'sle story sails on the Diomede with Dicky, through a gallant rescue, an adventure with the redcoats, and the capture of General Prescott. The two tales tell the old navy from the officers' deck and from before the mast.
6255-there-is-sorrow-on-the-sea:
A letter dated York Factory, Hudson's Bay, 23rd September 1747, opens this tale, addressed to a dear cousin Fanny. A year before, on April Fool's Day, the writer left her on the sands at Mablethorpe. He swore she would never see or hear from him again. Coast guards flashed their lights over the sands that night. One stumbled and dropped his lantern, and in the dark the cousins stole apart, she homeward with a whispered blessing.

Parker tells the rest through memory, as the writer, lonely in the far north, lives the bad night over bit by bit and tries to work it out. Distance brings a clearer sight of old games played in the sand and choices that cannot be undone. It is a short, sad tale of parting, told in a letter's voice, where sorrow sits on the sea between two people who once knew each other well.
63404-galatea:
Galatea is a pastoral romance by Miguel de Cervantes in English. It forms volume two of the Complete Works of Cervantes in twelve volumes. Jas Fitzmaurice-Kelly edited the volume for that collected edition. Oelsner and Welford shared the work of translation into English. Gowans and Gray of Glasgow issued it on November 1, 1903.

A publishers' note explains the types used to mark old Spanish quotes. Spelling of names and places follows the rules of the Spanish Academy. Quotes in ancient Spanish keep their first spelling as Cervantes wrote them. Shepherds, song, and crossed loves fill the romance that follows in full. Readers meet the young Cervantes before Don Quixote made him immortal.
63752-frank-merriwell-on-the-boulevards-:
Frank Merriwell on the Boulevards forms one number of the Medal Library. The head pages here are the publisher's own catalogue and praise. That line, issued weekly, sold famous stories for boys by famous authors. Burt Standish wrote the Merriwell tales for the line. Frank, the catalogue says, is a true American lad. He holds a strong determination to do right at any cost. Horatio Alger and Oliver Optic fill the neighbouring numbers. The December list promises Merriwell's Great Scheme among them.

The title itself sets this adventure in Europe, on the boulevards. Astonishing the Europeans is its second promise. Merriwell tours the old world with his usual pluck, sport, and clean record. The catalogue calls Alger the Dickens of juvenile literature in passing. Ten cents bought the number at any newsdealer, the advert claims.
64380-the-fauna-of-the-deep-sea:
Sydney J. Hickson wrote this book on the life of the deep sea, printed at New York in 1894. It is one of a set of books on the new science, set in order by Sir John Lubbock. The author held posts at Cambridge and at Oxford, and was a fellow of Downing College. A plate at its front shows a fish of the deep, Stomias boa, at half its true size. It was drawn up from a depth of near two miles of sea.

The list of parts gives the plan of the work. A short tale of the probes of the deep stands first. Then come the state of the abyss as to heat, light, and weight of sea. A part treats of the tie of the deep zone to the rest of life, and of the birth of its stock.
64643-maru-a-dream-of-the-sea:
Henry De Vere Stacpoole wrote Maru, a dream of the sea. Stacpoole was known for The Blue Lagoon and The Pearl Fishers. His tale is set on Tokahoe, a little South Sea island where the narrator visits a trader named Lygon. The night smells of vanilla and frangipani, rollers sound on the reef, and men spear fish by torchlight in the reef pools.

The island once drew ships for sandalwood. Now it yields only copra, barely enough for one trader. The last trader died there of drink, and his ghost is said to walk the beach on moonlit nights. Lygon turns the talk to ghosts: do you believe in them? The narrator answers with another question, and the two men debate the beliefs of Polynesians, Japanese, and Irishmen. Stacpoole lets the ghost talk open a story steeped in lagoon light, trade, and island superstition.
64789-bratton-s-idea:
Bratton's Idea is a short story by Manly Wade Wellman, first printed in the magazine Comet in December nineteen forty, as its note states. Old Bratton is janitor at a Hollywood radio station studio in the tale. He is gaunt and dark of mood, and he has no wish to act in films at all. A director once offered him a screen test on the street.

Bratton refused with loud anger when he heard the part was a mad scientist. The joke of the opening is that he is touchy on that point because he is one. From that setup Wellman builds a tale that mixes studio comedy with a wild invention. The copyright note says no renewal of the magazine copyright was found.
64861-the-love-of-azalea:
Onoto Watanna wrote The Love of Azalea, for Dodd, Mead in 1904. Rights were held that year by Winifred Babcock and by the house. Foudji drew the pictures for the October book. Watanna had written A Japanese Nightingale and The Heart of Hyacinth. A front plate shows a little figure waiting at a garden gate.

He had come quite close to the gate before he perceived her, it says. Other plates give the tale in glimpses. This is the American way, he says, stooping to kiss her, in one. She throws her tablets toward a little river in another plate. My house awaits your coming, and I have sworn to possess you, says a third. Night shadows cover her in a fourth plate. A sword flashes upward in the last of the pictured scenes. Watanna gives a romance of Japan and an American love.
653-the-chimes-a-goblin-story-of-some-be:
Charles Dickens writes a New Year goblin tale in this Christmas book, where bells ring an old year out and a new year in. The story opens with a warning that few people would care to sleep in a church at night, alone, while the wind moans round the pillars and tries the doors. Toby Veck, a poor porter, hears the chimes and meets their spirits.

Dickens writes with warm, urgent prose, full of winter wind, organ notes, and moral fire. The tale argues that the poor deserve hope, not blame. It endures as a beloved Christmas story, where bells teach a man to trust the future he feared.
6622-legends-that-every-child-should-kno:
Hamilton Wright Mabie edits a set of great legends for young people, with pictures by Blanche Ostertag and Guy, Earl of Warwick, on the cover. His introduction starts with words themselves, noting how they grew slowly from human need, not made to order like parts of a machine. That slow growth, he says, shows the brotherhood of men.

The legends that follow span times and lands, chosen for wonder, courage, and moral force. Mabie keeps the telling clear for young readers, without dulling the tales. Legends That Every Child Should Know is a solid, old-style gift book, made to start a child on the great stories of the world.
66922-an-account-of-two-voyages-to-new-e:
Two Voyages to New-England, by John Josselyn, is dated 1674 here. Veazie reprinted it at Boston in 1865. Only two hundred and fifty copies were printed, in small quarto. The reprint keeps the old spelling and italics exactly. Josselyn sailed in 1638 and again in 1663. A publisher's preface ties the book to his Rarities of 1672. That work gives his family history, the preface says. A chart from the Harleian manuscripts is added here, furnished by Drake. The first voyage came eight years after Boston was settled.

Josselyn travelled as a gentleman observer, the preface implies. His account preserves the look of a colony still new. Plants, beasts, and the manners of the settlers fill such early narratives. The 1865 editor prized the book as a record of first things in New England.
67259-the-big-idea:
Ray Cummings opens a coal-country tale at the Fallon Brothers Mine near Menchon, Pennsylvania. Jimmy Rand lines up at dawn with men in black, greasy mine clothes. They shuffle past the power-house toward the gate-house window. There each man gives his number for the great book.

Jimmy is twenty-two and one of the best loaders on the books. Metal tags on each car bear the loader's number, and the records prove his tonnage. His father and grandfather mined before him. He left school at fifteen to drive the mules. This April day he stops work at noon. He and Anne have planned a long walk together. Cummings, later famed for science tales, grounds this one in pit work and young love.
67613-the-story-of-chalmers-of-new-guine:
Janet Harvey Kelman wrote The Story of Chalmers of New Guinea, with pictures by Heath Robinson. Jack at London and Dutton at New York put out the book. James Chalmers was born in a little town in the West Highlands of Scotland. He was the son of a stonemason, and his home was a humble one. A preface tells how children once begged a Scotchwoman to tell on with her tales.

Chalmers himself knew how to answer that call, the preface says. He wrote of Kone and Aveo, of wild Pacific waves and wilder island men. Contents run from boyhood in Argyll to the mission ship John Williams. Rarotonga, the death of Bocasi, and the spirits of the height follow. War-canoes, the barrier reef, and the Fly River fill the later chapters. Kelman gives the missionary's brave life for young readers.
67614-the-boy-s-book-of-the-sea:
The Boy's Book of the Sea is an adventure collection by Eric Wood, printed at New York with four colour plates and twelve other illustrations. Wood also wrote The Boy's Book of Heroes. The first section compares naval warfare old and new, through the stories of Trafalgar and the Bight of Heligoland.

The men who discovered the world come next: the men who ventured on unknown seas and laid the foundations of nations and commerce. Some early buccaneers follow, hunters of wild animals turned scourers of the seas. Morgan, buccaneer and governor, gets his own tale: a born leader who later forsook his profession for the safer one of Governor of Jamaica. Under the Jolly Roger continues the pirate matter. A prefatory note says we need not go to fiction for adventures as thrilling as Robinson Crusoe's: here is a tale of shipwrecked and castaway mariners.
6847-cytherea:
Joseph Hergesheimer opens Cytherea with Lee Randon on a shorn hill, playing what he thinks is his last golf of the year. Country spreads in sere tones to a grey horizon, a stream holds a cold glimmer in frost-killed grass, and wind scatters soft crystals of snow. Alone, with no boy to carry clubs, Lee recalls a refusal by Peyton Morris, who married his niece and is fourteen years younger.

At worse than forty-five, Lee feels age and desire pull against each other, and a woman named Cytherea enters his life. Hergesheimer writes with a novelist's eye for mood and manners. Cytherea is a polished, adult novel of love, age, and longing in the 1920s.
68480-the-naval-cadet-a-story-of-adventu:
Boy’s adventure fiction drives The Naval Cadet, a story of adventure on land and sea by Dr Gordon Stables. The book came out from Blackie and Son of London, Glasgow, and Bombay. Pictures by William Rainey fill the volume. Chapter heads promise storms, wild lands, and war at sea.

The tale begins with the hermit of Kilmara and a night that came before its time. A storm and the story of the Skye clearings follow in the early chapters. The hero is lost in a Highland mist and searches for adventure. Later chapters put him on board the gunboat Rattler. War ahead, the city of blood, and the capture of Benin mark the turn to Africa. The book ends with a welcome back to Skye and life on the Osprey.
69554-the-boy-explorers-in-darkest-new-g:
Warren Miller wrote a boys adventure printed at New York and London in 1921, with illustrations by Frank Spradling. All the generous instincts of youth rose up in him at the sight, the frontispiece cries. Without thinking further he raised his pistol and fired at the nearest pygmy. Aru opens the chapters, then into the jungle and pirate visitations.

Nicky encounters a death adder, the Outanatas, and the curator's air pistol follow. Cassowary camp, pygmy land, and the fight at the crater fill the middle. Cinnabar mountain, the flight to the coast, and the escape to Aru close the road. I see it, exclaimed Nicky, peering through his glasses. It's developing out like a camera plate, high jungly mountains that seem to be floating in the clouds. Miller, a museum man who knew the South Seas, sends his boys where few white men had walked.
69735-new-nick-carter-weekly-no-197-the-:
Number 197 of the New Nick Carter Weekly appeared on October 6, 1900, priced at five cents. Street and Smith of New York issued the weekly, and the story is credited simply to the author of Nick Carter. The tale, The Little Glass Vial, opens with the famous detective back in his office on a snowy evening.

A telegram from Boston sends Carter north at once. On his way to a cab the next morning, he spots a small glass vial half buried in the snow and pockets it. That chance find points toward the case promised in the subtitle, in which a blackmailer is brought to bay. The story shows the fast, plain style that made the Nick Carter weeklies a staple of cheap American fiction.
6993-the-lord-of-the-sea:
M P Shiel's Lord of the Sea runs through forty seven chapters of exodus, hunting crops, meteors, guns, and ships of steel. Early chapters name the Fez, a swoon, Reid's, Pearson's Weekly, and the elm, before Hogarth's guns and Isaac set a harder note. Wroxham Broad, the rose, and a priest lead to a monsignor, a rope, old Tom's letter, and chloroform, with a great bell and an infirmary.

Later chapters bring the deep, a meteorite seen by Frankl, church building, a bag of light, and a claim of priority. Hammers, wonder, reefs of steel, the Kaiser, and a cup of trembling precede the Boodah and the battleships, the straits, and a manifesto. A wedding, a visit, a land bill, a regency, and Estrella the prophetess close a vast romantic saga.
70982-vagabonds-of-the-sea:
Rene Milan's Vagabonds of the Sea, the campaign of a French cruiser, was translated by Randolph Bourne. Dutton published it at New York in 1919. Three parts divide the book: the awakening of the cruiser, in the Adriatic Sea, and in the Ionian Sea. The narrative opens at the end of July 1914. Milan rides the last normally scheduled express from Paris to Toulon, full of naval officers recalled from leave.

The call of the country sends them toward the sea, the field of battle they have chosen. Milan knows the decisive duel will be fought in Flanders or the Vosges, yet the navy's Mediterranean effort will not be useless. The train passes Dijon, Lyons, Valence, and Marseilles through a France gone erect and watchful. Sentinels guard every nerve-center of mobilization. The officers' one fear is arriving too late for the battle. Bourne's translation keeps the memoir's lyrical, patriotic voice.
71230-desert-and-water-gardens-of-the-re:
Cyril Crossland, marine biologist to the Sudan Government, wrote Desert and Water Gardens of the Red Sea, issued by Cambridge University Press in 1913. The book gives an account of the natives and the shore formations of the coast. Its first plate maps the coast of the Anglo Egyptian Sudan, with sandstone hills, small islands, fringing reefs, and barrier reefs drawn in, and depths marked in fathoms.

Crossland adds a note that the book has a moral he never meant: real romance and beauty lie in things as they are. He holds that the man of science may find a truer worship in fact than the dreamer finds in idols of his own fancy. The dedication thanks his wife for bearing a large share of his exile.
71549-prentice-mulford-s-story-life-by-l:
Prentice Mulford's Story, Life by Land and Sea, is a memoir issued at New York in eighteen eighty nine. It belongs to a line called the White Cross Library. Contents run to thirty six chapters. The first tells of shadows of coming events, the second of going to sea. Early chapters treat getting sea legs and a mutiny amid much water.

San Francisco in eighteen fifty six takes a chapter, then the author as a sea cook. Whaling in a bay and a spell at the gold mines follow. Town tales, a California school, and life on a jury fill the middle. Editing against writing and running for office come near the end. The first California report he heard came from an old sea captain, he says. That captain had been captured by a pirate and showed his bullet scars.
71837-the-zoological-gardens-of-europe-t:
The Zoological Gardens of Europe, their history and chief features, by C V A Peel, was printed in London by F E Robinson and Company. Peel had written Somaliland and Wild Sport in the Outer Hebrides. A plate shows a group of performing animals at Carl Hagenbeck menagerie.

Ads at the front praise Peel Somaliland as a capital book of sport and travel, with Edmund Caldwell drawings of wild animal life. The Spectator said his two hunting trips would make many a man mouth water. The Saturday Review called it a pleasant book of sport, natural history, and adventure. The zoo book then turns from the wild field to the caged gardens of Europe, their past and their chief sights. Beast fans get a hunter view of the great menageries.
71880-pinocchio-under-the-sea:
Carolyn M Della Chiesa turned this Pinocchio tale into English from the Italian book Il Segreto di Pinocchio by Mongiardini-Rembadi. John W Davis edited the text, and Florence R Abel Wilde drew the art. The Macmillan Company of New York issued it in September 1913. A front plate shows Pinocchio looking at himself in the water.

The wooden boy recalls his past, then talks with a dolphin and takes a lesson in good manners. He rides a horse under the sea and pays a call on Beluga, the whale. Dinner with a white host and more sea trips fill the middle chapters. The tale sends the famed puppet into a new world of waves and sea beasts.
72051-the-pearl-divers-and-crusoes-of-th:
The Pearl Divers and Crusoes of the Sargasso Sea, by Gordon Stables, is a sea tale for boys. Stables served as a surgeon in the Royal Navy. He gives the book to his cousin Nellie. A word to his boy readers opens the story. His own children, he says, always ask if his tales are all true. No tale is all true, he answers, or it would not be a story. Yet he has knocked about the world and made many notes.

Most of his people, he claims, had real models. Antonio Garcia, with his glass eye, was met at Bombay. Davie Drake and Barclay Stuart stand for bold English boys he knew. A verse from Longfellow on graves beneath the sea heads the book.
73510-the-adventures-of-captain-o-shea:
The Adventures of Captain O'Shea, by Ralph Paine, was published in New York in September 1913. Front ads list Paine's campus and sea tales, from The Stroke Oar to A Cadet of the Black Star Line. Four long parts make up the book: The Castaways, The King of Trinadaro, a liner tale, and The Branded Man.

The Castaways opens in the days when Cubans under Gomez and Maceo fought Spain. Gun-running from American ports was brisk, and the Cuban Junta in New York needed bold seamen who could keep eyes open and mouths shut. Young Captain O'Shea had already jolted one president off his perch in Haiti and fired the coat-tails of another in Honduras. Paine writes fast, salty adventure.
75238-the-motion-picture-chums-new-idea:
The Motion Picture Chums' New Idea, or The First Educational Photo Playhouse, is a boys' novel by Victor Appleton. Grosset and Dunlap published it, with copyright in 1914. Appleton also wrote the Tom Swift series and the Moving Picture Boys. The frontispiece shows the start of a struggle between a man and Pep, one of the chums. The series list shows this as the fifth Motion Picture Chums volume.

The contents open with Something New, then an absent-minded visitor and a missing satchel. A railroad adventure follows in the early chapters, to judge by the list preserved in the copy. The chums are boys running a small moving-picture house in the pioneering days of film. Their new idea, promised by the subtitle, is an educational photo playhouse.
75608-the-city-in-the-sea:
De Vere Stacpoole's City in the Sea was published by Doran at New York in 1925, by the author of The Blue Lagoon. Robert Lestrange opens the tale, leaving his rooms in Cadogan Street one bright September morning. A map fronts the book: the island of Hyalos, from a sketch made on board the Lorna Doone, with soundings inside and outside the reefs. The contents promise a purchase of that yacht, deep sea gear, and a crew of blind men.

Martia and her secret stand at the center of the plot. Chapters run from London to Genoa, then towards Hyalos and its houses, a terrible danger, and the dumping of the Victory. A boat from Aegina, a man of war, and the customs all enter the later action. Thirty-four chapters carry the adventure back west to London and the end.
75741-on-both-sides-of-the-sea:
On Both Sides of the Sea, a story of the Commonwealth and the Restoration, is a sequel to The Draytons and the Davenants, by the author of Chronicles of the Schonberg-Cotta Family. The New York edition carries a card from the author stating which American editions bear her sanction. Chapters swap between Olive's recollections, Lettice's diary, and notes by Magdalene Antony.

Olive recalls the day London darkened on January 30, 1649, a day like none since England was. She finds it hard to part feeling from fact in such hours. Her memory holds a hushed, sunless city in black and white: the draped scaffold, the frosty ground, and the palace asleep by a mute, ice-bound river. Faith and family carry the tale.
76536-the-loss-of-the-swansea:
The Loss of the Swansea is a story of the Florida coast by W Alden. Drawings by Small dress the boys tale of wreck and wild shores. Past books by the hand tell of a boy named Jimmy Brown. Rights date the work to the year eighteen eighty nine.

Mutiny opens the tale, then the crew is cast ashore on a wild coast. A cave, a marooned stretch, and a maze of swamp mark the road south. Old Bills raid and the deep grass swamps raise the stakes for the boys. Held as guests of foes, they win back to blue water at last. The ship of the title meets its end in the last part of all.
76672-a-brief-narrative-of-the-life-of-m:
A Brief Narrative of the Life of Mrs Adele Jewel is the self tale of a wife who was deaf and dumb. It was put out in eighteen sixty-nine at a steam press in a school town. She gives the small sketch of her life as a means of keep, in hope of friends and grace. A line of the old book on like for like heads the work.

The front note tells of her youth as a bright girl of ten years, the sole child of fond kin. All that could give her joy was hers, to mend the loss fate had dealt her. Past a move west the friend lost sight of her past long years. They met once more to find her grown fair and skilled, yet sunk in grief. Sick took one eye, death took her father, and want took their home.
769-the-book-of-tea:
Kakuzo Okakura wrote this short book on tea as an art of life in Japan. He traces tea from its origins in China to the Japanese tea ceremony, where a bowl of tea becomes a rite of harmony, respect, and quiet beauty. The chapters move from the history of the leaf to the cult of tea and its place in art.

Okakura argues that the West, with its noise and haste, has much to learn from the tea room's calm. His prose is lyrical and aphoristic, full of contrasts between East and West. The book, first written in English, remains a beloved introduction to Japanese aesthetics, and to the idea that small acts can hold deep meaning.
76960-the-corsair-or-the-little-fairy-at:
The Corsair, or The Little Fairy at the Bottom of the Sea, is a stage piece. William Brough wrote it as a Christmas burlesque and pantomime in verse. Samuel French issued it in the Minor Drama acting edition at New York. It spoofs the ballet Le Corsaire for holiday crowds at the theatre.

Conrad the corsair is drawn gloomy, misanthropic, ironical, and Byronical in the cast list. Seyd Pasha, a terrible Turk, and his major domo Syng Smaul join him. Medora, a Grecian maiden, and Gulnare of the harem fill the love plot. Submarina rules the deep as fairy guardian and ocean police chief there. Costumes, entrances, exits, and stage business are spelled out for actors.
77774-by-the-deep-sea:
By the Deep Sea is a seashore natural history by Edward Step, printed in London by Jarrold in 1896. The third edition is the text here. Its subtitle promises a popular introduction to the wild life of the British shores. 122 illustrations come from Gosse, Pearce, and Mabel Step. A Byron verse stands at the front: there is a rapture on the lonely shore.

The contents, in 20 chapters, work down the shore. The sea and its shores open the book, then low life, sponges, and zoophytes. Jelly-fishes, anemones, and sea-stars with urchins follow. Worms, crabs and lobsters, and shrimps and prawns fill the middle. Barnacles, shell-fish, snails, and cuttles close the survey. The sea, Step writes, is the very fountain and reservoir of the life of this globe, as the heart is to man. His book made a generation of holiday rock-poolers.
7784-from-the-lips-of-the-sea:
Clinton Scollard's From the Lips of the Sea gathers sea lyrics that urge the reader to sit alone by the shore and listen. The opening sonnet promises Eddas of old kings, runes of forgotten lore, and solemn secrets of infinity trembling on the sea's dark lips, for those who hearken well.

Contents move from sea marvels, mist, and dirge for a sailor to bagpipes at sea, wild geese, a sea change, and night song by the water. Dawn, lilac seas, summer shores, and moonrise follow in turn. It is a book of music and mood, where the ocean speaks in rhythm and image.
7831-when-london-burned-a-story-of-resto:
G. A. Henty's When London Burned, a story of Restoration times and the Great Fire, defends Charles II's reign against a charge of mere disgrace. Court waste and vice, he admits, helped doom the Stuarts, yet trade and wealth grew fast, and sailors under York, Albemarle, Rupert, and Sandwich fought as bravely as under Blake.

Their wins took naval and commercial lead from Holland, even as plague and fire struck London hard. Through a boy's eyes amid court, plague, and flame, Henty tells how a battered nation still advanced, and how ordinary courage met disaster in the streets of a burning capital.
78708-the-burning-of-chelsea:
Burning of Chelsea is a record of a great fire by Walter Merriam Pratt. Sampson Publishing of Boston issued it in June of the year 1908. Numerous illustrations from original photographs fill the fire record. Pratt dedicates it to officers and men of the Eighth Company, Coast Artillery. He served with them on provost guard in Chelsea after the fire.

Contents run from historical Chelsea and statistics of the fire to its start. Beyond control, under control, and night among the ruins follow in order. Day dawns upon the ruins, the firemen, and the militia fill later chapters. Expressions of sympathy and the relief work close the main account. A front view shows the burning city from Powderhorn Hill in smoke.
7957-out-of-the-fog-a-story-of-the-sea:
C. K. Ober wrote this short sea story with a foreword by Dr Wilfred T. Grenfell, who had spent twenty years working along the Labrador coast. Grenfell introduces the tale as a record worth preserving, tied to his own efforts to improve charts and sailing directions for those dangerous waters. The narrative belongs to the world of coastal boats, fog, and hard weather off Labrador.

The story is brief and direct, told as a seaman's experience rather than a grand adventure. Its value lies in its setting: a coast where fog could strand a crew and where Grenfell's mission work tried to bring help. Readers who enjoy true-seeming tales of the sea will find a compact, atmospheric account of life and risk on the North Atlantic shore.
7974-the-pilot-a-tale-of-the-sea:
James Fenimore Cooper wrote this sea tale around a mysterious pilot who guides American ships along a hostile coast during the Revolutionary War. Dedicated to his naval friend William Branford Shubrick, the novel draws on Cooper's own seafaring experience and on the daring raids of John Paul Jones, whose figure stands behind the pilot. Storms, chases, and shore parties drive the action.

Cooper, who had already proved himself on land with the Leatherstocking tales, here proved he could write the sea with equal force. The pilot himself, secretive and commanding, remains one of his most memorable creations. Readers who enjoy naval adventure will find the book a founding example of the genre in American literature.
8255-the-world-english-bible-web-hosea:
Hosea was a prophet in the northern kingdom of Israel in the eighth century before Christ, and his book turns his own marriage into a parable. At God's command he married a woman who was unfaithful to him. He used that broken marriage to picture Israel's unfaithfulness, a people chasing other gods while still claiming God's love. The pain in the book is personal as well as prophetic.

Short oracles of judgment alternate with sudden outbursts of tenderness, as God refuses to give up the people he calls his child. Hosea's images of a husband, a father, and a farmer have shaped how later writers speak of love betrayed and renewed. It is a short book, fierce and heartbroken in equal measure.
8396-the-gentleman-a-romance-of-the-sea:
Alfred Ollivant, author of Bob, Son of Battle, sets this sea romance in July 1805, in the age of Nelson. Contents open with the death of Black Diamond. They follow the man on the grey, the galloping gent, the gunner of the sloop, and old Ding-Dong, through a tale of the navy in wartime. The gentleman of the title moves through a world of ships, guns, and honor.

Ollivant writes for readers who love sea stories with strong characters and period color. The 1908 novel belongs to the tradition of naval romance, where duty and daring test a man. Readers get action at sea and a hero shaped by the navy he serves, in a story told with warmth for its service.
9826-homeward-bound-or-the-chase-a-tale-:
James Fenimore Cooper wrote Homeward Bound, or The Chase, a tale of the sea and of American society. His preface explains the plan: fresh arrivals from Europe, meeting America at Sandy Hook, would see the nation's traits with sharper eyes. The tale was to open at the country's threshold and follow the travellers inward. Cooper, famed for sea and frontier tales, steers this voyage himself.

The chase of the title drives the plot across the Atlantic, as shipboard folk debate manners, politics, and home. Cooper writes with a sailor's knowledge and a critic's eye. A reader gets a lively Cooper novel, where a sea voyage becomes a mirror of young America.
994-riders-to-the-sea:
On a bare island off the west coast of Ireland, an old mother waits for news of her sons, who make their living from the sea. One by one the waves have taken them, and now her last two boys ride out to face the same tide. J. M. Synge built this short play from the speech and life of the Aran islanders.

Maurya, the mother, moves from dread to a grim calm as each loss lands, and her final words accept what no prayer could change. The sea itself acts as a force no one can bargain with. In under an hour of stage time, the play packs grief, faith, and the hard terms of island life.
a-dream-of-the-north-sea: James Runciman dreams of the North Sea in two books of storm and trial. The first book follows a dreamer through breeze, second gale, near disaster, and the mission hall after storms. The second book turns to January in the North Sea, a crucial test, and a plotter's denouement. Runciman, author of books on trawlers and skippers, writes of fishermen with sympathy.
a-maid-of-the-silver-sea: John Oxenham tells of a maid of the silver sea named Nance. Chapters tell how two lay in a cleft, how Nance came to be herself, and how a new mine captain came. Gard makes new acquaintances, fights gales, and follows Tom through the story. Oxenham writes a Cornish romance of sea, mine, and love.
a-message-from-the-sea:
Charles Dickens opens his Christmas tale in a Cornish fishing village built straight up a cliff, where Captain Jorgan marvels at the steep streets. A bottle found at sea carries a message that stirs old grief in the village. The story appeared in the Christmas Stories collection, in the 1894 Chapman and Hall edition used here.

Chapters named The Village, The Money, and The Restitution carry the plot from discovery to repayment of a long-hidden wrong. Dickens wrote the tale with Wilkie Collins for a Christmas number, and it mixes sea weather, village talk, and a family secret. It reads as a warm, compact piece of holiday storytelling.
a-voyage-to-the-south-sea: William Bligh voyages to the South Sea in this 1792 account, undertaken by command of the King to convey the bread-fruit tree to the West Indies in the Bounty. The volume includes the mutiny on board. It follows the subsequent voyage of part of the crew in the ship's boat from Tofoa to Timor. The advertisement explains that the mutiny narrative appeared first to give early information, and this fuller voyage now supplies the preceding part of the story.
adventures-in-new-guinea: James Chalmers, a missionary based at Port Moresby, recounts travel and work among the peoples of New Guinea in the late nineteenth century. He describes villages, canoes, and first meetings, along with the risks of coastal journeys and the slow building of trust. The book combines adventure narrative with a missionary's record of a region then little known to readers in Britain.
an-old-town-by-the-sea:
Thomas Bailey Aldrich writes about Portsmouth, New Hampshire, the old seaport where he was a boy. He opens with a poem to the Piscataqua River, longing for its shores from a city desk. The contents promise Captain John Smith, strolls about town, old Strawberry Bank, and personal reminiscences.

Aldrich walks the reader past wharves, gardens, and old houses, pausing for the sailors, merchants, and odd characters who filled them. He tells the town's story from the first sassafras hunters of 1603 onward, in graceful, unhurried prose. The book is both a small history and a love letter, preserving a New England port as steam and rail were changing it.
anne-of-avonlea:
Lucy Maud Montgomery's sequel follows Anne Shirley at sixteen, now the schoolteacher of Avonlea, the Prince Edward Island village where she grew up. The contents list thirty chapters. Anne helps found a village improvement society, teaches a classroom of strong personalities, and looks after neighbors old and young with her usual mix of energy and daydreaming.

Marilla, her guardian, takes in young twins Davy and Dora, and Davy's mischief drives much of the comedy. Anne also coaxes along the shy romance of Miss Lavendar, a lonely woman in a stone house, whose lost love returns by the final chapters. The book ends with a wedding at that house and Anne ready for college. It is gentler and more communal than the first Anne book.
ballads-of-lost-haven-a-book-of-the-sea:
Bliss Carman published this book of sea ballads with Lamson, Wolffe and Company of Boston in 1897. Carman, a New Brunswick poet, had already won notice with Low Tide on Grand Pré and the Vagabondia songs. Lost Haven is his imagined fishing port, and its wrecks, ghosts, and drowned lovers fill the verse.

A Son of the Sea and The Gravedigger lead off, then The Yule Guest, where a voice in the snow answers a monkish questioner with news of a goblin maid. The Marring of Malyn, The Nancy's Pride, and Arnold, Master of the Scud follow, with The King of Ys, The Kelpie Riders, and The Ships of St. John. Carman writes salt-water Romanticism: fog, bells, and lost crews, in ballad stanzas built to be chanted.
britannica-1911-abu-klea:
Abu Klea was a halting-place for caravans in the Bayuda Desert of the Anglo-Egyptian Sudan, on the road from Merawi to Metemma. The Britannica entry is brief because the place matters chiefly for two days of fighting in January 1885. A British force marching to relieve General Gordon at Khartum was attacked there by Mahdist forces.

Fighting on the seventeenth was beaten off, and a second attack two days later, nearer Metemma, also failed. Among the dead was Colonel F. G. Burnaby, killed on the first day. Sir Herbert Stewart, who commanded the British force, was mortally wounded on the nineteenth. The entry points readers to the wider history of the Egyptian campaigns.
britannica-1911-achaea:
Achaea was a district on the northern coast of the Peloponnese, a narrow strip of fertile land between mountains and the Corinthian Gulf. Tradition said the Achaeans were driven back into this region by the Dorian invaders of Greece. Herodotus names its twelve cities, which met as a religious confederacy at Helice. In Roman times the name Achaea was stretched to cover nearly the whole of Greece.

Later centuries changed its masters. After the Latin conquest of the Eastern Empire, Achaea became a Latin principality under William de Champlitte, surviving in pieces until 1430. The Turks conquered it with the rest of the Morea in 1460. The entry ends with the modern coast, given up to growing currants shipped from Patras.
britannica-1911-albert-lea:
Albert Lea, a city in Minnesota, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the county-seat of Freeborn county, about ninety-seven miles south of St Paul. Its people grew from 3,305 in 1890 to 6,192 in 1910, many of them Norwegian and Danish immigrants. Five railway companies served the city, an unusual web for a town of its size.

Set attractively between Fountain Lake and Albert Lea Lake, the city drew summer visitors. It held a public library, the county court house, Albert Lea College for women, and Luther Academy. Railways and manufacturing drove its economy, with grain elevators, foundries, machine shops, and brickyards. Factories made tiles, carriages, wagons, flour, corsets, refrigerators, and woollen goods. Large dairy interests centred there too, with many creameries across the county, and artesian wells supplied water of unusual excellence.
britannica-1911-alciati-andrea:
Andrea Alciati (1492–1550), an Italian lawyer born at Alzano near Milan in January 1492, changed how men read Roman law. He expounded the laws with great skill in letters. Among the first of his kind, he read the civil law through the past, the tongues, and the books of the ancient world. Fresh research took the place of the slavish glosses of the old commentators in his work.

Many books on law came from his pen, and notes on Tacitus, the Roman historian, besides. His Emblems, a set of moral sayings in Latin verse, won wide praise and passed into French, Italian, and Spanish, carrying his name far past the law schools. His history of Milan, Rerum Patriae, came out after his death, at Milan in 1625, in four books. He died at Pavia in 1550.
britannica-1911-apamea:
Apamea, in the 1911 Britannica, is a place entry that covers four towns of western Asia under one name. The first was a treasure city and stud depot of the Seleucid kings in the Orontes valley. Seleucus Nicator named it for his wife Apama. Wrecked by Chosroes in the 7th century and by a quake in 1152, it kept its weight down to Crusade times.

The second Apamea, in Phrygia, stood where the Marsyas joins the Maeander. It grew into a seat of Seleucid power and a hub of trade and mixed Greek, Roman, and Jewish life. Antiochus the Great mustered there the army he led against Rome, and peace was signed there two years later. The town stayed a great trade centre for ages, then fell as routes shifted to Constantinople. Short notes add towns on the Euphrates and in Bithynia.
britannica-1911-aranda-pedro-pablo-abarc:
Pedro Pablo Abarca de Bolea, count of Aranda (1719–1798), was a Spanish minister and general. He was born at Siétamo castle near Huesca. His Aragonese family was very ancient. He never forgot his noble rank. Bologna and Parma educated him partly. He entered the army in 1740. His father's regiment gave him a captaincy. His father's death made him colonel.

He served in the Italian campaigns. The War of the Austrian Succession was his school. He married into the Hijar ducal family in 1749. Travel then broadened his experience greatly. Frederick the Great's camp impressed him deeply. He introduced Prussian drill into Spain afterwards. Diplomatic service in Portugal followed briefly. His temper clashed with Pombal there. Madrid recalled him to high office. He became director-general of artillery. The entry follows his ministry and fall.
britannica-1911-archelaus-king-of-judaea:
Archelaus was a king of Judaea. He was Herod the Great's son. Herod's last will gave him the kingdom. An earlier will had favoured his brother Antipas. The army proclaimed him king immediately. He declined the title pending Augustus's approval. He travelled to Rome to submit his claim. Before leaving, he crushed a Pharisee sedition. Nearly 3,000 Pharisees died in that cruelty.

Antipas opposed him at Rome strongly. Many Jews feared his cruelty there. Augustus allotted him the greater kingdom part. Judaea, Samaria, and Ituraea composed it. His title was ethnarch, not king. He married Glaphyra, his brother Alexander's widow. Her second husband Juba still lived then. That marriage violated Mosaic law openly. Continued cruelty provoked Jewish complaints. Augustus deposed him in A.D. 7. Banishment to Vienne followed. Matthew's gospel mentions him briefly.
britannica-1911-ardea:
Ardea, an old town of Latium in Italy, is the subject of a study in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stood a short way in from the south-west coast. Its port lay at the mouth of a small stream, and a road ran to it from Rome. Tales give its founding to a son of Odysseus, or to Danae, mother of Perseus.

The town was the seat of Turnus, the foe of Aeneas in the old tale. Rome took it in time, and it stood among the thirty towns of the Latin league. It was made a Latin colony in 442 before Christ. The entry tells of its revolts, its sack by the Samnites, and its slow fall in the days of the empire. Ill air from the low land drove that fall. The old town wall of squared stone still guards the site.
britannica-1911-azalea:
Azalea is a genus of prized hardy and greenhouse plants of the heath family, barely separable in botany from Rhododendron. The fine garden varieties were bred from a few originals native to the hills of China and Japan, Asia Minor, and the United States. Few plants match them as indoor decoration.

Growers raise azaleas by grafting half-ripened shoots onto stronger kinds in moist heat, and large plain plants can be grafted over with choicer sorts. They want rich, fibrous peat soil with sand, made firm so it holds no excess water, and repotting a few weeks after bloom ends. Young plants are pinched back for shape; leggy ones are cut before growth starts. Thrips and red spider are their great pests. The entry closes by listing noted species, from the tall Pennsylvania kind to the Indian azalea.
britannica-1911-ballou-hosea:
Hosea Ballou (1771–1852) was an American Universalist clergyman, born in Richmond, New Hampshire, on 30 April 1771. Son of a Baptist minister and self-taught, he turned to preaching early, became a Universalist in 1789, and took a congregation at Dana, Massachusetts, in 1794. From 1817 he led the Second Universalist Church in Boston until his death.

Ballou founded and edited The Universalist Magazine and The Universalist Expositor, wrote some 10,000 sermons, and left many hymns and essays. The 1911 Britannica entry names Notes on the Parables, A Treatise on Atonement, and his 1834 work on future retribution as the books that made him the chief American voice of Universalism.
britannica-1911-baltic-sea:
The Baltic Sea is a sea of northern Europe lying between 54 and 66 degrees north, ringed by Sweden, Russia, Germany, and Denmark. Its greatest length is about 960 miles and its greatest breadth about 400 miles, with some 5,000 miles of coastline. Its long axis runs from south-west to north-east.

A winding channel past southern Scandinavia links it to the North Sea, split into the Skagerrak and the Kattegat. Danish islands then block the way south, so ships pass by the Sound or the Belts. The 1911 Britannica entry, a long one, goes on to the sea's deep basins, shores, and waters. It also traces its past, when ice-age shifts made it by turns a salt arm and a fresh lake.
britannica-1911-barents-sea:
The Barents Sea is the part of the Arctic Ocean bounded by the north coast of Europe and the islands of Novaya Zemlya, Franz Josef Land, and Spitsbergen, with smaller islands between. It was named after the Dutch navigator Willem Barents. The southern shore, off the Murman coast of the Kola peninsula, is sometimes called the Murman Sea.

Leaving out the great inlet of the White Sea in the south, the sea runs from about 67 to 80 degrees north and from 20 to 60 degrees east. The 1911 Britannica entry is a short geographic notice: it fixes the sea's borders, its islands, and its namesake, and refers the reader onward for fuller treatment of the region.
britannica-1911-battersea:
Battersea is a south-western borough of London, England, described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The Thames bounds it to the north, and Lambeth and Wandsworth close its other sides. Its people numbered 168,907 in 1901. Three bridges, the Victoria or Chelsea, the Albert, and the Battersea, cross the river from its bank. The district is mainly one of artisans' houses, working men's homes, with several large factories set by the river.

Open space is the borough's pride. Battersea Park runs along the Thames for nearly 200 acres, with a lake and a subtropical garden. It was made by banking up the river and raising marshy ground, and opened in 1858. Wandsworth and Clapham commons also reach into the borough. St Mary's church holds glass and tombs from an older church, among them one to Viscount Bolingbroke. A room in a riverside house that survives is linked with Pope and his Essay on Man.
britannica-1911-beale-dorothea:
Dorothea Beale (1831–1906) was an English schoolmistress born in London on the 21st of March 1831. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica tells how she was among the first to attend lectures at the new Queen's College for Ladies in 1848. From 1849 to 1856 she taught classes there herself.

After a short, unhappy spell at the Clergy Daughters' school at Casterton, she became principal of the Ladies College at Cheltenham in 1858. The college was then in very low water, but her tact, hard work, and sound handling of money set it firm by 1864. New buildings rose from 1873 as numbers grew, and the school became one of the great girls' schools of the country. Its rise helped change how far women's schooling could go, and she held her post until her death in 1906.
britannica-1911-berea:
Berea is a town of Madison county, Kentucky, 131 miles by rail south of Cincinnati. It held only 762 people in 1900 and is served by the Louisville & Nashville railway. The town sits pleasantly where the Blue Grass country meets the Mountain region of the state.

Berea is widely known for Berea College, founded from an anti-slavery school of 1855 to serve the mountaineers of Kentucky and Tennessee. The college had 65 instructors and 1,150 students in 1908, with halls for science, industry, printing and worship on seventy acres. State law in 1904 barred teaching black and white students together, and the school planned a separate branch for black students at once.
britannica-1911-black-sea:
The Black Sea, called Pontus Euxinus in ancient times, lies between southern Russia to the north, Rumania, Turkey, and Bulgaria to the west, and Asia Minor to the south and east. It joins the Sea of Azov through the strait at Kertch and the Mediterranean through the Bosporus, the Sea of Marmora, and the Dardanelles.

Depth and water conditions fill much of the entry. The greatest depth is 1030 fathoms near the centre, in a single basin. Below 100 fathoms the water holds much sulphuretted hydrogen, stays still, and supports no higher life. Surface currents, coastal shelves, and the shallow, fresher Sea of Azov are also described for sailors and geographers.
britannica-1911-bona-dea:
Bona Dea, the Good Goddess, was an old Roman deity of fruitfulness in the soil and in women. She was identified with Fauna, and later also with Ops and Maia. Her temple stood on the Aventine, and its dedication day was the first of May.

Women alone tended her cult. A second yearly rite, held in early December in the house of a senior magistrate, became notorious when P. Clodius broke into it in 62 B.C., with heavy political fallout. Wine and myrtle were banned from her worship, and myths grew up to explain the bans. Healing herbs and snakes were kept in her temple, fitting her care for health. Her offering was a sow, and she and her priestess also bore the names Damia and damiatrix.
britannica-1911-brightlingsea:
Brightlingsea, spoken as Brittlesea, is a port and fishing station in Essex, England, on a creek off the east shore of the Colne estuary. It ends a branch line from Colchester, 62 and a half miles east-north-east of London, and its urban district held 4501 people in 1901. The Colchester oyster beds lie mainly in this reach of the Colne.

Oyster fishing is the chief trade, with boat-building beside it, and the creek is a favoured yachting centre. All Saints church, mostly Perpendicular in style, holds fine monuments and brasses under a tall tower. Though in Essex, the town is a member of the Cinque Port of Sandwich in Kent. Across the creek stands St Osyth's priory, first a nunnery founded by Osyth, grand-daughter of Penda of Mercia, martyred about 653, later a house of Augustinian canons with a grand late gateway.
britannica-1911-briosco-andrea:
Andrea Briosco (about 1470–1532) was an Italian sculptor and architect from Padua, known by the nickname Riccio, meaning curly-headed. In building he is known by the church of Sta Giustina in his home city. Fame, though, rests on his work in metal, above all in bronze, where his finest pieces still stand in Padua churches.

Masterworks named are the bronze Paschal candelabrum, 11 feet high, set in the choir of the Santo, St Anthony's church, in 1515. Two bronze reliefs of 1507 in the same church showing David dancing before the Ark and Judith with Holofernes. His bronze and marble tomb for the physician Girolamo della Torre at Verona bore fine reliefs later carried off by the French to the Louvre. Workshop pieces are also credited to him, and a Dance of Nymphs relief in London is doubtfully put to his name.
britannica-1911-caspian-sea:
Caspian Sea is the subject of a long article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is an inland sea between Europe and Asia, known of old as the Mare Caspium. It runs seven hundred and sixty miles from north to south. Its breadth runs from one hundred to two hundred and eighty miles, and its area is near one hundred and seventy thousand square miles.

The sea fills the deep part of a wide hollow that was once a far larger inland sea. Its surface now lies some eighty-six feet below the level of the ocean. The basin falls in three parts, and the north part is the shallowest. Rivers such as the Volga, the Ural, and the Terek are fast silting it up with sand and mud. The article names the men who have mapped its waters and shores since the time of von Baer.
britannica-1911-centaurea:
Centaurea is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a genus of plants in the natural order Compositae. The genus holds between four and five hundred species. It is spread widely, but its main centre is the Mediterranean region. The plants are herbs with entire or cut leaves, often with spiny teeth. Their flower heads are ovoid or globose. Tubular florets fill them, the outer ones larger and neuter, the inner ones bisexual.

Four species are native in Britain. Knapweed grows in meadows and pasture. The cornflower, or bluebottle, is a well known cornfield weed. Star thistle is rare, found in dry waste places in the south. The entry then lists species worth growing in gardens. They grow readily in ordinary soil. White downy Cineraria, tall yellow babylonica, and blue flowered montana from the Pyrenees are among them. Silver haired ragusina from south eastern Europe closes the list.
britannica-1911-chaldaea:
Chaldaea was a land whose name is oft used for Babylonia in the Bible. Its land entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. At first the name meant the far south district of that region. Its old capital was Bit Yakin, seat of rebel Merodach baladan.

That rebel king vexed Assyrian kings Sargon and Sennacherib in his time. The home land stretched where the Tigris and Euphrates met the sea. In time the name spread to cover near all of Babylonia plain. Assyrian records from the ninth century show that wider use by then. A clear split between Chaldaeans and Babylonians lasted to a late date.
britannica-1911-clacton-on-sea:
Clacton-on-Sea is a watering-place in Essex, England, 71 miles east-north-east from London by a branch of the Great Eastern railway from Colchester. Steamers from London also serve it in the summer months, the entry notes. Its urban district counted 7,456 people in 1901, and clay cliffs of slight height rise from its sandy beach facing south-east. Marshes fringe the shore in the neighbourhood, in contrast to the cliffs.

The church of Great Clacton, at the village one and a half miles inland, is Norman and later and of considerable interest. Clacton itself provides a pier, a promenade and a marine parade for its visitors. Various convalescent and other homes have their seat in the town, fitting its resort character. Beach, pier and rest homes make up the whole picture this brief notice draws.
britannica-1911-consulate-of-the-sea:
The Consulate of the Sea is a famed set of sea customs and rules in the Catalan tongue. It was printed at Barcelona late in the 1400s. Its true title is The Book of the Consulate. The name comes from the consuls, trade judges of the Mediterranean ports. Their rulings in the sea cities form the book's core.

The first known edition came off the press at Barcelona in 1494. It has no title page or frontispiece. Its name shows in a letter placed before the table of contents. One copy of that edition is known, kept in the National Library in Paris. That letter calls the book a mended form of an older Book of the Consulate. Francis Celelles compiled it with help from shipmasters and merchants. Their long practice at sea stands behind its rules.
britannica-1911-cooperage-liquor-trade-a:
Cooperage, in this second sense, names a trade in strong drink, tobacco and other goods among North Sea fishermen. The word comes from Flemish and Dutch terms for a trader. The practice began in the middle of the 1800s. Flemish and Dutch traders sought out the fishing fleets to barter with the crews. Tobacco came first in their holds.

Their trade soon grew into floating grog-shops in all but name. The harm to the men drew public notice in 1881. A meeting at the Hague in 1882 weighed means to end the abuse. In 1887 six states signed a pact to bar sales of strong drink to fishermen at sea. Britain passed an act in 1888 to give that pact force. The fine ran to fifty pounds at most, or a term in prison. Mission ships that serve deep sea fishermen close the account.
britannica-1911-crustacea:
The hosted text opens partway through a long anatomical survey of the Crustacea, at the gastric teeth of crab and lobster. Those teeth, set in the stomach wall on moving plates, grind food in a gastric mill. The hosted pages then work through the gut and its liver-like outgrowths. Set sections treat the circulatory, excretory, and nervous systems in turn. Further sections cover eyes, sense organs, glands, light-giving organs, and the reproductive system.

Figures show the stomach of the common crab and lobster laid open, with their grinding teeth enlarged. The survey is built system by system, each part compared across the groups of the class. It closes with a full classification table. That table sets out the sub-classes Entomostraca and Malacostraca and orders from Branchiopoda to Amphipoda. The arrangement, the entry warns, does not always match the newest views of kinship among the groups.
britannica-1911-decelea:
Decelea is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an Attic deme, or township. It stood on the pass over the east end of Mount Parnes. That road led toward Oropus and toward Chalcis. From its spot it commands a view over the Athenian plain. Its hero, Decelus, gives the place its name. Legend says he showed the Tyndaridae where Helen was hidden. Theseus had hidden their sister Helen at Aphidnae.

That tale bred a lasting friendship with Sparta. The friendship shaped events in the Peloponnesian War. On the advice of Alcibiades, Sparta fortified Decelea. They made it a base for lasting occupation of Attica. That occupation ran from 413 to 404 before Christ. From there they could harass the Athenians without pause. The post became a centre for runaway slaves and deserters. The royal palace of Tatoi now stands on the site.
britannica-1911-euboea:
Euboea, called Euripos or Negropont, is the largest island of the Grecian archipelago. The Euboic Sea parts it from the mainland. It runs about 90 miles from north-west to south-east and narrows in places to 4 miles. A mountain chain runs its whole length in three knots. In the north, hot sulphur springs near Aedepsus, the Baths of Heracles, were used by Sulla. The cape of Artemisium recalls the Greek naval victory over Persia in 480 B.C.

Mount Dirphe, now Delphi, rises 5,725 feet at the centre, its sides clothed in pine, chestnut and plane. Mount Ocha closes the south at 4,830 feet. The island's later story runs through Venetian and Turkish hands. At the close of the Greek War of Independence in 1830 it joined the new Greek state. It now yields much grain, and magnesia and lignite are exported in quantity. In 1899 it became a separate nome, with 116,903 people in 1907.
britannica-1911-eusebius-of-caesarea:
Eusebius of Caesarea (about 260 to about 340) was a historian of the church, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens his life with his teacher. He called himself Eusebius Pamphili, for his love of his friend Pamphilus. He was born most likely in Palestine, between 260 and 265. He died as bishop of Caesarea in 339 or 340.

Little is known of his youth beyond one key link. Early on he joined Pamphilus, a presbyter of the church at Caesarea. Pamphilus had founded a school of theology in that city. He gathered a circle of earnest students around him. They gave themselves to the study of the Bible above all. They copied out biblical books by hand, and they defended the writings of Origen. Origen was the master they held in honour.
britannica-1911-garcao-pedro-antonio-joa:
Pedro Antonio Joaquim Correa Garcao lived from 1724 to 1772 and was a Portuguese lyric poet. His 1911 Britannica life notes his birth into a house close to the royal court. Frail health marked his youth in Lisbon, where Jesuits taught him. At home he learned English, French, and Italian tongues with care.

He went to Coimbra in 1742 to study law and took his degree in 1748. Two years later he was made a knight of the Order of Christ. A rich marriage in 1751 let him live at ease and write. With friends he helped found the Arcadia Lusitana in 1756. That group sought to purge bad taste from Portuguese verse.
britannica-1911-gephyrea:
Gephyrea is the subject of a short science article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The name was used for groups of worm like animals that look much alike. Scholars were not sure how the groups were truly linked. Older editions of the work grouped three families under this one name.

The article explains how that old group has been broken up. One part is now seen as true ringed worms. A second part stands as its own group of sea worms. A third part stays of doubtful place. A fourth part is now placed near a quite different stock. In short, the piece shows how science moved past a loose label. It points readers to the newer articles for each part.
britannica-1911-hemans-felicia-dorothea:
Felicia Dorothea Hemans (1793–1835) was an English poet. She was born in Liverpool on 25 September 1793. Her father was a merchant of Irish extraction. Her grandfather was Austrian and Tuscan consul there. Her father's failure moved the family to Gwrych in Wales. Her education was desultory but voracious. She mastered Italian, Spanish, Portuguese and German.

Her Juvenile Poems appeared in 1808 when she was fourteen. The Monthly Review criticised them harshly. Marriage to Captain Alfred Hemans came in 1812. Five sons were born during the following years. Domestic care and failing health never stopped her writing. The Restoration of Works of Art to Italy appeared in 1816. Modern Greece and Camoens translations followed. Her husband left for Rome in 1818, never to return. Note: this record's hosted file is a shared page chunk; the Hemans entry stands complete within it.
britannica-1911-hosea:
Hosea, son of Beērī, stands first in order among the minor prophets of the Old Testament. His name is the same as that of the last king of Ephraim. Nothing is known of his life beyond what his prophecies give. He was plainly a citizen of the northern kingdom: in his book, the land means Israel, and our king means the king of Samaria.

The title dates him by the kings of Judah, Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, and by Jeroboam son of Joash in Israel. The study argues the book belongs before 734 B.C. The Syro-Ephraimitic war, opening that year, is nowhere mentioned, and Gilead still stands as Israel's ground. Hosea links his eldest child's birth to the coming fall of the house of Jehu, before Jeroboam's death in 743. Chapters i–iii reflect the wealth of Jeroboam's reign; iv–xiv speak into the disorder that followed.
britannica-1911-hydrangea:
Hydrangea is a well loved garden flower and shrub. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica centres on the kind called Hydrangea Hortensia. It is a low shrub that drops its leaves in winter. Pairs of large oval leaves line its stems. A great round head of blooms caps each shoot. The showy parts are in fact wide grown sepals. The true flowers are small and mostly barren of seed parts.

The blooms are pink by nature. Alum or iron in the soil can turn them blue. A white kind called Thomas Hogg is singled out. The group holds more than thirty kinds in all. They come chiefly from Japan, the hills of India, and North America. Growers force the plants to bloom out of season for house use. Their heads stay fresh for a long span once cut or potted.
britannica-1911-idumaea:
Idumaea is the Greek name for Edom, a land south east of the Dead Sea. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica links the name to a root meaning red. The red sandstone hills of Petra may explain it. That root is not sure, the entry warns. The name may come from a god called Edom. The Bible's early books often call the land Seir.

The first folk known there were the Horites, cave dwellers of old. Tales say the kin of Esau drove them out in time. Through most of Bible history, tribes who claimed descent from Esau held the land. Israel owned them as kin folk. Signs in the tales show the two stocks mixed by marriage. Egypt's records shed little light on the land's first ages.
britannica-1911-jordan-dorothea:
Dorothea Jordan, an Irish actress who lived from 1762 to 1816, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. She was born near Waterford, daughter of a Dublin actress. Her father, named Bland, was perhaps an army captain, more likely a stage hand. She first appeared at Dublin in 1777, as Phoebe in As You Like It.

After work in Ireland and the Yorkshire towns, she reached London in 1785. As Peggy in A Country Girl at Drury Lane, she won the town in one season. Her comic acting was ranked second only to Kitty Clive's. She stayed at Drury Lane until 1809, playing a wide range of parts. Her Lady Teazle, Rosalind, and Imogen were specially liked. So were her breeches parts, played in male dress. She moved to Covent Garden in 1811 and left the London stage in 1814.
britannica-1911-joseph-of-arimathaea:
Joseph of Arimathaea is a Bible entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It tells of a rich Jew who had turned to follow Jesus Christ. All four Gospel books name him and agree on the main tale. After the cross he asked the Roman ruler for the body of Jesus.

The entry notes small clashes between the four accounts of the burial. One book calls the tomb his own, while the rest stay vague. Two books call him a councillor, a word that sparks much debate. The entry weighs whether he sat in the high Jewish council. Tales that call him a friend of both sides are judged late and weak.
britannica-1911-judaea:
Judaea was the name given to the southern part of Palestine as held by the Jewish community in the days after the exile. Persians, Greeks, and Romans in turn ruled over it. In Luke and in Acts the term is at times used loosely for the whole of western Palestine. Its borders were never fixed with care and shifted from age to age, above all on the north.

After the death of Herod, Archelaus became ruler of Samaria, Idumea, and Judaea. When he was cast down, Judaea was joined to the province of Syria. It was then governed by a procurator whose seat was at Caesarea. For the look of the land the entry points the reader to the article on Palestine. For the history it points to the articles on the Jews and on Judah, with a further note to Mommsen's work on the Roman provinces.
britannica-1911-kara-sea:
The Kara Sea is a part of the Arctic Ocean fenced in, save on the northwest, by Novaya Zemlya, Vaygach Island, and the Siberian coast. Three straits give entry from the west: Matochkin, between the two islands of Novaya Zemlya, and Kara and Yugor, north and south of Vaygach. On the southeast, Kara Bay cuts deep into the mainland.

The sea is shallow throughout, its deepest parts lying off Vaygach and the north of Novaya Zemlya. It long had the name of being bound in ice almost without pause. Then the Norwegian captain Johannesen showed in 1869 that it could be entered, and Nordenskiöld crossed it to the Yenisei in 1875. Many then saw it as a trade route between European Russia and the north of Siberia. The open season is in any case very short, and the western straits are at times ice bound for a whole year.
britannica-1911-labyrinthulidea:
Labyrinthulidea is the name Sir Ray Lankester gave in 1885 to a group of Sarcodina that form a net-like plasmodium, the denser masses joined by fine threads, hardly distinct from some Proteomyxa. Its article sits inside a chunk file with the labyrinth and lac articles. Labyrinthula, found by Cienkowsky, spreads a network of fairly stiff threads, its pseudopods, scattered with large spindle-shaped bodies, each an amoeba with a single nucleus.

The amoebae multiply by fission while active. They reproduce by drawing together and encysting in an irregular heap; one amoeba emerges from each cyst, or rarely four. Chlamydomyxa, named by Archer, has a freely branched plasmodium with yellowish chromatophores and small vesicles holding a tannin-like substance. Its body carries many nuclei and feeds two ways, swallowing other Protista and also assimilating through its chromatophores, the product being oil rather than starch.
britannica-1911-marshalsea:
Marshalsea is a short article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a former prison in Southwark, London. The prison belonged to the court of the same name, held by the steward and marshal of the king's household. When it was first set up is not known, but it stood as early as the reign of Edward the Third. In 1842 it was merged with the Queen's Bench and Fleet prisons, and shut for good in 1849.

At the merger the Marshalsea held debtors and those kept for contempt of the courts of the Marshalsea, of the queen's palace at Westminster, and of the high court of admiralty. It also held admiralty prisoners under sentence of courts martial. The article ends with a pointer readers still use: the Marshalsea is the grim house of debt at the heart of Charles Dickens's novel Little Dorrit.
britannica-1911-medea:
Medea, a famed sorceress in Greek legend, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. She was the daughter of Aeetes, king of Colchis. Her father threw her into prison, fearing harm from her witchcraft. She escaped by her art and fled to the temple of the Sun god, her grandfather as the tale is told.

The article follows her dark path. She fell in love with Jason when he reached Colchis, and took a dread revenge when he proved false. After the murder of his second wife and of her own children, she fled Corinth in a car drawn by dragons. At Athens she wed King Aegeus and bore a son, Medus. A plot against the life of Theseus forced her out again. She went home to Colchis and set her father back on his throne. Corinth held her a goddess.
britannica-1911-north-sea:
North Sea is a place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It describes the sea that lies between Britain and the mainland of Europe. A narrow strait at its south end joins it to the English Channel. To the north it spreads wide, then narrows once more by Norway.

The entry gives two sets of size and depth counts from sea scholars. Both sets agree that the sea is shallow as great seas go. Its floor forms part of the shelf on which the British Isles stand. Depth grows less in a fair slope from north to south shore. A broad bank of sand bars the mid sea from east to west.
britannica-1911-palladio-andrea:
Andrea Palladio, an Italian architect who lived from 1518 to 1580, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Vicenza and studied Vitruvius and Alberti while young. His patron Count Trissino took him to Rome for his student years. In 1547 he came home to Vicenza and designed a host of fine buildings.

Among his Vicenza works stands the Palazzo della Ragione, ringed with two storeys of open arcades. Palaces for great local families followed, and stately churches rose in Venice. The article notes that many were built of brick faced with stucco, against his wish for stone. That flaw, it says, does not touch the merit of the designs. His last great work was the Teatro Olimpico at Vicenza, finished by his pupil Scamozzi. His country villas were widely copied, and his Four Books of Architecture, printed at Venice in 1570, spread his fame.
britannica-1911-panacea: Panacea, a cure for all diseases, is the subject of a brief entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica.
