The word is Greek, built from terms for all and to heal, and means all healing. In the middle ages it named a mythical herb thought to hold that power over sickness. Many real herbs have had the power of curing all diseases ascribed to them over time. Hence they took the name of all heal. Among them the entry names mistletoe, woundwort, yarrow or milfoil, and the great valerian.
britannica-1911-pea:
Pea is a botany article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, with a labelled figure of the flower. The pea genus belongs to the legume order. Its plants are herbs with compound leaves that end in tendrils. By those tendrils the weak stems hold themselves up. Large leafy growths sit at the base of each leaf.

The flowers have the typical butterfly shape of the family, the entry explains. A large upper petal stands above two side petals, and two front petals form a keel below. Ten stamens stand inside, nine joined and the tenth mostly free. That split lets insects reach the honey at the base. The fruit is the familiar pod, which bursts when ripe into two halves. Large round seeds, the peas themselves, sit along the edges of the pod.
britannica-1911-phoronidea:
Phoronidea is a small group of sea worms with just one genus, named Phoronis. The worms are found in seas all round the world. They live in tubes that they make, and the tubes can twist in a dense mass. The entry is a close study of their form from the nineteen eleven reference work.

The text sets out the worm from its crown of fine arms to its gut. That crown is shaped like a shoe for a horse and bears the mouth at its base. Two plates show the parts in fine detail. The gut loops down and back up in a U shape, and the text maps each part.
britannica-1911-portuguese-guinea:
Portuguese Guinea is a Portuguese colony in West Africa. It runs along the Guinea coast from Cape Roxo in the north to the Cogon estuary in the south. French land rings it on the land side, with Senegal to the north and French Guinea to the east and south. The colony covers about 14,000 square miles. Its people are put at from 200,000 to 800,000 in the count.

Most of the colony is a low delta land. A group of small islands, the Bissagos, lies off its coast as part of it. The coast line is cut deep by estuaries. Into them flow a great many rivers whose sources lie in high land on the east border. The largest estuary is the Geba. It takes in the Geba river, the Mancoa, and the Rio Grande.
britannica-1911-roscrea:
Roscrea is a market town near the north west edge of a county in Ireland, set in fine ground that links two hill ranges. The 1911 Britannica entry gives its rail span from Dublin and its town count at the turn of the age. A branch rail line runs north from the town to a sister market town.

Flour milling and the tan of hides are its trades, and fairs for cattle are held each month. A branch house of a strict order of monks sits there. The old remains draw the eye, the entry says: parts of an abbey founded by a saint in the first ages, built into the church of today. From that abbey a church district grew. A famed book of the Gospels was made there, kept now in a Dublin book room in a rich shrine.
britannica-1911-sacchi-andrea:
Andrea Sacchi, Italian painter of the later Roman school born at Nettuno near Rome in about 1600, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. His father Benedetto, a painter of small note, gave him his first lessons. Andrea then passed into the studio of Albani. He was the last and most famed pupil of that master.

Raphael was the painter Sacchi loved most of all. He stood as a keen rival to Pietro da Cortona and, still more, to Bernini. In time he became one of the most learned designers of the Roman school and one of its soundest hands with colour. Trips to Venice and Parma let him study Venetian colour and the style of Correggio. His rule was plain: a painter should make few pictures, but make them perfect.
britannica-1911-southsea:
Southsea is a seaside resort in Hampshire, England, and part of the borough of Portsmouth. Its place entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It forms the south and home quarter of Portsmouth, with its own rail stop. The town looks out on Spithead and the Isle of Wight beyond.

The entry notes two piers and a parade along the sea wall. Sea bathing there is described as good, which drew resort trade. Southsea Castle stands at the south tip of Portsea Island. Henry the Eighth built that castle to guard the coast. Readers get a brief sketch of a resort quarter and its Tudor fort in a few lines.
britannica-1911-swansea:
Swansea, a seaport and market town in Glamorganshire, South Wales, is described in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. It sits between high hills on the river Tawe, near its mouth in Swansea Bay. That bay is a fine recess of the Bristol Channel. Rail lines reach it from London and Cardiff.

The older part of town stands on the west bank of the river. That part is now given over to business, the entry says. Newer parts stretch north along the river and east along the sea. Several rail lines come in from the north and east, through a works district. One line from the west passes through fine woods and skirts the bay. Light rail runs along the shore to Mumbles Pier.
britannica-1911-tea:
Tea is a long article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica on the leaves of the tea bush, made into a drink. The entry gives the word's Chinese roots and notes that the term is also used for drinks made from other leaves. It can even name the afternoon meal at which tea is served. The article then turns to history.

The early history of tea, it warns, is mainly a matter of tradition. Knowledge of China's past was still thin when the entry was written. Scholars might one day learn who made the first cup and who planted the first bushes, it says. For now, knowledge is mixed with much that is plainly myth. A Chinese legend credits an emperor of deep antiquity with finding the virtues of tea.
britannica-1911-tegea:
Tegea was an old Greek city of Arcadia, on a high plain. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica rings that plain with named peaks. The Tegean land filled the south half of the plain. Mantineia held the north half. The flat ground fed herds and grew corn well. It was prone to floods, since its streams had no free outlet. Drains cut under the ground carried the overflow south.

Control of those drains set Tegea and Mantineia at odds for ages. Roads from Laconia to Argos crossed the plain too. That place put Tegea in Sparta's path. For centuries it stood as a shield of Arcadia against Sparta. Sparta beat it about 550 before Christ, yet left it its freedom. Tale credits a king called Aleus with joining its hamlets into one city. At Plataea the Tegeans were first to charge, the entry says.
britannica-1911-urea:
Urea, also called carbamide, is a chemical found in the urine of mammals, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out. It was first found in 1773 by Rouelle. Human urine holds about two to three per cent of it, and a grown man makes about 30 grammes a day. It is also found in blood, in milk, and in other fluids of the body.

Great weight is given to its making in the lab by Wohler in 1828. That was the first time a compound of life was made from stuff with no life in it. The text then lists many other ways to make urea in the lab. Each way starts from a named salt or gas and ends with the same white compound.
britannica-1911-water-flea:
Water-fleas, the mites of ponds, are shown in a beast entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Early lens men gave that name to small fresh water shell beasts. Swammerdam used the name for them as far back as 1669. The true water-fleas teem in fresh water at all points of the globe. Daphnia pulex, a chief kind, haunts ponds and ditches near us.

That mite runs less than a tenth of an inch in length. A clear two-valve shell wraps its whole small body in glass. Two branched, feathery feelers row it through the water in bounds. One big black eye marks the head that juts from the shell. Five pairs of leaf limbs beat as gills in the shell. The female keeps her eggs in a brood pouch till they hatch.
britannica-1911-winchelsea:
Winchelsea is the subject of a place entry in the 1911 Britannica. The village lies in Sussex in England near Hastings. It stands on a steep spur above flat low land. That low land was once a great inlet of the sea. The village was a famed port till the 1400s. Its count in 1901 was under seven hundred souls. Two old gates still look out over the marsh.

King Edward the First laid out the town in straight streets. A church stands in an open space at its heart. Only part of that church was ever built. What stands shows fine carved work and grand tombs. The first town of the name lay out at sea. Waves ate its site away year by year. The sea wiped it out in 1288. The king then set the new town on safe ground.
britannica-1911-zeno-of-elea:
Zeno of Elea, son of Teleutagoras, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He is thought to have been born toward the start of the fifth century before Christ. He was the pupil and friend of Parmenides, the thinker of the One. Zeno sought to back his master's doctrine by attacking the common belief in the Many.

That method of indirect argument won him the name of inventor of dialectic. In that art, disputation aims not at victory but at finding or passing on truth. He is said to have joined a plot against a tyrant and borne torture with firm constancy when it was found out. Plato shows a young Socrates meeting Parmenides and Zeno in debate. The entry doubts such a meeting could fit the dates, but trusts Plato on Zeno's teaching.
broken-homes-a-study-of-family-desertion:
Joanna C. Colcord wrote a study of family desertion and its social handling, printed at New York in 1919. She headed the Charity Organization Society of that city. The Russell Sage Foundation put out the book in its Social Work Series. Mary E. Richmond edited the series.

Ten chapters map the field. Why men desert holds the long second place. Shifts in how workers treat such cases come next. Hunts for the gone husband fill a full chapter, with probe lists after it. Two chapters give case handling step by step. The man who stays home yet gives no support gets his own study. Last come next steps, first to cure and then to stop the harm. A worker's line fronts the core tale: before the deserter there was a broken man, broke in health, hope, or means.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acacius-bisho:
Acacius, Bishop of Beroea, was born in Syria about 322, dying about 432. While still very young he joined the solitaries' community under Asterius just outside Antioch. He proved a fervent champion of orthodoxy through the Arian troubles, suffering greatly for his courage and constancy. When Eusebius of Samosata returned from exile after Valens's death in 378, he ordained Acacius to the see of Beroea.

Acacius next appears in Rome as deputy for Meletius and the Antiochene synod when Apollinaris's heresy came before Pope Damasus. He signed the Two Natures profession of faith, and his efforts helped end the schisms at Antioch. He later attended the second general council at Constantinople in 381, joined the illegitimate consecration of Flavian, and died at the remarkable age of one hundred and ten.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andrew-of-cae:
Andrew of Caesarea was Bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia. Krumbacher assigns him to the first half of the sixth century, though others place him anywhere from the fifth to the ninth century. Almost nothing else is known of his life. His principal work is a commentary on the Apocalypse, printed in Migne's Patrologia Graeca, volume 106, columns 215 to 458.

The commentary matters because it is the oldest surviving commentary on the book, and most later commentators drew on it. The writer knows early patristic literature far more widely than most Byzantine commentators. Later writers drew on it heavily, so it preserves earlier tradition as well as offering its own reading of Revelation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arethas-of-ca:
Arethas of Caesarea was born at Patrae in Greece about 860 and was a disciple of Photius like all eminent men of his time. He became archbishop of Caesarea in the early tenth century and ranks among the most learned theologians of the Greek church. He compiled the oldest surviving Greek commentary, or scholia, on the Apocalypse, the Book of Revelation, drawing heavily on his predecessor Andrew of Caesarea. It first appeared in print in 1535 as an appendix to Oecumenius's works.

Through his interest in earliest Christian literature, caught perhaps from Andrew, we owe the Arethas Codex, Paris Greek 451. Through it the writings of the Greek Christian apologists have largely reached us. He also commented on Plato and Lucian, and the famous Plato manuscript called Codex Clarkianus, carried from Patmos to London, was copied by his order. The entry presents a scholar whose copying saved ancient texts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aurea:
Aurea, meaning golden, was a title given to certain famed works and documents, listed here as five. First comes the Golden Bull, the charter of Emperor Charles IV. It fixed the law of future imperial elections on 10 January 1356, in union with the estates of the empire. Next is the Catena Aurea, a chain of Scriptural commentaries gathered by St Thomas Aquinas. Third is the Legenda Aurea, a collection of saints' lives by Jacopo da Voragine, Archbishop of Genoa.

Fourth is the Summa Hostiensis, also called the Summa of the Archbishop. It expounds the chief parts of Gregory IX's Decretals, by Henricus de Segusio, Cardinal of Ostia, who died in 1271. Last is the Tabula Aurea, an index to Aquinas's Summa Theologica prepared by Pietro da Bergamo. The entry gives no more than these identifications, yet the five titles together sketch a golden shelf of medieval law, Scripture study, and saints' lives.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bagnorea:
Bagnorea, anciently Novempagi or Balneum Regium, is a diocese in the Viterbo district of Italy. It answers immediately to the Holy See, and its city holds about 4,500 people in a diocese of 20,000. Tradition says St Ansanus preached there in the third century, and a church outside the Alban Gate marks his prison. No record dates the diocese, but Gregory the Great attests Deacon John as bishop about the year 600.

Montefiascone belonged to Bagnorea until Urban V made it a separate diocese, and an alleged 1449 union with Viterbo lacks proof. Its churches include an ancient Gothic cathedral and a new one built by Bishop Nardi in 1698. It preserves an arm of St Bonaventure, a citizen of the town, with some of his writings. Barbarian Goths and Lombards took the city often between the sixth and ninth centuries, and Louis I joined it to the Papal States in 822.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-balanaea:
Balanaea was a titular see of Syria, a city founded as a colony of Aradus. Stephanus places it in Phoenicia, though it belongs rather to Syria. Its first known bishop attended Nicaea in 325, and three more are known to the sixth century. It then served as suffragan of Apamea, metropolis of Syria Secunda. When Justinian built the province of Theodorias, Balanaea joined it civilly yet stayed under Apamea in church matters.

By the tenth century it stood exempt, directly under the Patriarch of Antioch. Crusaders raised a Latin see there, known about 1200, and its bishop lived at Margat, a Hospitaller castle. Franks called it Valania and Muslims Bulunvoas, and its river marked Jerusalem's border with Antioch. Today Banias is a village of about 1,550 people, mostly Maronites, growing onions, olives, and fine tobacco.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-basil-of-amas:
Basil of Amasea, or Basileus, was a bishop and martyr of Pontus. Jerome's Eusebius text puts his death under Licinius, in AD 321 to 324. His name appears among bishops at Ancyra and Neo-Caesarea in 314. Eusebius records Licinius's cruelty at Amasea, where rulers gave bishops the pains of crooks.

Athanasius counts the great Basileus of Pontus among bishops holding the Son of like substance with the Father. Philostorgius's tale that Basileus went to Nicaea must be wrong, since Nicaea's lists name Eutychianus of Amasea. His Acts, said to be by the eyewitness priest Johannes, are false and wholly fabled. His feast falls on 26 April in Greek and Roman books.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-beroea:
Beroea, a titular see of Macedonia, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. It lies at the foot of Mount Bermios, now called Veria by Greeks, and still keeps its ancient name. Rome took it after the battle of Pydna in 168 BC, and Pompey wintered there in 49 to 48 BC.

Its Jewish synagogue heard St. Paul preach with success, and on leaving he left Silas and Timothy behind. Onesimus, once the slave of Philemon, counts as its first bishop in the Apostolic Constitutions. The entry joins classical geography to apostolic memory in a short note.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caesarea:
Caesarea in Cappadocia began as Mazaka, named for the legendary hero Mosoch, and later took the name Eusebeia, then Caesarea, named for Tiberius when Cappadocia became a Roman province in A.D. 17. It stayed the metropolis of Cappadocia Prima and the first metropolis of the Patriarchate of Constantinople. Bishops listed from the first to the eighteenth century number fifty, among them Saint Basil the Great and Firmilian, correspondent of Saint Cyprian.

Its saints include the whole family of Saint Basil and the martyrs Mamas, Gordius, and Julitta, praised by Basil himself. Councils met there in 314, 358, and 371, and at Basil's time the diocese counted fifty country bishops. Today it is Kaisarieh in Turkey, with about 72,000 people, Greek, Armenian, and Muslim, and ruins of the old city a quarter mile west.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canea: Canea once served as a titular see of Crete, until a decree of 1894 suppressed it. Canea is the Italian name of Cydonia. The two names were used at the same time as separate titles. Cydonia, the Greek name, and Canea, the Italian name, thus stood side by side as two titles for one Cretan see.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-corea:
Gustave Mutel's entry covers Corea, a vicariate apostolic coextensive with the Empire of Corea, created distinct in 1831. For nearly half a century before, Corea held fervent Catholics. In a manner perhaps unique in Church annals, the Faith arrived without preaching, before any missionaries had penetrated the country. Educated people, eager for new knowledge as their country closed jealously, procured through the annual Peking embassy every possible book on science, literature, and other subjects.

Some Christian books reached their hands, and, grace aiding, they recognized the truth. One, Ni-seung-houn, journeyed to Peking in 1784 and was baptized there as Peter. Returning, he baptized his learned, high-placed companions. Persecution broke out in 1839, with many Christians arrested, tortured, and killed, and missionaries hunted without mercy. The Kang-hoa expedition, avenging murdered French missionaries, lacked vigour. 1907 statistics list one bishop, 46 French missionaries, ten Corean priests, eleven French sisters, 41 Corean sisters, and 72 schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dead-sea:
A geographical entry describes the Dead Sea, the lake on Palestine's south-eastern border, known by many biblical names. The Old Testament calls it the Salt Sea, the Sea of the Arabah, and the East Sea. Josephus and Pliny called it the Lake of Asphalt, and local people call it Bahr Lut, the Sea of Lot. Only once does the Old Testament use its present name.

The Dead Sea ends the Jordan valley's chain of waters. The chain runs from Mount Hermon through Lake Merom and the Lake of Tiberias. Travellers compare the Dead Sea to Lake Geneva in size and shape. It is forty-seven miles long, about ten miles wide, and 360 square miles in area. Its surface lies 1,292 feet below the Mediterranean. Its bitter, buoyant waters, asphalt deposits, and bordering wilderness are described with the region's exploration history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-diocaesarea:
Diocaesarea is the later name of Sepphoris, a town the rabbis called Sippori, meaning the bird. Though absent from the Bible, it ranked among the largest towns of Galilee. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how Gabinius set one of five provincial councils there in 56 before Christ. Herod the Great retook it in 39 before Christ, and rebels seized it again in the year 3.

Herod Antipas rebuilt the ruined town and named it for the emperor, giving it the name Diocaesarea. The entry also treats two other sees of the same name, one in Thrace and one in Egypt. Bishops from the fourth century onward fill out a story of a town known more from councils and lists than from ruins.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dioclea:
Dioclea was a titular see in Phrygia, a land of Asia Minor. Ptolemy names Diocleia, likely the Greek dress of a native name, Dokela. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry proves its self-rule from coins struck under the emperor Elagabalus. It appears in the Synecdemus of Hierocles and in later lists of bishoprics as a see of Phrygia Pacatiana, whose chief city was Laodicea.

Only two bishops are known, one in 431 and one in 451. An inscription found near Doghla, a village in the region of Smyrna, points to the site of Dioclea, though no ruins remain. The entry is a small study in how coins, lists, and a single stone can fix a lost bishopric on the map.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-elaea:
Elaea was an ancient port city of Asia Minor, now only a titular see, said to have been founded by Menestheus. It stood twelve stadia from the mouth of the Caicus river and one hundred and twenty stadia from Pergamus. It was the port of Pergamus. It enters history about 450 before Christ, in the days of the Athenian naval league. It passed from Alexander to the kings of Pergamus.

Antiochus of Syria besieged it in 190 before Christ, Prusias ravaged its land in 156, and an earthquake partly wrecked it in the year 90. In Roman times it struck its own coins. As a suffragan of Ephesus it appears in church lists to the twelfth or thirteenth century. Only three of its bishops are known: Isaias in 451, Olbianus in 787, and Theodulus in the twelfth century. Its ruins lie a few kilometres south of Kilisee Keui. Mongols or Turks likely destroyed the city.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-euroea:
Euroea was a small ancient see of Epirus Vetus in Greece, suffragan to the metropolitan of Nicopolis, now carried as a titular bishopric. The geographer Hierocles names it, and the emperor Justinian moved its people to an islet in a nearby lake and built a strong city there. Only five of its bishops are known, a thin record that still sketches a long life. The first, Saint Donatus, lived under Theodosius I, and the last appears in a letter of Pope Saint Gregory the Great written about 603.

The site itself is lost, and the entry weighs the guesses of scholars. Lequien placed it at Paramythia, called Aï Donal, or Saint Donatus, by the Turks, in the region of Janina. Others put it at Limboni, since shown to be Photice, or at Janina itself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eusebius-of-c:
Eusebius of Caesarea, called the Father of Church History, was bishop of Caesarea in Palestine in the early fourth century, born about 260 and dead before 341. The entry builds his life from his own letter to his diocese explaining why he signed the Creed of Nicaea. It weighs rival readings of that letter. One view holds that the creed he offered was the local creed of Caesarea, learned at his baptism and taught through his priesthood. 

The bulk of the article is a guide to his books. It covers his Church History, his apologetic works answering pagan and Jewish critics, and his commentaries on Scripture. It also covers his writings on doctrine, his orations, and his letters. It judges his strengths and limits as a historian, his part in the Arian dispute, and his standing at the court of Constantine.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eusebius-of-l:
Eusebius of Laodicea was a third-century Alexandrian deacon who became bishop of Laodicea in Syria and died about 268. His story comes from Eusebius of Caesarea's Church History. As a deacon he stood with his bishop Dionysius before Aemilian, prefect of Egypt, under the emperor Valerian. All were sentenced to banishment. Eusebius stayed behind in hiding, served confessors in prison at great risk, and buried the bodies of martyrs.

When revolt and plague struck Alexandria in 260, he nursed the sick and wounded. He then won leave from the Roman general besieging the Bruchium quarter for all who wished to leave, and he tended the exhausted refugees like a father and physician. In 264 Dionysius sent him to Syria as his delegate in the affair of Paul of Samosata. The Syrians, impressed by him and his friend Anatolius, kept them both, making Eusebius bishop of Laodicea.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-first-council:
The First Council of Nicaea met in 325 to meet the heresy of Arius. Constantine, now sole emperor, called bishops from every country to restore religious peace. The emperor supplied transport and upkeep, and opened the sessions with great solemnity. Some 318 bishops attended, most of them Greek, with Hosius of Cordova presiding.

The council condemned Arianism and framed the Nicene Creed, drawn up on 19 June. It also dealt with the paschal controversy and other matters before closing. The young deacon Athanasius was present, at the start of a life of conflict and glory. Sessions closed on 25 August, after the symbol and the remaining business were settled.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-frederic-naus:
Frederic Nausea, bishop of Vienna, was a wagonmaker's son from Franconia who rose through learning to the Council of Trent. Born around 1480, he studied at Bamberg, Pavia, Padua, and Siena, taking degrees in law and divinity, then served Cardinal Campeggio as secretary at diets across Germany. Driven from Frankfurt by Lutheran riots, he preached at Mainz and became court preacher to King Ferdinand.

Named coadjutor of Vienna in 1538 and bishop in 1541, Nausea worked for reunion with the Lutherans, even asking Rome to allow married clergy and the communion cup for the laity. He reached Trent only in 1551, spoke chiefly on the sacraments, and died there of fever within the year. His writings range from sermons and a catechism to a treatise on the resurrection.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-d-an:
Giovanni d'Andrea was a canonist born at Mugello near Florence about 1275, who died in 1348. Educated by his father and at the University of Bologna, he taught canon law at Padua and Pisa before becoming a professor at Bologna. His teaching ran for forty-five years. A Catholic Encyclopedia article sums his career in his epitaph: Rabbi Doctorum, light, censor, and rule of morals.

Trithemius, Baldus, Forster, and Bellarmine paid him the highest tributes. He died in the plague of 1348, and was buried, the article says, in San Domenico at Bologna. His works include glosses on the sixth book of decretals and on the Clementines, a commentary on Gregory IX's decretals, and additions to the Speculum of Durandus. Later writers honored his name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heraclea:
Heraclea, a titular see of Thracia Prima, was the name given some four centuries before Christ to Perinthus. It was an ancient Samian colony shaped like an amphitheatre on a peninsula in the Sea of Marmora. Famous for resisting Philip of Macedonia, it prospered as a port at the junction of great sea routes. Justinian repaired its aqueducts and a palace. It survives as Eregli in the vilayet of Adrianople, with ruins on a cape nearby.

Heraclea gained see status early, by Greek tradition from apostolic times, and once counted the Bishop of Byzantium under its jurisdiction. Its suffragans rose from five to seventeen, then fell to two in modern days, Myriophyton and Metrae. Its metropolitan, titled Exarch of Thrace and Macedonia and resident at Rodosto, hands the new Patriarch of Constantinople his crozier. Lequien lists forty-eight titulars, from martyrs and Arians to patriarchs of Constantinople.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hierocaesarea: Hierocaesarea was a titular see of Lydia, suffragan to Sardis, mentioned by Ptolemy and known from its coins to have worshipped Artemis Persica. Its site lay between the villages of Beyova and Sasova, south-east of Thyatira on the Koum-Chai, a tributary of the Hermus. It appears as a bishopric in the lists of sees until the twelfth or thirteenth century, with only three bishops known: Cosinius, Zacharias, and Theodore.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-idea:
Idea is a philosophical term carrying more shades of meaning than perhaps any other, yet its sense often holds the key to a philosopher's whole system. From Descartes onward usage grew confused and inconstant, and Locke, above all, ruined the term in English writing, where it ceased to hold any fixed meaning. Locke himself calls idea whatever the understanding takes as its object when a person thinks.

For Locke it covers, indifferently, a sensation, a perception, an imagined image, and an intellectual concept. It can also mean an emotional feeling, or the external material object perceived or imagined. The entry traces the word from its Greek root, to see, through ancient, medieval, and modern philosophy. It shows how one word came to bear so many loads and why its history matters for reading philosophers fairly.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-idumea:
Idumea is the country of Edom's descendants, its name the Greek form of Hebrew Edom, apparently from the red colour of its sandstone cliffs. It lay south of Juda and the Dead Sea, though its wilderness borders are hard to fix. Genesis says Esau settled on Mount Seir, then home of the Horites, after leaving Canaan.

Mount Seir is commonly identified with Jebel esh-Shera, prolonging Moab's mountains east of the Arabah. Yet signs point to a more westerly site in the highlands between Cades and the Dead Sea's southern end. The Amarna tablets name She-e-ri south of western Palestine and a city of Edom there. The entry traces Idumea's shifting bounds, peoples, and history from Esau's settlement onward.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ivrea:
Ivrea, a suffragan see of Turin in northern Italy, stands beside the Dora Baltea river and looks out finely toward the Great St Bernard. It started as a town of the Salassi people, Rome set a colony there in 90 before Christ, and in Lombard times it grew into the seat of a dukedom.

In 870 Emperor Guy of Spoleto handed the Mark of Ivrea to his brother Anscarius, whose heirs, Berengarius II and Arduinus, chased Italy's kingship. Afterward Ivrea battled for communal freedom against the marquesses of Monferrat, and in 1248 Frederick II handed it to Savoy's count. French troops laid siege to it and took it in 1554, 1641, 1704, and 1796.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-dawson-g:
John Dawson Gilmary Shea was an American historian who pioneered the study of early Catholic missions and exploration in America. Born in New York in 1824, he learned Spanish as a clerk in a Spanish merchant's office. He published at fourteen and studied law. He entered the Jesuits at Fordham in 1847, leaving the order in 1852 under the scholarly influence of Father Martin at Montreal.

He then began systematic research into early Indian missions. He published the Discovery and Exploration of the Mississippi Valley in 1852 with original narratives of Marquette, Allouez, and Hennepin. The Westminster Review and the Athenaeum praised it. His History of the Catholic Missions among the Indian Tribes followed in 1854. His Cramoisy Series republished rare pamphlets on early voyages, while his Library of American Linguistics gathered grammars and dictionaries of Indian languages.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jose-maria-de:
José María de Zalvidea was a Spanish Franciscan who spent four decades as a missionary in California, from 1805 until his death in 1846. Born in Bilbao in 1780, he joined the order in 1798 and passed through the missionary college of San Fernando in Mexico. He then served in turn at San Fernando, San Gabriel, San Juan Capistrano, and San Luis Rey.

He was known as a model friar and a shrewd manager of mission lands and goods. Under his care Mission San Gabriel reached its peak of prosperity, and he joined a 1806 expedition seeking new mission sites while baptizing the dying along the way. The entry also notes his skill in Indian languages and his refusal to swear a political oath he saw as meddling.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-of-ari:
Joseph of Arimathea was the wealthy Jew who buried Jesus after the Crucifixion. All certain knowledge of him comes from the Gospels. A member of the Sanhedrin, the Jewish supreme council, and a secret disciple who had not agreed to Jesus' condemnation, he was a good and just man awaiting the kingdom of God.

After the Crucifixion, Joseph boldly asked Pilate for Jesus' body. With Nicodemus, who brought spices, he wrapped the body in linen and laid it in his own new rock tomb in a garden, rolling a great stone across the entrance. Later legends of his voyage to Gaul and Glastonbury, the entry warns, are fabulous and unworthy of credence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-judea:
Judea was the Jewish homeland around Jerusalem after the return from captivity. Its name comes from the Aramaic Yehudai, and its first bounds ran from Bethsur in the south to Bethoron in the north, Emmaus in the west, and the Jordan in the east. Jews scattered elsewhere did not live in Judea proper.

The entry follows Judea from a Persian province through Alexander, Egypt, and Syria to Maccabean independence from 130 to 63 BC, then Roman tribute under Pompey. Under Herod, Christ was born at Bethlehem, and under Roman procurators, Pilate condemned him and Felix and Festus handled Paul. Its history is often confused with Jerusalem's.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lady-elizabet:
Lady Elizabeth Herbert of Lea (1822-1911) was an author and philanthropist, daughter of General Charles A'Court, a soldier and member of Parliament. At twenty-four she married Sidney Herbert, a rising young politician and later Secretary of War in the Crimean campaign, when she worked closely with Florence Nightingale.

Widowed in 1861 with four sons and three daughters, she converted to Catholicism at Palermo in 1866, largely through Manning's influence, though only one child followed her. From then she led Catholic charities and poured out books, original and translated, that sold readily. Best known are Impressions of Spain, Cradle Lands on Egypt and Palestine, Wives and Mothers of the Olden Time, and Wayside Tales, plus lives of saints and statesmen.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-laodicea:
Laodicea was a titular see of Asia Minor, metropolis of Phrygia Pacatiana, first called Diospolis and Rhoas, then renamed by Antiochus II between 261 and 246 before Christ for his wife Laodice. It stood on a spur of Mount Salbacus near the Lycus river.

Achaeus ruled it in 220 before Christ, Pergamus held it next, and Mithridates' war battered it before Rome restored its prosperity. By the first century before Christ it ranked among Asia Minor's chief cities for woollen cloth and sandals, a free city and centre of a judicial district of twenty-four towns. Wealthy citizens raised fine monuments, a medical school flourished, and sceptic philosophers Antiochus and Theiodas were born there. Mongol and Turkish invasions later ruined it, leaving a stadium, theatres, and aqueduct near Denizli.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-leonard-alea:
Leonard Alea was a French polemical writer of the early nineteenth century. Born in Paris at an unknown date and dead by 1812, he was from a family of bankers. In 1801 he published anonymously his first book, L'antidote de l'atheisme. The next year a new edition, enlarged to two volumes, appeared under a new title, La religion triomphante des attentats de l'impiete, bearing his name.

The book answered Sylvien Marechal's Dictionnaire des Athees, lately published, and its timely, fair, and pointed reply won a warm welcome. Marechal himself praised his adversary's moderation. Cardinal Gerdil praised the work highly. Portalis, to whom Alea dedicated the second edition, was delighted and later tried in vain to bring him into the Council of State. Alea's only other work is Reflexions contre le divorce, also of 1802.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lorea: Lorea was a titular see in the Roman province of Arabia, a lesser bishopric under Bostra. Its city shows up only in tenth-century lists of bishops under Antioch, spelled Lourea, Dourea, and Lorea in different manuscripts. No geographer names it, its site is unknown, and nothing more is recorded of it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-medea:
Medea, a titular see of Thrace under Heraclea, takes its name, like modern Midieh, from ancient Salmydessos or Alydessos. Herodotus says its people yielded to Darius after some resistance, and Xenophon with his men subdued it only with great trouble. Sophocles, Aeschylus, Diodorus, Strabo, and Ptolemy all place its harbour on the Black Sea, open to winds, with a sandy shore bad for ships. Aeschylus wrongly sets it in Asia.

Theophanes names it Medeia in 763. Emperor John Cantacuzenus took it in 1352 and nearly died there at Turkish hands. It appears as a suffragan of Heraclea about 900 in Leo the Wise's Notitia, and again under Manuel Comnenus about 1170 and Michael VIII about 1270. Under Andronicus II it became an autocephalous archbishopric, and about 1330 a metropolitan see. The entry follows the town from classical port to Byzantine church centre.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-neocaesarea:
Pontus Polemoniacus holds Neocaesarea as a titular see, though Cabira was its first name. Mithridates the Great favoured the place as a home and raised a palace on the spot; King Polemon and those who followed him favoured it too. Pompey gave it city rank under the name Diopolis. Polemon's widow Pythodoris then chose it for her capital, calling it Sebaste. By the day of Pliny it bore the name Neocaesarea, a change its coins suggest fell under Tiberius.

The city grew into the civil and religious centre of Pontus. Gregory Thaumaturgus, a native son, took up its bishopric around 240, when only seventeen Christians lived there; by his death in 270, only seventeen pagans remained. A great council gathered there in 315, and its acts survive. Quakes levelled the city in 344 and again in 499. Through the Middle Ages Muslims and Christians fought over it, until Ottoman rule began in 1397.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-new-guinea:
New Guinea, the world's second largest island and one of its least known countries, lies immediately north of Australia. It stretches from the equator to about 12 degrees south and 130 to 154 degrees east. It is 1,490 miles long, up to 430 miles broad, covering some 310,000 square miles, with a purely conjectural population of 875,000. D'Abreu, long credited with its discovery in 1511, reached only Further India's eastern coast.

Whether Menzes, Saavedra and Grijalva reached it remains uncertain, but Ortiz de Retas landed in 1545 at the Saint Augustine River's mouth, took possession for Spain, and named it Nueva Guinea. Torres in 1606 first circumnavigated most of the island, and Tasman, Vuik and Kayto mapped southern and eastern coasts. The entry follows later exploration, the island's peoples and geography, and the Catholic missions dividing its coasts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicaea:
Nicaea, a titular see of Bithynia Secunda on Lake Ascanius in a fertile but summer-unhealthful plain, was first colonised by the Battaei as Ancora or Helicora. Destroyed by Mysians, Antigonus rebuilt it about 315 BC after beating Eumenius and called it Antigonia. Lysimachus later enlarged it and named it Nicaea for his wife.

Bithynian kings resided there almost as often as at Nicomedia, with which it struggled for influence. It was the birthplace of astronomer Hipparchus and historian Dio Cassius, and Pliny the Younger often mentions its monuments. After the first Ecumenical Council in 325, Constantine titled it metropolis, which Valens withdrew but it kept ecclesiastically. It took suffragans from Nicomedia, and in 787 hosted the second Ecumenical Council, the seventh, against Iconoclasts, with over 300 bishops.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicotera-and-:
Nicotera and Tropea, a united diocese in Calabria, joins two coastal towns battered by earthquake and Turkish raids. Nicotera, ancient Medama, was wrecked in 1783, and its first known bishop, Proculus, received a letter from Gregory the Great in 599.

Tropea, perched on a reef in the Gulf of Saint Euphemia, gave birth to the painter Spanò and the philosopher Pasquale Galluppi, and its cathedral rose again after 1783. United in 1818, the diocese counts 72 parishes and 78,000 inhabitants, with Franciscan and Sisters of Charity houses. Bishop Charles Pinti saw the city pillaged by the Turks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pamphilus-of-:
Pamphilus of Caesarea, martyred in 309, gave his name to one of the great early Christian libraries. Eusebius's life of him is lost, but his Martyrs of Palestine tells that Pamphilus came of a noble Beirut family, sold all he owned for the poor, and joined the perfect men. At Alexandria his teacher Pierius headed the famed catechetical school, and Photius drew on Pamphilus's Apology for Origen.

Settled at Caesarea, Pamphilus was ordained priest, gathered his famous library, and opened a school of theological study. His chief labour was making accurate copies of Scripture, praised in manuscript colophons. Jerome says he copied most of Origen's works with his own hand, and kept twenty-five volumes of Origen commentaries copied by Pamphilus as a precious relic. Eusebius catalogued the library in his lost life of the martyr.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-de-vine:
Peter de Vinea was the chief minister of Emperor Frederick II, born at Capua about 1190. Legal learning and elegant Latin carried him to the top of the imperial court, where he strengthened Frederick's drive toward absolute rule in Church and State. As chief judge he shaped justice and law in Sicily, and he probably helped draft the Constitutions of Melfi issued in 1231.

By 1247 he stood alone at the head of the imperial chancery as prothonotary and logothete of Sicily. The height proved his ruin. He enriched himself and his kin until, by the emperor's own account, his thefts threatened the empire's finances. Suspected also in a plot to poison Frederick at Cremona in February 1249, he fell from favour and died that year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-procopius-of-:
Procopius of Caesarea, Byzantine historian, was born in the fifth century's late years at Caesarea in Palestine and died no earlier than 562. No word survives of his parentage or schooling, save that legal training fitted him for the civil service. Ere Justin died, in 527 at the earliest, he joined Belisarius as counsellor, assessor, and secretary, following his fortunes and campaigns for twelve or fifteen years. He ranks among the greatest of the later Greek historians.

His eyewitness tale of Belisarius' wars runs to eight books. Two cover the Persian war, two the Vandalic, three the Gothic, and the eighth closes with a broad survey down to 554. His scope runs past war: he is the best source for Justinian's reign.  His peerless worth lies in his personal and official knowledge of the folk, places, and events he tells.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-red-sea:
The Red Sea, Hebrew Yam-Suph and Latin Mare Rubrum, carries a history in its name. This encyclopedia entry notes that classical historians and geographers used Red, or Erythraean, Sea for the waters of the Indian Ocean and the Persian Gulf. In modern geography the name means the north-west arm of the Indian Ocean, some 1,400 miles long, lying between Arabia to the east and Africa to the west. It runs from the Strait of Bab el-Mandeb to the head of the Gulf of Suez.

At Ras Mohammed the Sinai Peninsula splits it into the Gulf of Suez to the west and the Gulf of Akabah to the east. The entry then weighs the Exodus crossing. Some scholars favour Akabah over Suez, but that view clashes with the most natural reading of the biblical data. The traditional Suez identification should stand, though scholars still dispute the exact crossing place.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rhaphanaea:
Rhaphanaea was a titular see in Syria Secunda, suffragan of Apamea. Ancient writers mention it rarely. Josephus alone notes a nearby river that flowed six days and stopped on the seventh, probably the intermittent spring now called Fououar ed-Deir near Rafanieh in the Orontes valley. In Ptolemy's time the Third Legion, Gallica, was stationed there.

Hierocles and Georgius Cyprius list it among the towns of Syria Secunda. Crusaders passed through at the end of 1099, Baldwin took it, and it was given to the Count of Tripoli. Its known bishops include one present in 451, Zoilus about 518, and Nonnus in 536, and the see still appears in the tenth-century Notitia of Antioch.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rosea: Rosea was a titular see. The Roman Curia's official catalogue formerly listed a titular see of Rosea in Syria. The title is now held by Félix Jourdan de la Passardière, a Paris-based priest of the French Oratory. Rosea was only a corruption of Rhosus, and the latter name replaced it in 1884.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-second-counci:
The Second Council of Nicaea, seventh ecumenical council of the Catholic Church, met in 787 to settle iconoclasm, the quarrel over sacred images. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia picks up after a first attempt at Constantinople failed before violent iconoclast soldiers, sending the papal legates toward Rome. The story turns on an empress's resolve.

Reaching Sicily, the legates were recalled by Empress Irene. She replaced Constantinople's mutinous troops with officers she trusted, then in May 787 convoked a new council at Nicaea in Bithynia. The pope's letters to empress and patriarch prove Rome approved the gathering, and he later wrote to Charlemagne that the synod had been held according to his directions. The empress-regent and her young son did not attend in person, but the council restored image honour.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-seleucia-trac:
Seleucia Trachea, a metropolitan see of Isauria in the patriarchate of Antioch, was built about 300 BC by Seleucus I Nicator. He likely joined the older towns of Olbia and Hyria under his own name. This entry traces its Roman career as an autonomous city and later capital of Isauria. Its council of 359 drew some 160 bishops. They backed the homoiousian formula and condemned the chief errors of the Anomoeans. Hilary of Poitiers was present.

Fame came chiefly from the tomb of Saint Thecla, the virgin of Iconium converted by Paul. Her shrine, rebuilt by Emperor Zeno in the fifth century, ranked among the most celebrated in the Christian world. The entry also notes the imperial governor's two legions and the Christian burial ground west of town. The ruins are still called Meriamlik.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sir-ambrose-s:
Ambrose Shea, born in Newfoundland on 17 September 1815, died in London on 30 July 1905. At twenty-two he took up journalism successfully for eight years, then turned to trade. Elected to Newfoundland's House of Assembly in 1848, he sat continuously except for a short break in 1869 until 1886, serving as speaker in 1855 and again in 1860. He negotiated Newfoundland's entry into reciprocity treaty arrangements in 1855 and sat unofficially in the executive government from 1864 to 1869.

He went as Newfoundland's delegate to the Quebec confederation conference in 1864. In 1883 he served as commissioner to London's International Fisheries Exhibition, then went to Washington, where he brought the State Department into harmony with Canada over extending the Washington Treaty of 1885. Knighted in 1883 for distinguished service, he was named Governor of the Bahamas in 1887. There he revived a stagnant colony, starting the sisal fiber industry, organizing a public bank, laying the Bahamas-Florida cable, and fostering trade in every branch.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-dorothea:
Two very different women share this entry, and the piece gives each her own space. The first Dorothea, virgin and martyr at Caesarea in Cappadocia, died on 6 February 311 under Diocletian's persecution. Mocked on her way to execution by the lawyer Theophilus, she sent him roses and fruits from her bridegroom's garden. He confessed the faith at once and was himself put to death. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 calls this the oldest form of her legend.

Gardeners still claim her as patroness, and trees are blessed on her feast in some places. The second Dorothea, of Montau, was a fourteenth-century recluse who married a hot-tempered sword-cutler at seventeen. Together the pair show how one name can carry both a martyr's tale and a mystic's hard married life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-gregory-of:
Gregory of Neocaesarea, called the Wonder-worker, built a church from seventeen souls into a Christian city. Born at Neocaesarea in Pontus about 213, originally named Theodore, gift of God, he grew up pagan and knew nothing of Christianity until his father's death left him fourteen. With his brother he set out for Beirut and Roman law, but at Caesarea they met Origen, head of Alexandria's catechetical school. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 dates his death at Neocaesarea to 270 or 275.

Origen's charm won both youths, who forgot Beirut and gave themselves to the great teacher. Consecrated at forty over a community of only seventeen, Gregory ruled thirty years with zeal the record can only infer. His pastoral work is little known and his writings survive incomplete, yet ancient references let his work be rebuilt in detail. The entry honours a bishop eclipsed by his own wonder-working title.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-theodore-o:
Theodore of Amasea, surnamed Tyro, was a soldier martyr whose cult spread from Pontus across the East. Tyro marks not a young recruit but his service in the Cohors Tyronum. He suffered at Amasea, and his body was carried to Euchais, renamed Theodoropolis in his honour. His martyrdom seems to have fallen on 17 February 306 under Galerius and Maximian.

The Greek and Armenian calendars also keep him on Lent's first Saturday. Rome's Martyrology lists him under 9 November. In the twelfth century his body moved to Brindisi, where he is patron, and his head is enshrined at Gaeta. Churches bear his name at Constantinople, Jerusalem, and Damascus, and a round church at the foot of the Palatine in Rome is dedicated to him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stratonicea:
Stratonicea was an ancient city of Caria in Asia Minor, and this entry gathers what is known of its past and its bishops. Antiochus Soter founded it, perhaps on the site of older Idrias, and named it for his wife Stratonice. Later rulers adorned it with fine monuments until it ranked among the chief towns of the region.

Ceded to Rhodes, besieged by Labienus, and praised by Pliny as a free town, it also hosted the assembly of Carian cities at the nearby temple of Zeus Chrysaoreus. Only three bishops are known by name, from councils in 451, 692, and 787. Today the place is the small town of Eski Hissar, its theatre, tombs, and columns still standing among extensive ruins.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-priory-of:
A Cambridgeshire house of Austin Canons, founded for Mary and Saint Nicholas, is sketched here from scanty remains. Henry I stands behind its founding, though Dugdale found no foundation charter. A deed of 1333, ceding patronage rights at elections from Elizabeth de Burgh, Lady de Clare, supports Leland and Speed in naming Richard de Clare as founder or patron. 

Edward Mortimer, Earl of March, under Henry V also patronised the house. No register survives, and ruins run meagre. Lysons noted remains inside a later mansion on the site, no older than Elizabeth's reign. Chief among them stood an undercroft thirty-six feet by twenty-two, groined and pillared, now split into two rooms, with a row of bracketed arches.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-titular-see-o:
Phocaea was a titular see subject to Ephesus, founded in the eleventh century BC by colonists from Phocis led by two Athenians. They settled first on a small offshore island granted by the Cymaeans, between the bays of Cyme and Hermaeus, twenty-three miles north of Smyrna. Admitted to the Ionian Confederation, it became one of the great seafaring cities of antiquity, with two fine ports and an enterprising people.

Rome took the town in 189 BC under the praetor Aemilius Regillus, who left its boundaries and laws untouched. The Phocaeans later backed Aristonicus against Rome, but Massilia's plea saved them from harsh punishment. In time the harbour silted up, trade faded, and the people left. Venetians traded there after 1082, Genoese supplanted them, and in 1275 Michael VIII gave the city and its alum mines to Manuel Zaccaria.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-zeno-of-elea:
Zeno of Elea was a Greek philosopher born at Elea about 490 B.C. At his birthplace Xenophanes and Parmenides had founded the Eleatic school, whose chief doctrine was the oneness and immutability of reality. It distrusted sense-knowledge, which seems to testify to multiplicity and change. Zeno's contribution, a treatise now lost, argued indirectly against the reality of motion and the existence of the manifold.

This method of indirect proof, or reductio ad absurdum, appears to have been used first by Zeno. The arguments are fallacious, resting on false notions of motion and space, as Aristotle readily shows, yet they were specious enough to puzzle opponents before logic became a science. They earned Zeno the title of first dialectician, helped prepare the way for Sophist skepticism, and foreshadowed the eristic method of strife.
cerberus-the-dog-of-hades-the-history-of:
Maurice Bloomfield, professor of Sanskrit and comparative philology at Johns Hopkins, traced one myth across cultures in a 1905 book from the Open Court Publishing Company, dedicated to Max Müller. His frontispiece shows a Greek vase: Herakles drags two-headed Cerberus from Hades by a chain through its jaw, while Persephone protests and Hermes watches.

Bloomfield starts with Homer's souls gibbering like bats on their way to the asphodel meadow. He then turns east, to the two dogs of Yama in the Rig-Veda, one black and one spotted, read as moon dog and sun dog. Greek and Indian watchdogs of the dead are set side by side. The argument is comparative mythology in full dress.
chronicles-of-avonlea:
L M Montgomery set Chronicles of Avonlea among the neighbors of Anne Shirley's Prince Edward Island village, dedicating the stories to a dear friend gone beyond. Anne herself opens the first tale, The Hurrying of Ludovic, curled on a window-seat watching the stars while slow Ludovic needs hurrying into marriage. Twelve stories follow the island's courtships, feuds, and kindnesses.

Old Lady Lloyd, Pa Sloane's purchase, the quarantine at Alexander Abraham's, and the winning of Lucinda, whose anger melts into malicious smiling on the walk home, fill the middle. Montgomery writes village comedy with a poet's eye for blossom and lane. Readers of Anne of Green Gables will find the same world widened to its grown-ups.
cytherea:
Joseph Hergesheimer's Cytherea is a novel of middle age, desire and discontent, opening on a golf course late in the year. Lee Randon, past forty-five, stands alone on a shorn hill above frost-killed grass, realising that this is probably his last game until spring.

No partner would join him this late in the year, and his younger kinsman Peyton Morris has refused with a frankness that leaves Lee cross. From that wintry, solitary opening Hergesheimer unfolds a story of a man reassessing his marriage, his work and his appetites. The novel suits readers who like polished, psychologically attentive fiction about people whose outward lives look settled while their inner lives stir.
doe-osti-17010971-peer-exchange-demystif:
Slide deck from an August 13, 2026 peer exchange, led by Michael Deru and colleagues at the National Laboratory of the Rockies, explains dual fuel heat pumps for building managers. A dual fuel unit pairs an electric heat pump with a gas or propane furnace in one rooftop system. The session was built to clear up common myths about such units.

One myth holds that dual fuel units raise utility bills, which the slides trace to poor control settings. Another holds that controls cannot aid demand flexibility. Answers cover fixed and dynamic switch over points, balance point switching based on live fuel prices, and variable speed compressors and fans. The takeaway is that control choices can lower cost and ease grid demand.
doe-osti-17124817-multi-port-converter-i:
Logan Snow of GE Research reports on a multi port converter for district energy systems, under award DE-EE0010279. District systems serve many buildings from shared plants, and each added solar array, battery, or heat source usually needs its own converter and interconnection. A single multi port unit promises to tie them together through one box.

The converter is built from modular power boards around a silicon carbide module rated at 2 kilovolts and 400 amperes, supporting a 1500 volt direct current bus. Modules can be arranged as inverters, battery converters, isolated converters, or multilevel bridges. Economic modeling found yearly return about 33 percent above a baseline system, with capital cost down 17 percent and no interconnection delays. Five use cases were picked for deeper checks.
doe-osti-17198164-proposal-of-tactically:
Megan Tribble, Jerome Stofleth, and Venner Saul of Sandia propose a new work line on tactically deployed microreactors, in report SAND2026-27239R dated September 2026. Microreactors promise power for hard tactical settings, but the technology is young and design effort still centers on performance and reliability. The authors argue that threat thinking deserves equal weight, early.

Fixing weaknesses after deployment is far costlier than designing them out. Sandia's breadth in engineering and energetics, plus its test facilities, fits the task well, they argue. The proposal calls for a standing system for tactical threat assessment and mitigation development. Background chapters survey commercial and tactical microreactor efforts before the short conclusion.
doe-osti-3007483-improved-pare-pressuriz:
Los Alamos report LA-UR-25-31816, by Murray Moore and six co-authors, describes improved PARE equipment, the pressurized rig used to measure how much powder becomes airborne in an accident. Two fractions matter for safety work: the airborne release fraction and the respirable fraction that can reach deep into lungs. One co-author joined from the University of California, Davis.

The document, which supersedes LA-UR-24-30006, details the rig and its instruments, including an aerodynamic particle sizer that counts particles by size. It also works through test-powder density, showing how loose bulk density and a shape factor set the density the sizer must assume. Cerium oxide serves as the test powder in the worked examples. Safety analysts use such rigs to bound what a spill or fire could put into the air.
doe-osti-3007887-recommendations-for-a-f:
Don Kovacic, Tom Pham, and Joe Giaquinto, with three co-authors, set out what a material control plan should hold for TRISO fuel plants in an October 2025 Oak Ridge report, ORNL/SPR-2025/4252. TRISO fuel packs uranium into tiny coated particles, which changes how a plant counts and guards its nuclear material.

The plan follows the parts the Nuclear Regulatory Commission expects in a Fundamental Nuclear Material Control plan. It covers stock counts, count gaps, and how measurement error is worked out. Random and systematic errors are treated apart, each backed by repeat readings and standards. Future work points to a full generic plan, nondestructive assay checks, and Raman spectroscopy checks.
doe-osti-3013833-a-computational-tool-co:
North Carolina State University's Yousry Azmy led this final report for NEUP project 22-26770, INL/RPT-25-89328, dated December 2025, on a shape optimization tool that works with the NEAMS nuclear simulation codes. Reactor designers usually test a handful of hand-drawn shapes. This tool instead lets the physics search shape space on its own, using a simulated annealing strategy driven by neutronics results.

The OpenFSAM code was attached to the MPACT neutronics package and demonstrated on a two-dimensional fuel pin cell. Three framings were tried: swapping fuel and moderator pixels on a 20-by-20 grid, flipping pixels freely, and varying the radii of an annular pin. Objectives moved from simply maximizing the multiplication factor to a revenue proxy balancing reactivity against coolant pressure drop and fuel cost.
doe-osti-3015142-instrument-requirements: Installation requirements for two Los Alamos instruments bound for IAEA work fill LA-UR-26-20532, issued January 26, 2026, by Schreiber, Schoenemann, and Kim. The hosted text is a specification sheet rather than a study: the SOFIA spectrometer needs 1.5 by 2.5 meters of lab space and a 220 volt 20 amp circuit for its compressor. Its DRC-100 cryostat stands 102 centimeters tall and weighs about 45 kilograms, cooled by a Cryomech PT403 compressor on two ten-foot hoses. A DES section follows the same format.
doe-osti-3016267-illinois-basin-regional:
The University of Illinois Illinois Sustainable Technology Center submitted this final report on February 4, 2026, for award DE-FE0032375. Kevin C OBrien was principal investigator and Chinmoy Baroi lead engineer. The report covers the feasibility phase of a planned Illinois Basin regional direct air capture hub. Such a hub is a cluster of plants that would pull carbon dioxide from the air.

Anchor capture technologies came from CarbonCapture Inc and Heirloom, and the team scoped an initial hub design around them at pre-design stage. Appendices identify storage and use sites across several states, many within 15 miles of planned capture sites. They also review the status of Class VI well permits. A phased buildout plan assumes private capital arriving beyond 2030. The filing gives reviewers the ownership, transport, and business outlines for judging the hub.
doe-osti-3021299-calendar-year-2024-unde:
DOE Environmental Management Nevada Program letter report DOE/EMNV--0056, Revision 1, dated September 2025, reports calendar year 2024 groundwater sampling under the Underground Test Area activity at the Nevada National Security Site. Decades of underground nuclear testing left contamination in groundwater, and this program samples wells year after year to track it. The letter report is the annual record for the characterization and monitoring locations sampled in 2024.

The document gives well completion diagrams and laboratory results by location. At characterization well ER-EC-15, samples collected on September 24 and 25, 2024, were analyzed for low-level tritium, with results reported as below detection limits of roughly 2.2 to 2.7 in the stated units. Similar tables cover the other wells. Regulators use these annual letters to confirm that sampling happened as the closure plans require.
doe-osti-3021664-new-principles-of-self-:
Paul W. K. Rothemund's final technical report for DOE award DE-SC-0020993, from the California Institute of Technology, dated March 5, 2026, reports a $769,000 project on self-organization at the molecular scale. Inside cells, motor proteins haul cargo along microtubule tracks, and DNA condenses into droplets. The project asked what new forms of organization emerge when DNA condensates, microtubules, and motors act together, and whether those principles can be engineered deliberately.

The work combined experiments on these three components with theoretical analysis. One thread applied ideas from ray optics to predict how moving particles are trapped or guided, computing trapping probabilities across geometry ratios and times. The report closes with conclusions, recommendations, and lessons learned for building synthetic systems that organize themselves. Total project costs equaled the DOE share, with no recipient cost share.
doe-osti-3024523-final-technical-report-:
Roger Ghanem of the University of Southern California reports award DE-SC0021307, done under the FASTMath institute, on putting error ranges on high-dimensional systems. Engineers often must predict behavior with little data, tangled dependencies, and models known to be imperfect. His framework hunts for low-dimensional manifold structure hiding inside the outputs that matter, then works on that smaller stage.

Polynomial chaos expansions, projection-based dimension reduction, and chance-based learning on manifolds combine into one operator-based view. Functional sensitivity scores extend the usual idea: they show how input doubt shapes whole regions of the output spread, including failure zones, not just single numbers. Model error enters by treating spectral coefficients as random values that Bayesian updating can refine against observations. Applications span fluids, structures, materials with General Motors, and plasma physics with Princeton's laboratory.
doe-osti-3025188-scalable-solar-fuels-pr:
Xin Qian of Saint-Gobain Ceramics and Plastics led award DE-EE0010739, from October 2023 to March 2025, with Sossina M Haile at Northwestern and Ahmed Ghoniem at MIT. The project pursued solar fuels from a reactor train: sunlight heats perovskite oxides until they shed oxygen, then steam gives the oxygen back and leaves hydrogen. The materials must survive that redox cycling thousands of times.

The team synthesized single-phase CTM5050 perovskite and a calcium titanium manganese oxide family with titanium fractions from 0.4 to 0.8, and made porous monoliths at 40 to 66 percent porosity. Above 1150 degrees, water splitting was limited mostly by gas phase thermodynamics, not material speed. Some compositions held fuel output above 12 milliliters of hydrogen per gram of oxide after long cycling, with reduction at 1350 degrees.
doe-osti-3031151-porous-polymer-to-modif:
John C. Stormont of the University of New Mexico led this project under award DE-EE0009787, running from March 2022 to June 2025, with Utah and Sandia partners. Enhanced geothermal systems crack hot rock so water can carry heat to the surface, but some fractures steal too much flow. The team built polymer materials that can be injected down a well and lodge in chosen fractures far from the bore, changing how easily fluid passes.

The carriers are tiny capsules with acrylic shells that break down at set heat. Heat tests darkened the capsules and confirmed shell breakdown, and a third store-bought monomer mix ruptured at lower temperatures. The team also packed a hardening agent inside capsules with high efficiency and showed the injected polymer setting at the target hot zone conditions.
doe-osti-3363538-coupled-investigation-o:
Kayla A. Kroll of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory leads this final technical report for a University of Utah award (DE-EE0007080, October 2021 to March 2026) on enhanced geothermal systems. Partners included Penn State's Chris Marone and Los Alamos researchers. The project asked how fracture permeability changes reservoir stress and seismic slip as fluid circulates through hot rock.

The team combined core flood experiments with reactive transport models that couple heat, flow, mechanics, and chemistry. Two core samples from the Utah FORGE site, drawn from about 5,477 and 10,955 feet deep, anchored the simulations, which were calibrated against the laboratory measurements. The work informs how stimulation and circulation can be run without inviting damaging earthquakes.
doe-osti-3376034-reassessing-double-ende:
Idaho National Laboratory report INL/RPT-26-90155, dated January 2026, asks whether a fifty-year-old reactor safety rule still earns its keep. Five authors wrote it, led by Kevan Weaver and John Wagner of the lab. The rule guards against a double-ended guillotine break: a main coolant pipe snapping clean in two, at both ends at once. Plants spend heavily on restraints and shields sized for that worst case. The team weighs five decades of run data against the rule's roots.

Three lines of proof are laid out. Run history comes first, then odds math, then the materials science of how pipes truly fail. The leak-before-break concept shows the prize. NRC staff credit it with savings in the hundreds of millions of dollars, by sparing backfits at many plants. The authors argue that guarding against events no longer seen as credible wastes money and adds upkeep load.
doe-osti-3376517-audible-noise-modeling-:
Sandia National Laboratories report SAND2026-22713, printed in June 2026, models the sound of a hydrogen leak inside rail maintenance shops. Kevin Mangala Gitushi, Marina Miletic, and Brian D. Ehrhart wrote it. Hydrogen locomotives are coming to rail yards, and their fuel lines will be serviced indoors. A pressurized leak screams. That noise can pass safe hearing limits long before the gas itself is a fire risk, so crews need to know how loud a leak gets, and how fast.

Tests compared leak noise across gases and pipe sizes. Hydrogen's sound level sat within five decibels of the comparison gas for most mixes, at a leak rate of 4.17 cubic feet per minute. Pipes of quarter-inch and three-eighths-inch bore were used. Crimped pipes stood in for lines crushed in a crash, a worst case since gas speeds up in a pinch. Sound was read from twenty hertz to forty thousand.
doe-osti-3377246-non-neutron-transmutati:
Argonne National Laboratory final report ANL/NSE-26/2 lays out ways to burn down used nuclear fuel without a fast neutron reactor doing all the work. T. K. Kim heads a team from Argonne, Brookhaven, Idaho, Michigan, MIT, and Berkeley. The long-lived fission products in spent fuel drive its hazard for ages. Transmutation can shorten that span. The study tests photon and hybrid routes in place of pure neutron burning.

One design pairs a photon source with a neutron blanket. A laser Compton source makes the photons. They strike a central target loaded with long-lived fission products. Around it, 896 pins hold 214.46 kilograms of technetium-99. Heavy water reflects stray neutrons back in. Tables give pin pitch, blanket thickness, and rates per year. The point is a yardstick: how much waste each route destroys, and at what cost in gear and power.
doe-osti-3436734-specifications-of-fipd-:
Argonne report ANL/CFCT-23/15 Revision 1, by Kun Mo and Aaron Oaks, specifies fission gas release data in the FIPD database. FIPD stores irradiation and physics data for fast reactor metallic fuels. Clear specs keep old test records usable.

Formulas in the pages derive capsule pressure from measured volumes and pressures. Helium backfill readings feed those calculations step by step. Many repeat readings were averaged for reported values. Results flow into post-irradiation records, reports, and memos. Data users can trace each reported gas value back to its own raw pressure readings.
doe-osti-3662051-himu-high-multiplicatio:
Lawrence Livermore report LLNL-TR-2003059, dated September 2026, is a benchmark evaluation called HiMu. Evaluators Jesse Norris, William Zywiec, and Daniel Siefman are printed, with David Heinrichs as internal reviewer. The work covers subcritical measurements of water-moderated fuel rod lattices. Rods held low-enriched uranium dioxide fuel in a square pitch. Such benchmark data help check the computer codes used for nuclear criticality safety.

Sections describe the subcritical assembly, its tank, grid plates, water reflector, and helium-3 detector wells in fine detail. Test cases step down from just over a thousand fuel rods to smaller loadings. Material data include fuel enrichment checks on ten pellet samples drawn at random from the stock. Uncertainty work weighs random and systematic errors side by side. The report is dedicated to Gary Harms of Sandia, whose earlier experiments laid the base for the work. Two past benchmark evaluations are built on directly.
doe-osti-3816356-ornl-infrastructure-sta:
Oak Ridge letter report ORNL/LTR-2025/4131, dated September 2025, updates planning for the BEA research reactor shipping cask. Kory Linton, Jason Harp, and Susan Case of Idaho are the printed authors. The cask will move irradiated fuel and materials between Oak Ridge and Idaho for user research. Before loaded runs can start, the lab must clear rules, contracts, and safety reviews. Fiscal Year 2025 carried most of that groundwork.

The Nuclear Regulatory Commission issued the cask's certificate amendment in June 2025. Oak Ridge panels then cleared the work, with the top safety panel signing off in August. A transport services firm finished upkeep on the tracking unit in September. Loaded shipments still wait on inner basket hardware from Orano, ordered in July with delivery due March 2026. An empty cask dry run is set for October 2025 to prove the crew can receive, handle, and return it.
from-the-lips-of-the-sea:
Scollard gathers a book of short poems on the sea. An opening sonnet urges the reader to sit by the shore. The sea, it says, keeps the secrets of old kings and myths. Poems follow on mist, tides, and a sailor's dirge. A sea rover, a shell, and a mist barque supply images.

The moods shift with the hours of the day. Dawn, dusk, and moonrise by the sea each get a lyric. Wild geese and autumn weather widen the range. One long piece builds into a symphony of the sea. The verse is musical and pictorial throughout. Scollard writes the ocean as speaker, sibyl, and master. It is a slim volume for lovers of sea poetry.
further-chronicles-of-avonlea:
L. M. Montgomery's Further Chronicles of Avonlea collects fifteen stories of the Green Gables country. The subtitle promises personalities and events in and about Avonlea, home of Anne Shirley. Aunt Cynthia's Persian Cat opens the volume, to its narrator's lasting anguish. The Materializing of Cecil, Jane's Baby, and The Return of Hester follow.

Sara's Way, The Education of Betty, and The Conscience Case of David Bell fill the middle. Tannis of the Flats, the story of a half-breed girl's love and death, closes the book in a darker key. An introduction compares Montgomery's Prince Edward Island to Longfellow's Acadia. Anne herself appears only at the edges; the islanders take the stage. Humour and pathos, the introduction rightly says, are compounded in every tale. The Chronicles volumes are the short-fiction attic of the Anne books, full of their weather.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FlyingEagleMoti: Sean Mansfield of Flying Eagle Motion Pictures wrote to Harold Weisberg on September 30, 1992. A film company's letter to the veteran assassination researcher suggests screen interest in his subject, though the surviving record gives no letter text or project details. The entry stands as a dated piece of correspondence between a motion picture company and Weisberg.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PicturesTomAlye: Postal Return Receipt (Fragment): the fragment of a postal return receipt connected with Weisberg - no document can be identified. A slip, kept. A single fragment. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the files and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-pursue-release-01-do: FBI File 62-HQ-83894 is a headquarters file, and Release 01 in the PURSUE set covers serials 246 through 301. A serial is a single document inside a bureau file, numbered as it was added. The release gathers excerpts from the FBI's Central Records Center. Readers get the bureau's paper in its own order: memos, letters, and reports as clerks filed them, rather than a summary written later.
govdocs-archive_org-pursue-release-02-do: United States Air Force inspectors examined security at Sandia Base and reported on April 7, 1949. The report came from Detachment D of the 1100th USAF Special Reporting Group. Sandia, in New Mexico, was central to the early atomic weapons program, so its guards, fences, and procedures mattered greatly. Inspection reports like this one show how the young Air Force policed the secrets of the first Cold War years.
hermann-and-dorothea:
Johann Wolfgang von Goethe's Hermann and Dorothea, translated by Ellen Frothingham, is praised in its introductory note as nearly perfect in its kind. The poem, in nine cantos of hexameters, tells how refugees fleeing the French Revolutionary armies pass a German town in 1796. Its basis was a 1731 story of Salzburg Protestants expelled for their faith.

Hermann, the innkeeper's son, carries help to the fugitives and finds Dorothea among them, drawing water at a spring with stone benches and living waters bubbling forth. His parents, the pastor, and the apothecary debate the match before the betrothal. Goethe's domestic epic of war at the doorstep became Germany's best-loved household poem.
hills-and-the-sea:
Hilaire Belloc gathered these essays and travel pieces under one title. Belloc writes as a walker, sailor, and keen Catholic man of letters. The pieces roam hills, roads, and coasts, mostly in England and France. A long comic dedication to a friend sets the warm, combative tone.

Some pieces recall marches, thirst, and night quarters on the road. Others muse on faith, history, and the look of old towns. Belloc's prose is firm, rhythmic, and full of strong views. Readers who like travel writing with mind and muscle in it will find a rich, varied set of pieces here.
homeward-bound-or-the-chase-a-tale-of-th:
James Fenimore Cooper wrote this sea tale, here in a complete one-volume new edition of 1871. His preface explains the first plan. The book was to show the present state of American society. Travellers fresh from Europe would see the country's features with sharper eyes than natives.

The Effingham party's voyage home gives Cooper his stage. Captain Truck, rough in his humanity, frees an Arab prisoner with a kick and a laugh in one scene. A chase at sea supplies the action of the subtitle. Manners, politics, and shipboard life mix throughout. The tale sets up the homecoming that its sequel then judges.
irish-wit-and-humor-anecdote-biography-o:
Irish Wit and Humor, an anecdote biography of Swift, Curran, O'Leary, and O'Connell, was issued at New York in 1872. Dean Swift heads the contents, from his birth to his charity and humor. Resolutions when I come to be old and a meditation upon a broomstick are among the Swift pieces. Curran's cases follow.

Curran advises a farmer who left a hundred pounds with a publican who denied it. Have patience, my friend, is his opening counsel in the tale. Courtroom retorts and dinner wit fill the lives. The anonymous book gathers Irish talk as short, pointed stories for popular reading.
jack-archer-a-tale-of-the-crimea:
George Alfred Henty's Jack Archer tells the Crimean War through a young midshipman, in this full edition. The chapter list matches the 1883 tale, from school to Sebastopol's capture. Count Preskoff's disgrace at court deepens the Russian strand in this copy. Smerskoff presses for Katinka's hand against her father's refusal.

The marriage would advantage all parties, Smerskoff argues, and will not take refusal as final. Jack's escapes, Polish insurgents, and a lion's den fill his own strand. Balaklava and Inkerman supply the famous battles. This edition presents the tale in its complete twenty-six chapters.
journal-of-landsborough-s-expedition-fro:
