William Landsborough's journal records his expedition from Carpentaria in search of Burke and Wills. It was published at Melbourne in 1862, with a map of his route. Four search parties went out after anxiety grew for the missing explorers. Howitt led from Melbourne, McKinlay from Adelaide, Walker from Rockhampton, and Landsborough from Brisbane.

Howitt soon learned the sad fate of Burke and Wills, but the other parties had already started. The brig Firefly carried Landsborough's party and horses from Brisbane to the Gulf of Carpentaria in August. The steamship Victoria assisted the search from the sea. This pamphlet presents Landsborough's own journal and letters, the record of the northern search party's work.
legends-that-every-child-should-know-a-s:
Hamilton Wright Mabie edited Legends That Every Child Should Know for young people. Blanche Ostertag drew its pictures and decorations. Guy, Earl of Warwick, fronts the book as an example hero.

Mabie's introduction argues that word histories open a rich past. His selections gather great legends from many times and lands. Heroes, saints, and wonder tales stand side by side here. Each story is shortened for child readers without losing wonder. Families used such collections to pass classic tales to the next generation. William Tell and King Arthur stand among its heroes. Mabie aimed at the stories no child should grow up missing.
miscellanea:
Juliana Horatia Ewing left these papers unpublished at her death, and her sister gathered them for the SPCK. The preface admits the pieces appear to complete her works rather than for their own worth. Ewing herself never republished them. Her sister notes her gift for mimicry, in acting and in writing alike.

The first four stories imitate the early sensation novels, like Lady Audley's Secret and The Moonstone. The Mystery of the Bloody Hand even adds a glimpse of the supernatural to everyday scenes. Other pieces grew from the family manuscript magazine of Ewing's girlhood. The volume preserves the experiments of a beloved children's author, juvenilia and all.
nasa-tm-19710001489-diagnostics-of-a-sup:
Fredric A. Baker, Masayuki Omura, and Austin H. Somes of the Ames Research Center wrote this report in November 1970. It describes a microwave tool for studying a supersonic plasma stream. Plasma is a gas so hot that its atoms split into charged parts.

Their interferometer measures electron density and collision rates across the jet. Unlike most such tools, both of its horns sit inside the plasma stream itself. The report weighs the gains and drawbacks of that bold placement. A main system did the measuring, and a second system checked its results. Readings of this kind help engineers design gear that must fly through plasma.
north-south-and-over-the-sea:
M. E. Francis, also named as Mrs Francis Blundell, published North, South and Over the Sea in 1902. H. M. Brock drew the pictures. A note says some tales first ran in the Cornhill Magazine, Longman's Magazine, and Country Life. The book sits in a Country Life library of fiction.

The contents sort the stories by place, under North, South, and Over the Sea. Golden Sally and The Conquest of Radical Ted stand under North. Heather in Holborn crosses country and city in its title. Under South come The Romance of Brother John and Giles in Luck. The Wold Love and the Noo speaks in dialect. Village love and luck fill the set.
out-of-the-fog-a-story-of-the-sea:
Charles K. Ober's Out of the Fog is a sailor's testimony with an introduction by Dr. Wilfred T. Grenfell, the Labrador medical missionary. Grenfell says he urged the narrative into print. For twenty years he worked on the Labrador coast, charting its dangerous waterways. His errand was to translate God's fatherhood into plain language there. He calls Ober's story one of the tracks left by those who found the way before.

Ober begins at nineteen, when the lure of the sea prevailed and he shipped for a four-month fishing trip on the Newfoundland Banks. What follows is a conversion story in oilskins: fog, fishing schooners, and a young man's road to faith, framed by Grenfell's hearty prayers for its unprecedented circulation.
parker-s-second-reader-national-series-o: The sample hosted here shows only the front matter of Parker's Second Reader, the title pages and the start of its 1851 copyright entry, with no reading lessons visible. The title page names Richard G. Parker, principal of a Boston school, as the author and describes the book as the second part of a national series of reading selections for younger classes in schools and academies. It was sold by A. S. Barnes and Burr of New York.
patty-and-azalea:
Carolyn Wells's Patty and Azalea, published in 1919, finds Patty Fairfield grown up and married. The opening chapter puts her in the sun parlour at Wistaria Porch with her husband Bill, called Little Billee, and their baby daughter. Bill calms Patty's fear that the baby is choking; she is only laughing.

Into this settled home comes Azalea, a new relative whom one chapter calls "that awful Azalea." Mysterious callers, a disappearance, and Azalea's own story follow. The book mixes domestic comedy with a light mystery, as Patty's household absorbs a difficult guest.
podcast-dannyjones-I4Rzxmr63EA:
Ice swimmer Ryan Stramrood tells Danny Jones why swimming through shark-filled ice water is good for the brain. Stramrood, a South African endurance swimmer, has completed extreme cold swims around the world. His claim is that the shock rewires stress and sharpens the mind.

Stramrood describes what the cold does to the body in the first brutal minutes. He explains the calm that follows and how he trains his brain to choose it. Jones asks about the sharks, the risks, and who should never try it. Hardy and curious listeners get a bracing talk on the cold-water cure.
reminiscences-of-scottish-life-character:
E. B. Ramsay, Dean of Edinburgh, wrote these sketches of Scottish life and character, here in a twenty-second edition of 1874, enlarged with his last corrections. A memoir of Dean Ramsay by Cosmo Innes stands at the front. The contents that follow map a vanished Scotland of faith, food, and talk.

Chapters treat Scottish religious feelings and observances, then old Scottish conviviality. The old Scottish domestic servant gets a chapter of her own, and Scottish judges get theirs. A long chapter collects humour drawn from Scottish expressions and proverbs. Ramsay, a churchman with an ear for stories, preserves the speech and habits of a passing world.
riders-to-the-sea:
J. M. Synge's one-act play Riders to the Sea is printed here with an introduction telling how it was made. On Synge's second visit to the Aran Islands, the introduction says, he heard of a man washed up on the far coast of Donegal. The dead man was known by his dress as a native of Inishmaan, the middle island of the Aran group.

A tale of second sight, common among Celtic peoples, gave the play its title and its other strand. The scene is a cottage on Inishmaan. The introduction calls the result a tragedy of dramatic irony and noble pity, with no equal among its contemporaries, wrought from elemental forces in a far place.
rivers-to-the-sea:
Sara Teasdale gathered these lyrics under the title Rivers to the Sea, dedicating the book to Ernst. Part one alone fills the contents shown, in a list of more than thirty poems. Spring Night leads, and The Flight, New Love and Old, and The Look follow in a vein of love and season.

City and travel stand beside the love songs: From the Woolworth Tower, Broadway, In a Restaurant, and In the Train. Swans, The Kiss, and The Lighted Window give the set its images of grace and longing. I Shall Not Care, one of her best-known titles, stands near the end of the part, with Desert Pools to close it.
saved-at-sea:
Mrs. O. F. Walton, author of Christie's Old Organ, A Peep Behind the Scenes, and Little Dot, wrote Saved at Sea, a lighthouse story. A front picture is captioned On the Look Out. The contents list twelve chapters, opening with My Strange Home, The Flare at Sea, and The Bundle Saved. Later titles include Little Timpey, The Unclaimed Sunbeam, The Old Gentleman's Question, A Thick Fog, Waiting for the Boat, A Change in the Lighthouse, Our New Neighbour, and On the Rock. The list closes with The Sunbeam Claimed.

Chapter I, My Strange Home, opens on the day the narrator was born, and it was a strange day. Waves beat against the lighthouse, and wind roared and raged against everything. Had the lighthouse not been built firmly into the solid rock, it and all within it must have been swept into the deep sea. It was a terrible storm.
stories-by-english-authors-the-sea:
Stories by English Authors: The Sea gathers The Extraordinary Adventure of a Chief Mate by W. Clark Russell, Quarantine Island by Sir Walter Besant, The Rock Scorpions and two more tales by unnamed writers, The Master of the Chrystolite by G. B. O'Halloran, and Melissa's Tour by Grant Allen.

Russell opens with a newspaper report from 1876. The ship Hercules felt a quake in the North Atlantic. Land rose two miles off. Chief officer Michael Balfour fell overboard and was given up for lost. Balfour then tells his own side. Storms, strange islands, and shipboard peril fill the rest of the volume.
stories-of-ships-and-the-sea:
Jack London's Stories of Ships and the Sea came out as Little Blue Book No. 1169, edited by E. Haldeman-Julius and printed at Girard, Kansas, under a 1922 copyright held by Charmian London. The small, cheap volume holds five sea tales.

The contents list Chris Farrington: Able Seaman, Typhoon Off the Coast of Japan, The Lost Poacher, The Banks of the Sacramento, and In Yeddo Bay. The first opens with an old sailor scolding young Chris for thinking himself as good as an able seaman on an American ship. London writes from his own years before the mast, with salt speech and hard weather throughout.
sunk-at-sea:
R. M. Ballantyne's Sunk at Sea, dated 1869 in this printing, is a boys' adventure tale whose first chapter treats of the hero's early life and touches on domestic matters. The hero, William Osten, was a wanderer by nature, born with a thirst for adventure nothing could quench.

Baby Will kept his mother in a fever of alarm and all but broke his nurse's heart by escaping the nursery on hands and knees long before he could walk. Yet he never cried, and seemed a natural philosopher, grave and inquiring, silent except when hard pressed by hunger or pain. Ballantyne builds from this roving child to the seafaring disasters the title promises, in his usual hearty style.
tanakh-jps-1917-hosea:
Hosea opens the set of short prophetic books in this 1917 Jewish Publication Society Bible, based on the Masoretic Text. Hosea son of Beeri is placed in the days of four kings of Judah and of Jeroboam, king of Israel.

God tells Hosea to wed a wife whose unfaithfulness will mirror the land's breach of trust. His children gain stark names: Jezreel, Lo-ruhamah, and Lo-ammi, each name a sign of wrath or lost mercy. Yet the book also holds out hope that Israel's numbers will grow like sand. Readers meet fierce love and anger bound up as one, in a life made to act out a nation's story.
the-book-of-tea:
Kakuzo Okakura opens The Book of Tea with a part called The Cup of Humanity. Tea began as a drug, he says, and grew into a drink. In China in the eighth century it joined the polite arts. In the fifteenth century Japan raised it into a creed of beauty, which he calls Teaism. That creed rests on love of the fair.

Teaism, for Okakura, teaches purity and accord, kind acts, and social grace. It is a cult of the flawed, a soft bid to do what can be done in this hard thing called life. It is health, since it bids us keep clean. It is thrift, since it finds ease in plain things, not in cost.
the-cell-of-self-knowledge-seven-early-e:
Seven early English mystical treatises, printed by Henry Pepwell in 1521, are gathered here under the title The Cell of Self-Knowledge. Edmund G. Gardner edited the volume, with an introduction and notes, in a 1910 edition. A frontispiece comes from a British Museum manuscript, and two mottoes, from St. Catherine of Siena and Richard of St. Victor, frame the whole.

The contents open with a devout treatise named Benjamin, on the powers and virtues of man's soul and the way to true contemplation. That work is credited to Richard of Saint Victor, a doctor famed for holiness and devotion. The Victorine passage quoted up front urges the reader to cleanse the spirit like a mirror, so that a ray of divine light may appear. The set gives modern readers a planned path through old English writing on prayer, self-knowledge, and the inner life.
the-chimes-a-goblin-story-of-some-bells-:
Charles Dickens wrote The Chimes as a goblin story about bells that rang an old year out and a new year in, transcribed here from the Scribner's Works of Charles Dickens. Chapter I, called First Quarter, opens with a direct bargain between teller and reader. Both sides, Dickens insists, should reach a mutual understanding as soon as possible.

His first claim is a bold one: few people of any age or condition would care to sleep in a church. He does not mean dozing at sermon time in warm weather, which has been done, but sleeping there at night and alone. Many, he grants, will be astonished by the claim in broad daylight, so it must be argued by night. He offers to prove it on any gusty winter's night, in an old churchyard before an old church door, against any single opponent.
the-communist-threat-in-the-taiwan-area:
A Department of State pamphlet, Publication 6708 in the Far Eastern Series, gathers the United States government's statements on the Taiwan Straits crisis. It was released in September 1958. The contents promise a statement by Secretary Dulles, a White House statement, President Eisenhower's report to the American people, and his letter to Premier Khrushchev.

Secretary Dulles's statement of September 4, 1958, opens the set. He reports a detailed review with the President of the serious situation caused by aggressive Chinese Communist military actions in the Taiwan area. His first point is plain: neither Taiwan nor the islands of Quemoy and Matsu has ever been under Chinese Communist authority. For over thirteen years since the Second World War they have stood under Free China, the Republic of China. He adds that the United States is bound by treaty to help defend Taiwan from armed attack.
the-digger-movement-in-the-days-of-the-c: Lewis H. Berens, author of Towards the Light, wrote The Digger Movement in the Days of the Commonwealth. It was printed in London by Simpkin, Marshall, Hamilton, Kent and Company in 1906, and respectfully dedicated to the Society of Friends. The subtitle promises the movement as revealed in the writings of Gerrard Winstanley, named on the title page as the Digger mystic and rationalist, communist and social reformer. A German motto from Goethe stands at the front. Only the title page and dedication are present here.
the-gentleman-a-romance-of-the-sea: Alfred Ollivant wrote The Gentleman as a romance of the sea in the days of July 1805, giving the book to the Navy. Only the front matter and contents are present here. The contents split the tale into parts with heads like The Death of Black Diamond, The Galloping Gent, The Gunner of the Sloop, Old Ding-Dong, and The Lugger Kite. Ollivant's past books named here include Bob, Son of Battle. No chapter text shows up in these pages.
the-journey-to-the-polar-sea:
Sir John Franklin's narrative of his polar sea journey gets an introduction here. R. F. Scott signed it. Scarcely ninety years have passed since the adventures, he marvels. The world has changed beyond measure since. Mr. Beck missed his Yarmouth ship, Scott notes. He rejoined her at Stromness after nine days of travel. He had rested almost not at all. Post-chaises and sweating horses fill that vision.

In Franklin's vast dominion, change ran faster still. He followed lonely trails to Fort Cumberland. He sailed Lake Winnipeg's solitary shores. A hundred thousand people would dwell there within a century. The region would supply much of his countrymen's bread. The Barren Lands stay as Franklin found them. So does the ice-bound limit of the continent. Scott commends a great traveler and a gallant man.
the-lady-from-the-sea:
Henrik Ibsen's play appears here in Eleanor Marx-Aveling's translation. The cast lists Dr. Wangel, his second wife Ellida, his daughters Bolette and the not-yet-grown Hilde, the schoolmaster Arnholm, Lyngstrand, Ballested, and a Stranger, in a small fjord town in northern Norway. Act I opens on a warm, brilliantly clear summer morning in Wangel's garden, where Ballested arranges flag ropes under the flagstaff beside his easel and paints.

Bolette brings a vase of flowers and asks whether the work goes smoothly, then whether he expects visitors today. The scene is all stillness and preparation: an arbour, a hedge gate, the road along the shore, and beyond the trees the fjord and high mountain peaks. Ibsen places Ellida's sea-longing, the drama of a woman married inland and haunted by a stranger from the sea, inside this bright, enclosed garden.
the-lively-poll-a-tale-of-the-north-sea:
R. M. Ballantyne's The Lively Poll, a tale of the North Sea dated 1886, opens aboard a fishing fleet of nearly two hundred smacks. Their admiral, Manx Bradley, wears a pilot coat and sou'-wester rather than lace and brass buttons, yet the whole fleet watches his flagship for signals. On his order the smacks sweep into line and shoot their great trawl-nets together, since tangled gear would mean wrecks and no fish for London's breakfast tables.

Ballantyne then narrows to one smack, the Lively Poll, skippered by Stephen Lockley. Her crew spends two and a half hours at the capstan in the dark, spray bursting over the side, hauling a trawl that feels like a lump of wreck. Readers get hard physical detail about deep-sea fishing work in the age of sail.
the-lord-of-the-sea: M. P. Shiel's The Lord of the Sea is dated 1901 in its heading. Front matter alone is present: a title page and contents, with none of the novel itself. The contents shown end at chapter nineteen, The Great Bell, after titles including The Exodus, The Fez, The Meteor, Hogarth's Guns, Wroxham Broad, The Priest, and Chloroform. A companion record of the same book lists two further chapters, The Infirmary and In the Deep, so the two contents lists do not match.
the-mafulu-mountain-people-of-british-ne: Robert W. Williamson wrote The Mafulu Mountain People of British New Guinea, published by Macmillan in London in 1912 with illustrations, a map, and an introduction by A. C. Haddon. Only the title page and part of the contents are present here, so the chapters themselves do not appear. The contents shown move from an introductory chapter through physique and character, dress and ornament, and daily life. Then they turn to community, clan, and village systems and chieftainship. Villages, houses, and modes of communication between villages close the list shown.
the-ocean-waifs-a-story-of-adventure-on-:
Captain Mayne Reid published The Ocean Waifs, a story of adventure on land and sea, in 1869. An albatross flying over the Atlantic spots three craft adrift. One is a tiny raft with a man and a boy. Another is a large raft crowded with more than thirty men. The third is a ship's gig with six men who have dropped their oars in despair.

All three came from the Pandora, a slave ship that burned in mid-ocean. She was bound from the Guinea coast to Brazil with five hundred captives. The fire ended in an explosion. The only sound boat escaped in the dark with the captain and five others. Reid sets up a grim survival tale.
the-pathfinder-or-the-inland-sea:
James Fenimore Cooper wrote The Pathfinder, or The Inland Sea. In his preface Cooper says the plan came to him many years before, though the details are new. A publisher took his pledge to write a tale joining seamen and savages in incidents of the Great Lakes, and the pledge is now tardily redeemed.

Cooper warns that an old friend, his principal character, appears under new circumstances. Using the same hero in four separate works risks tiring readers with sameness, he admits. He also defends placing vessels on Lake Ontario in the middle of the eighteenth century, saying like vessels sailed that inland sea even earlier. Frontier settlements there, he notes, rival old American towns in age.
the-pilot-a-tale-of-the-sea:
J. Fenimore Cooper's The Pilot, a tale of the sea, opens with a letter dedicating the volume to William Branford Shubrick of the United States Navy. Cooper calls Shubrick his old messmate. He writes of the gaps that war, disease, and a hazardous profession had opened among his naval friends. The dedication is offered as a tribute to an enduring friendship that time and separation had not shaken.

A preface follows, arguing that a true history of human affairs would credit sudden impulse and accident with far more of our acts than reason claims. That opinion, Cooper says, holds strictly true for the making of this book. The opening pages thus frame a sea novel by a man who had himself served at sea. He also kept close ties with serving officers.
the-rose-of-dawn-a-tale-of-the-south-sea:
Helen Hay published The Rose of Dawn, a tale of the South Sea, with R. H. Russell in New York in 1901, with a drawing by John La Farge. The opening is verse rather than prose, and it begins before sunrise over a sleeping ocean.

Darkness lies somnolent and inert while a luminous haze stirs across the water, too soft for the islands to hear. A little cry breaks the silence, a dusky form glides through the palm trees, and the forest brings forth men. Their eyes are bright with morning as they set out where the great bonita play, on a sport the verse calls dangerous.
the-satyricon-volume-04-escape-by-sea:
Volume four of W. C. Firebaugh's unexpurgated Satyricon translation is titled Encolpius, Giton and Eumolpus Escape by Sea. It opens at chapter the ninety-ninth. The bracket code of the earlier volumes still marks the text. Passages by Nodot, Marchena, and De Salas are each flagged.

Eumolpus urges flight in a speech on his way of life. He has lived each day as though its light would never return, he says. Ascyltos persecutes Encolpius here, so they should get out of his way. Eumolpus has taken a berth on a vessel sailing that very night. He is well known on board, and they will be well received. Encolpius weeps and begs forgiveness for his jealousy. He vows to give no further cause for offense.
the-two-lovers-of-heaven-chrysanthus-and:
Denis Florence Mac-Carthy's translation of Calderón's Two Lovers of Heaven, Chrysanthus and Daria, a drama of early Christian Rome, was published at Dublin in 1870 with dedicatory sonnets to Longfellow. The front matter explains Calderón's family motto, 'Por la Fe Morire,' for the faith welcome death. Mac-Carthy traces it to Don Sancho Ortiz Calderon de la Barca, a commander of Santiago serving Alfonso the Wise in the thirteenth century. Captured by the Moors before Gibraltar, Ortiz refused life on condition of apostasy.

His answer, that since his God died for him he would die for God, became the family's watchword and the key note of this drama. Don Ortiz was put to death with great cruelty. Mac-Carthy's note joins the play's martyr lovers to the poet's own ancestry, a heritage of faith unto death carried in a coat of arms.
the-world-english-bible-web-hosea:
Hosea, book twenty-eight in the World English Bible, dates its prophet by four kings of Judah. Jeroboam also rules Israel during his ministry. Hosea is identified as Beeri's son. God's first command to him is shocking. He must marry a wife of prostitution. The marriage mirrors the land's unfaithfulness toward God, the text explains.

Hosea takes Gomer, daughter of Diblaim, as his wife. Their first son is named Jezreel as a sign. God promises to avenge blood shed at Jezreel. Israel's kingdom will cease, the oracle warns. More children receive symbolic names of judgment. Love and betrayal frame this prophet's painful message to a straying nation.
there-is-sorrow-on-the-sea:
Gilbert Parker's story opens as a letter from York Factory, Hudson's Bay, dated September 23, 1747. Dick writes to his cousin Fanny a year after fleeing Mablethorpe on April Fool's Day. Coastguards hunted the sands for him with lights while Fanny helped him escape.

He recalls their childhood among Lincolnshire dykes, sand-hills, and fishing smacks with red sails. Both children dreamed of sailing to distant lands. Readers get a historical tale told in a fugitive's own voice, mixing homesickness, love, and the wish to become a sailor. The letter form lets Dick tell his own flight in his own words.
thrilling-adventures-by-land-and-sea:
James O. Brayman edited Thrilling Adventures by Land and Sea, a collection of remarkable historical facts from authentic sources. His preface attacks books that merely excite readers while teaching nothing and harming morals. He compares such reading to a drunkard's bowl or a gambler's tools.

Brayman offers adventure as an intermediate step toward higher literature and science. Daring and heroic deeds, joined to noble purposes, should awaken noble impulses. Readers get startling incident and exciting adventure chosen to instruct as well as entertain, with a Shakespeare line about disastrous chances by flood and field as epigraph.
when-london-burned-a-story-of-restoratio:
G. A. Henty wrote When London Burned, a tale of the reign of Charles the Second. His preface pushes back at the view that the reign was a shameful one. Court waste and vice were real, he grants, and they fed anger that later felled the Stuarts. Yet trade and wealth grew fast in the same years.

Henty praises English sailors under York, Albemarle, Rupert, and Sandwich. Their wins took sea and trade power from Holland, he says. Plague and the Great Fire struck hard, but merchants still raised England high. The tale that follows puts a young hero in that mix of fire, plague, and war at sea. Henty frames the age as dark but brave.
